Uniform title:
Kālottara Main title: Kālottaratantra Secondary title: Kālottarāgama
Manuscript: NGMPP Reel No. B 118/7, Manuscript No. 5-4632. Description:
This manuscript contains various versions of the Kālottaratantra, namely:
1) Jñānapañcāsikā.
2) *Śatika*, also known as *Kālajñāna*—the *One Hundred Verse Kālottara*;
3) *Kālottara-sārddhaśatika*—the *One Hundred and Fifty Verse Kālottara*;
4) *Dviśatika*—the *Two Hundred Verse Kālottara*.
5) *Adhyuṣṭaśatika*—The Three Hundred and Fifty-Verse *Kālottara*;
6) *Saptaśatika*—The Seven Hundred-Verse *Kālottara*;
7) *Trayodaśaśatika*—The Thirteen Hundred-Verse *Kālottara*.
Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: February 16, 2013.
Publication country: India.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
In the ritual installation of Śiva and other deities, in sacrifice, and especially in initiation,
he is the supreme bestower of grace upon all castes alike.
Twenty quadrillion, ten trillion,
and a multitude of billions of years— such was the mass of mantras that issued forth from Īśa.
Seventy-two thousand, one hundred million, ten billion,
and fifty thousand mantras have issued forth from the mouth of the Mantra.
Thirty thousand crores, seven hundred and eight,
and thirty-six million mantras have emerged from Rudra.
Nine thousand crores, eighty-five ayutas,
and five hundred crores of mantras have issued forth from Vāmā.
Seven thousand million, thirty-seven hundred,
one hundred, and one hundred thousand [mantras] have issued forth from Sadyojāta.
By means of the mantras originating from the five faces, spoken by Śiva, which bestow both accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti).
One should install [the deity] with the six faces and so forth, and not with others enjoined by the Vedas and such.
Īśa, Vaktra, as well as Aghora, Guhya, and Jāta—
these are the five faces of the God, for the sake of meditating upon his five limbs.
Kāmin, Yogarjācintya, Kāraṇa, Vājita, Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasrāṃśu, Maṃśumat, Suprabha, and Daśa—
these ten are declared to be the divisions of Śiva; after that follows the division of Rudra.
Vijaya, the one known as the "Exhalation-Song of the Supreme Lord" (Pārameśvaryaniḥśvāsodgīta), Prodgīta, Mukhabimba, Siddha, and Santāna.
Nṛsiṃha, Candrahāsa, Vīra, Svāyaṃbhu, Raurava, Mākoṭa, Kiriṇa, Tvasvita, and Vīrasaṃpara.
The divisions of Rudra are fully described as those arising from the ten and eighteen [syllables]:
Hara, Huṃkāra, Bindusāra, and Kalāmṛta.
Devatrāsa, Sūyāsa, Sāvara, Kālasāvara,
Pakṣirāja, Śikhāyoga, Śikhāsāra, and Śikhāmṛta.
1b) The analysis of the five elements, the determination of the divisions of emptiness,
Nīlakaṇṭha, Kālāgama, Kālakūṭa, and Paṭadruma.
Kamboja, Kaṃvala, Kaṅka, Kālatuṇḍa, Kaṭāhaka,
Suvarṇarekha, Sugrīva, Trottala, and Trottalottara.
These twenty-eight divisions of the Gāruḍa are proclaimed:
Svacchanda-bhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmatta-bhairava;
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Kāpālīśa, Samuccaya, Aghora, Ghorāsa, Ghora, Nisvāsa, and Caradurmukha.
Bhīmāṃsa, Ḍāmarārāva, Bhīmavetālavarddhaka, Ucchūṣma, Vāhika, Bela, Śekhara, Puṣpa, and Advaya.
The Triśira, the Ekapāda, the Siddhayogeśvarīmata,
the Pañcāmṛta, the Prapañca, and the Yoginījālasaṃvara.
The Viśvārikakaṇṭhasaṃkoca, the Tilakoṣāgama, and the Bhairava;
thus, these two of us [possess] thirty-two Tantras along with their supplements.
Having thoroughly cleansed the sixty-four passions that arise from them,
he [attains] the method, the supreme method, the mute, delusion, and the nectar that overcomes delusion.
The ritual procedure for hand-worship (karapūjā), followed by the reality of the lute (vīṇātattva),
as well as Jaya, Vijaya, Ajita, and Aparājita.
The eternally risen Siddha, the Jyeṣṭha, the Cintāmaṇi of great prosperity,
the Vāgbhava, the Kubjaka, and the Kāmadhenu-kadambaka.
Ānandarudra, Rudrākṣa, Kiṅkara, Kiṅkarānuga, Anantavijaya, Sauka, Daurvāsa, and Bhījabhedaka.
Having known Vāmada, spoken by Vāmadeva, which encompasses twenty-four divisions,
as well as Hātvāhata, Hayagrīva, Karakoṭa, and Kaṭaṅkaṭa;
Karoṭa, Muṇḍamāla, Karkoṭa, Khararāmaṇa,
Caṇḍāsidvārahuṃkāra, Hāhākāra, and Śivārava.
Terrifying with a loud, boisterous laugh, emitting a gurgling sound that strikes fear into the wicked; pure yet formidable, exceedingly fierce with its beautiful form.
And Yamaghaṇṭa, Bhūtāṅka, and Ajātajam with its twenty divisions.
Thus, the collection of the Śiva-sūtras consists of one hundred and sixty-four aphorisms;
furthermore, this compendium of scripture is divided into a further hundred thousand distinct sections.
From Śiva it was received by the gods, from the gods likewise by the sages (ṛṣis),
and from the sages by human disciples who brought forth all the scriptures.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord, it is not possible to know [it] through excessive prolixity;
O Mahādeva, it has been revealed in many ways within the Vāthula.
Only that which stands on the path of the head has been proclaimed among the descents;
likewise, the southern path and the leftward path have been kept secret.
O Maheśvara, please explain in brief the true nature of reality as it is, which is the means for liberation, bestows prosperity, and grants spiritual accomplishment.
The Lord said:
Earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as the other five subtle elements (tanmātras), together with those consisting of the organs of cognition and action.
The mind, ego, and intellect are known as the qualities (guṇas), while dissolution is their designation;
furthermore, there are the Person (puruṣa), limited agency (kalā), time (kāla), attachment (rāga), and the regulator (niyāmikā).
This is called the "cocoon" (kañcuka), which differentiates the mantra from the *tāra*;
it should be understood as being like the cocoon of *māyā*, while the *kalā* and the other [sheaths] are like husks.
The innate impurity (mala), perfected by the ordinance of Śiva’s will like Māyā itself,
is that single principle consisting of Māyā which [gives rise to] the categories beginning with Earth and culminating in Pradhāna.
The second is declared to be bondage through the application of illusion (māyā);
it is the womb, as well as illusion, which is the supreme consciousness.
Īśvara and she known as Pramadā, Kuṭilā and Śarvadhāriṇī;
the subtle net of primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as obstacles and the intervals between obstacles.
Therefore, those whose knot is even more subtle are proclaimed as "subtle" (sūkṣma). Beyond that is the Lord Śiva; by knowing him, one is released from the grasp [of bondage].
The peaceful [mantra] is employed, and one should recite it up to the end of the peace-mantra (śāntyanta).
O God, Śiva, the solitary hero (ekavīra), is imperishable and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The mudrā known as Bala should be offered to the Supreme Lord after sprinkling [the deity] with water and worshipping him, until finally [the deity] is established within oneself.
O sinless one, by means of a single oblation alone, one becomes consecrated;
having drawn forth the essence situated in space, which arises from the supreme nectar.

Then, for the sake of accomplishing the success of the mantra, one should empower that person of firm intellect with the consecration and appoint them to the office of *ācārya* upon the support of the Sun.
First, however, you must encircle that which is at the beginning with the Vāyavya [mantras];
from the sound of the wind, that lord of yogis will undoubtedly be raised up by the wind.
Thus, with long [vowels], it is situated within fire and encircled by the fire-maṇḍala;
then the practitioner indeed becomes fire within the fire-maṇḍala.
In the arrangement of the pitcher (kalaśa), it should be completely enveloped with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa; thus its nature as Varuṇa arises, and one should place Śiva in the center.

Now, one intent on the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra] should know that the syllable *huṃ* resides within the sixteen parts (*kalā*) upon an eight-petalled lotus, while outside it is known to extend for two *nāḍikās*.
The deity situated within the center of the *kaṅkha* (the head) and established in the *śakti* becomes immortal.
The short vowels are said to belong to the wind (*vāyu*), while the long ones are designated as belonging to the external fire (*tejas*).
The letter *u* is said to belong to the Māhendra [group], while *aṃ* and *aḥ* are declared to be Vāruṇa.
The letters *va* and *gha* are proclaimed as Vāyavya, and those belonging to Agni are well-known as *ra*, *ṛ*, and *ṝ*.

Those known as Māhendras are to be understood as belonging to the higher [category], while those of Varuṇa are to be known as belonging to the lower; for the purpose of inciting enmity, one should use the feathers of a crow and those produced from an owl.
By means of the opposition of the castes and the application of that maṇḍala,
one causes everything to become hostile, even if the opponent were equal to Śakra himself.
For one by whom [the enemy] is quickly pierced with thorns through the *asthi-homa* (bone-oblation) accompanied by the utterance of *phaṭ*, there shall be the breaking of joints,
the drying up of water, the quenching of fire, and the piercing of pillars from the very midst of immortality.
One should join the lunar nectar to the moon; for by doing so without deliberation, one acts [thus].
Then, by means of the application of the *haṃsa*, one should inhale the poison within the maṇḍala.
If one withdraws the vital breath from the sun [the heart] by means of exhalation (recaka), what wonder is there?
Kārttikeya said:
O God, please describe what kind of worship leads to grace;
tell me that, O Lord of Gods, by the grace of the Wielder of the Trident.
Īśvara said:
One should join the one called the Seed-Self (bījātman) upon the seat, established in the form of a lotus;
having joined the nectar in the pericarp, one should then install the deity once more.
Through the division into Sakala and the others, one should apply the deity endowed with Mahāmudrā to the body by means of those eight states.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) by means of the individual and collective application of the limbs, the knower of mantras should perform this sacrifice which has been described to you; now hear concerning the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
One should sprinkle water upon and worship the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a square hearth (vaca);
five oblations with the Sakala-mantra are for the successful establishment of the fire.
One should offer oblations and worship the deity; one should perform the supreme initiation of the single syllable and, by means of the Viṣuva yoga, unite [the soul] with the supreme Śiva.
He shall never fear the faults of killing a Brahmin or other such sins;
truly, truly, O Mahāsena, he is liberated from the bondage of birth.
But by means of subtle practice received from the mouth of the Guru,
through the descent of Śiva’s power, the grasper becomes a liberator.
There is no bathing, nor any concern regarding impurity, nor any doubt whatsoever;
for one whose mind is disciplined is truly liberated, with the reality of the Self established in his heart.
But cognitions produced by different sense organs, though arising in succession, are to be known by a single knower; this is my firm conviction.
The activity of the sense-faculties, however, is governed by their respective domains;
direct perception, which illuminates its object and is free from defects, would be the means of valid cognition.
Then, with a concentrated mind, the practitioner of mantra should recite the form consisting of sound;
becoming one-pointed and standing before me, his consciousness should be absorbed in that sound.
Within six months, one attains the irreproachable divine form;
for in the practice of the divine, one should contemplate the deity situated within the resonance (nāda).
One should perceive the divine situated in the midst of the sky within the voids;
by the power of the reality-principle (tattva) of Śiva, it becomes like the sky upon the head.
Whichever deity there may be, having divided its initial syllable into ten parts, Śiva stands above it.
That deity becomes submissive within a year; of this there is no doubt.
[The letters] beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* reside upon the twenty-five-fold path.
At the conclusion of Pradhāna, everything shall remain under the control of the practitioner;
likewise, for the accomplishment of the elements, [the syllables] beginning with Ya and ending with Ava are employed.
In the accomplishment of the principle (tattva) of Pātāla, [the mantras] ending with the syllable *śādhyaha* are used;
one should collect ashes from a cremation ground on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Having recited this one hundred and eight times in a terrifying cremation ground,
or standing well-restrained in the midst of a village or even a city;
One should project the thread everywhere by means of the path of the great lord of yogins;
for the yoginīs indeed emerge through the power of Bhairava.
Upon that which is adorned with the sixteenth [digit], let your mind be fixed;
having made the mind thus, one should swallow the lower [element] there, united with the state of being.
For by that practice, one would not be subject to death,
just as if one were to possess a single, unbroken skull-cup.
Having taken it, one should recite [the mantra] while focusing on the grace that is the very nature of Bhairava;
O child, within six months, by the power of that yoga, one shall fly up.
One should perform a night patrol and strike the drum at a crossroads,
on a riverbank, or at an auspicious temple.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra) accompanied by the deities must indeed be made there;
O child, the vision will surely occur—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O Lord of Vatsa, one should offer liquor, meat, sesame seeds, black grain, and *tattūka* into the fire in a cremation ground or a forest; these are the most excellent offerings for rain.
Alternatively, one should visualize the god Tuṃburu, who bears four faces,
has eight arms, is a great hero, and is surrounded by four yoginīs.
One should worship [the deity] seated upon the Mātṛkā-throne, encircled by the sixteen [vowels],
with the Prasāda placed in the center, within that Maṇḍala of the Mothers.
Success is attained within a single month if one is devoted to reality;
[so too are] the Brahmāṇīs and the other Yoginīs, accompanied by the hosts ending with the Lord of Yogins.
When the notes are properly arranged in the *prasāda* scale, the deities in heaven are accomplished;
likewise, [it is used] for the mastery over spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and rākṣasas.
Thus has the Nyāsa been taught for Vāthulā, of this there is no doubt;
O child, the Jānapañcadaśikā must not be given to just anyone.
O Mahāsena, in the Vāthula [Tantra], the supreme and great true nature of Śiva, whose form is beginningless, is revealed;
there is no means beyond this.
O observer of excellent vows, O Lord of Vatsa, through the application of all principles and the yoga of mantra, I have explained to you this supreme and great tradition.
O sinless one, for those beings who dwell wherever they may be, this mantra is auspicious;
it should be known as equal in splendor to the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), and there is nothing superior to it.
Knowing this, O Mahāsena, one is indeed liberated from non-investigation;
thus, out of affection for my son, I have revealed this tradition to you.
"Truth, truth, and again truth has been told to you, O observer of noble vows.
Thus ends the *Jñānapañcāsikā* from the *Kālottara*.
[The Hundred-Chaptered Treatise] Īśvara said:
Henceforth, O Lord, I shall proclaim this unsurpassed ritual (iṣṭi),
extracted from the Kālottara Tantra like butter from curd.
And just as honey is the most excellent essence extracted from flowers,
so too is that supreme seed called Nāda, which resides within all beings.
Having known that, O Mahāsena, the teacher becomes a destroyer of bonds;
by him, the bound souls, having attained [liberation], go to the stainless Śiva.
What is the use of many other seeds that cause distraction of the mind?
By means of this one seed, all the fruit of many [seeds] is obtained.
But by means of subtle application perceived through yoga, the knower of mantras,
through the union of mudrās and seed-syllables, should contemplate the supreme seed-syllable.
Neither an auspicious lunar day nor a constellation, nor fasting,
is prescribed for one who is devoted to the gods, the sacred fire, and the guru, and who is free from envy.
Having worshipped that auspicious reality according to the prescribed rite— whether on a mental altar, on a physical sacrificial mound, or wherever the mind finds pleasure— one receives its grace.
I have declared this supreme consecration to be of two kinds:
for the purpose of adorning the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and as the supreme bestower of liberation when performed mentally.
Having placed the *haṃsa* seed-syllable on the hand, the wise practitioner should bind the mudrā;
then, the adept should form the *yogamudrā* by means of the *karaṇa*.
One should touch both feet with the two hands, extending them up to the head;
this is declared to be the mudrā of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Kārttikeya said:
O Mahādeva, tell me that by which liberation may become certain;
O Lord of Gods, abandon all dependence and speak to me that which is independent of anything else.
By the mere knowledge of which one liberates the bound soul (paśu) in an instant.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the practice according to its true nature, which is indeed very difficult to obtain.
One should utter the seed-syllable once, which abides as both the supreme and the non-supreme.
Just as [one applies it] to oneself, so should the wise one apply it to the disciple according to the ritual rule; thereafter, he should perform the fire-oblation with a mind of serenity.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). This procedure applies to the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila); however, in the case of a mental [rite], it should be performed mentally.
But those men who perform initiation without knowing the supreme reality undergo labor in vain; they shall certainly not obtain its fruit.
Having understood the three paths through their distinctions,
the wise teacher bestows grace upon all people in the world.
Whatever he touches with his hand and whatever he sees with his eye—
all that becomes auspicious (*śiva*), struck by the rays of the moon of Śiva.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Knowledge of Time.
The Lord said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the characteristics of the temple;
the knower of mantras should always observe whether it is short, long, or protracted.
The short [form] burns away sins; the long [form] becomes the bestower of liberation.
The prolated [form], endowed with a bindu at its head, is declared to be for the purpose of nourishment.
In recitation, meditation, and likewise in fire-offerings, the wise one should contemplate the extended [form];
it is employed in all rites of pacification as well as for subjugation.
When employed at the time of ritual action, they should be joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and the word of salutation (*namaskāra*) at the end; otherwise, they remain merely formal forms.
All rites are accomplished according to the practitioner's desire;
thus, one who knows the ritual procedures attains success—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Knowledge of Time.
I shall explain the sacrifice correctly and in due order:
the syllable *oṃ*, the lotus of the pericarp, and likewise the [lotuses] of Dharma, Jñāna, and so forth.
Detachment and likewise sovereignty are situated in the pericarp;
thus the Praṇava is proclaimed as being endowed with thirty-eight kalās.
The wise one should invoke the heavens with the *praṇava*;
likewise, the presence (*sānnidhya*), the respectful water for the feet (*arghyapādya*), and the bath (*snāna*) should be offered with the *praṇava*.
One should offer perfume, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, and a lamp with the syllable *praṇava*;
likewise, an offering of food, a sacrificial oblation, and a golden waist-band.
One should cause the giving of garments and ornaments with the *praṇava*;
indeed, everything that is enjoined by rule should be performed with the *praṇava*.
Having thus performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rite with a concentrated mind, even a slayer of a Brahmin shall attain perfection; let him undertake this procedure.
Those who awaken through grace do not awaken as bearers of the trident;
by means of the seed-syllable of the mantra of knowledge, one shall not undergo rebirth again.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Knowledge of Time.
Īśvara said:
I shall explain the fire-ritual; listen as it is declared by me.
The wise practitioner, having delineated the sacrificial pit with the syllable Om (praṇava), [should proceed].
Having performed the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and the final expiation (niṣkṛti),
everything ordained by the rules is to be done with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra, being always composed, should perform the previously described procedure for the lotus; he who offers oblations in this manner at all times.
He obtains the fulfillment of all desires and goes to the world of Śiva;
those who are joined with recitation and fire-offerings attain perfection—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on the fire-ritual in the Knowledge of Time.
Henceforth, O Skanda, I shall fully explain to you the supreme characteristic of the dhāraṇā of the great elements, which illuminates all ritual actions.
A king should always wear an earthen amulet that is endowed with color, distinguished by its superior and inferior qualities, and consecrated with the five-fold fire-ritual.
It was joined by the wind of the mind, crowded with the abodes of cities,
endowed with regions, cities, villages, and archways, and possessed of straight thoroughfares.
One should meditate on the hard, immovable [earth], devoid of wind, fire, and water;
it is neither depressed nor elevated, level, and completely enveloped by calves.
One should employ this in all applications of ritual pillars and in rites for nourishment;
one certainly performs the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) at the time of initiation.
O best of waters, you have warded off the rain from the great thundering clouds that falls like clubs,
which would otherwise have flooded the world of the gods and the earth.
This [mantra], joined with the ocean of Varuṇa, is the destroyer of the great flames of poison-fire and the noose of Time; it indeed performs rites of pacification.
The entire surface of the earth was set ablaze by the cresting flames of the fire of cosmic destruction;
the mass of waters was utterly consumed, leaving only heaps of ashes remaining.
Abundant with the letters of the fire-element (āgneya), easy to recite, and designated as "Fire" (agni),
this [mantra] destroys the affliction caused by the exhaustion of the Nāgas.
One should contemplate the entire surface of the sky as being filled with dust, stirred up by a fierce wind that has rent asunder the garments of the quarters.
One should contemplate the self as empty of intrinsic nature, established in infinity;
situated therein is the Blessed Lord, the deity, the reality that is both with parts and without parts.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon that [deity] raining down nectar;
then, by that [nectar], everything up to the lotus of the *āyoga* is filled.
Abiding within the lotus of that yoga, one perceives the Self in the form of the *liṅga*,
which is the most subtle and supreme abode of the Great Soul’s grace.
This is always the "Conqueror of Death" for yogins who maintain its name.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Knowledge of Time.
The Lord said:
Therefore, I shall speak in reverse order; listen as I declare it to you:
from the subtle elements (tanmātras), which have been individually agitated by egoism (ahaṃkāra).
Indeed, space, wind, fire, water, and earth are born;
from earth comes solidity and support, and from water comes fluidity and cohesion.
Tejas is said to be that which cooks, which provides supreme illumination,
and which is also described as being mobile, expansive, and drying.
Likewise, in the ether (vyoman) there are capacity for space and authority;
such are the foundations (pratiṣṭhās), each endowed with fivefold aspects.
Even within bodies, living beings are divided according to the physical constituents arising from the body—
namely, fat, flesh, bones, and indeed the sinews.
The earth is divided fivefold within the bodies of embodied beings;
from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), they arise again in succession, one by one.
Space has sound as its characteristic; wind likewise has sound and touch;
and fire has these three qualities: sound, touch, and form.
Sound, touch, form, and taste are the qualities in water;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth [are the qualities] in earth.
Earth is described as being endowed with five qualities:
supporting the earth, and protecting those who are oppressed by the wicked.
The supreme method for immortalizing the bodies of those who have been nourished is as follows:
sweat, blood, marrow, fat, and likewise phlegm.
The water-element within the bodies of embodied beings is divided fivefold:
desire, anger, envy, wrath, and energy as the fifth.
The fire within the bodies of embodied beings is fivefold:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The vital air (anila), divided fivefold within the bodies of embodied beings,
resides in the mouth, the nose, the heart, and likewise the stomach.
Space is divided fivefold within the bodies of embodied beings;
this is the gross body, while the subtle body arises from the subtle elements (tanmātras).
These alone are to be known as the subtle elements (tanmātras) and are proclaimed as the objects of the senses;
yet, when not perceived by the intellect, they are called the inner controller (antaryāmī).
The living being who bestows all elements is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
he always rejoices in the field characterized by the bliss of sense objects.
Because it is colored by the qualities of that state, it is known as their abode;
even when cut or pierced by weapons, or afflicted by diseases.
One abandons the body through suffering, but never through dispassion;
yet one may attain dispassion once again when impelled by the power of knowledge.
Having seen this body, I feel revulsion, for I am utterly deluded by the great Māyā— though I am that very Self which dwells within this foul-smelling sprout of a beggar’s wretchedness.
In a realm crowded with various diseases and corrupted by passion,
those intoxicated by pride are deluded by the thieves that are the serpents of sensory objects.
Repeatedly tormented by desire, anger,
and the pains of "mine-ness," it is exceedingly full of suffering and crowded with old age and death.
Alas! The body is filled with anxiety and grief, it is afflicted by suffering, bound together like leather, foul-smelling, and born from semen and blood.
How indeed can I take delight in that which is mixed with feces, urine, and semen?
It is like a reflection in mirrors, or like a form existing within a painting.
The wise man regards this body as being like a useless log;
having thus attained detachment, he strives for the perfection of knowledge.
The attainment of knowledge leads to liberation, as well as to right conduct and wrong conduct;
this scripture, the Knowledge of Time originating from Śiva, serves both purposes.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kālottara.
Beyond this, the vital breath (prāṇa) exists established in a tenfold manner:
the five winds beginning with prāṇa, as well as the five channels that destroy [the] nadīs.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
The body is traditionally held to be twofold: that which is born of the mother and that which is born of the father;
it is declared to consist of six sheaths due to the union of semen and blood.
There are three crores of body hairs, as well as an upper crore;
thirty-two teeth have been declared, and twenty nails are proclaimed.
One thousand palas of flesh, one hundred palas of blood are recorded;
ten palas of fat, and the skin is equal to that.
The marrow is twelve palas, the great blood (mahārakta) is three palas;
the semen should be known as two kuḍavas, and the bile is recorded as one kuḍava.
Phlegm is half an *āṭaka*, while feces and urine are immeasurable;
now hear the detailed explanation of the five winds that have been mentioned.
The first wind is indeed Prāṇa, and he is the lord of all nine;
Prāṇa is composed of breath, and the vital breaths are the emissions and the fillings.
Abiding within the chest of living beings,
this vital breath (prāṇa), conjoined with the individual soul (jīva), constantly fills it through exhalations, inhalations, and coughs.
Because it moves forward (prayāṇa), it is therefore proclaimed as prāṇa;
because it has moved downward (apānayat) and swallowed food, it is known as apāna.
The wind that carries semen and urine is celebrated as apāna;
by it, what is drunk, eaten, and smelled, as well as blood, bile, phlegm, and wind, are conveyed.
The wind named Samāna leads [the food] equally into the vessels;
it causes the lower lip and the mouth to quiver, and its agitation is merely this much.
The vital air named Udāna causes the limbs to tremble;
Vyāna produces contractions and obstructions, and Vyāna is the agitator of diseases.
*Prīti* is said to be the destroyer; *vārddhikya* is called *vyāna*. The *prāṇāghna* parts have been declared; now the *nāgāghna* parts are being described.
Nāga is said to be present during belching; Kūrma resides in the opening of the eyes; Kṛkara is present when one is hungry; and Devadatta is present during yawning.
O Six-faced One, Dhanañjaya resides in the state of drying; even when one has died, he does not abandon it. This is briefly described as the host of Vāyus.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Kālottara.
I shall now explain the movement within the body, as well as the day and night, the solstices, the transits, the equinoxes, the intercalary months, and the nights of the people.
This state known as the equilibrium of power (śaktisamarasa) is the southern course of Miḍā;
when the Self is in the middle region, the wise know it as the equinox (viṣuvant).
When a person moves from Cūlita to Madhyadeśa,
or likewise from the north to the south, that is designated as a Saṃkrānti.
The night belongs to the hungry people, while the intercalary month (adhimāsa) belongs to Vijṛmbhaka;
the upward-moving breath (prāṇa) is indeed the day, and the downward-moving breath (apāna) is the night.
Understand also that the power which pervades all beings is present;
and in the third extension (āyāma), there is the sixth vowel preceded by the letter 'd'.
And it is heard: "When a human being, having heard and understood [the teaching], becomes powerless [with regard to worldly bonds], he dissolves into Śiva;
and when the body is cast off, he goes to Śiva."
Mantras devoid of power do not bestow the grace of initiation;
lacking power, they do not achieve success, nor do they lead to the supreme goal.
Śiva is to be known as all-pervading and devoid of name and form;
he is to be known as the Person consisting of pure consciousness, Śiva who abides pervading all.
One should meditate, united with Śiva through the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*).
Having thus become of equal flavor, one goes to the other Śiva.
Alternatively, having diligently fixed the supportless Self upon the crown of the head,
one should perform all rites— sacrifice, yoga, recitation, and meditation.
Having established Śiva within oneself, one is not tainted even while performing actions;
one attains the perfection of yoga and proceeds toward union with Śiva.
I have proclaimed this yoga of knowledge, which bestows success and liberation without hardship;
it must not be given to one who has not been examined, even if he has resided [as a guest] for three years.
To a Brahmin endowed with good conduct, to a Kṣatriya of virtuous character,
to a Vaiśya possessed of compassion, and to a Śūdra who is devoted to his duties— [to these one should give].
Otherwise, the true nature of Śiva must not be given to wicked mortals who follow censurable reasoning and who walk upon the path of injustice.
This supreme reality should not be given to one devoid of devotion to Śiva, to one who lacks devotion to the guru, or to those who seek it out of mere curiosity or a desire for knowledge.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Knowledge of Time.
Īśvara said:
He who resides within the body is to be known as *sakala* (with parts), while he who is devoid of the body is *niṣkala* (without parts).
He is attained when one reaches Him; He is accessible from all directions and abides as something indescribable everywhere.
Free from conceptual proliferation, peaceful, and hidden within the supreme secret,
it is established everywhere through the relationship of cause and effect.
That very Blessed One is all-pervasive, existing like oil within a sesame seed;
yet it is obtained directly and manifest from every direction through the mouth of the Guru.
Since Śiva, who resides within one's own body, utters [it] himself,
therefore that alone is declared to be the victory for those persons who know the reality.
Having understood that which is within the vital breath at a distance of twelve finger-breadths from its end,
one should know that which resides therein— the all-pervading, stainless One.
The individual soul is led by the vital power (śakti), and within that [process], that power also ceases;
having understood this coming and going, one is liberated— of this there is no doubt.

Thus, that all-pervading Blessed One will perform coming and going; yet because he is all-pervading, there is no actual movement, for the Lord, remaining right where he is, performs the yoga of pervasion.
Regarding the expression "Haṃsa, Haṃsa," the wise should understand that the deity who is the Haṃsa is Sadāśiva,
according to the analogy of the mother and the sweetmeat.
To the east of Devayāna and to the north of Pitṛmāna,
having gone to the middle of Setubandha, one is not born again.
Although the mind perceives one object and the vision is cast upon another,
nevertheless, the yoga of practitioners proceeds without interruption.
Know that which is endowed with non-differentiation as the true reality to be given;
this has been told by me, my dear son, without doubt and without elaboration.
There is nothing higher than this; there is no auspiciousness higher than Śiva.
The knower of reality is not tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
One who has not yet attained perfection, yet possesses the knowledge of reality, goes to the presence of Śiva upon the fall of the body.
Thus ends the Śatika [chapter] on the Knowledge of Time.
[The Kālottara in One Hundred and Fifty Verses] p. 1a) Oṃ, salutation to Śiva!
Salutations to you, the knower of time; salutations to you who transcend time. Salutations to you, O Lord of Time, the impeller of all times.
O Lord of the Universe, who manifests in the form of Time within the vessel through your cosmic powers,
salutations to you, the primordial impeller of time!
Having thus praised Mahādeva, the Supreme Lord, with devotion, I entreat you, O God who wields the trident: be gracious.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord, you have previously explained to me its eightfold division,
merely by way of indication, in the two hundred [verses] known as the *Kāla*.
O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods, you are able to declare the definitive conclusion regarding that which was spoken by you as the equinox when the time for initiation had arrived.
O Maheśvara, [explain] the iconographic representation of the eight principles (tattvas),
as well as the division of their placement upon the body and how the division of yoga occurs.
Īśvara said:
The differentiated is situated within the five colors, while the undifferentiated is like the luster of a jasmine flower;
it is known as pure being, the void that transcends all letters, O Six-faced One.
The syllable AṂ, possessing the luster of saffron, bestows divine accomplishments;
situated within the sphere of the upper direction, it is known as the bestower of yoga through practice.
The reality (tattva) is like pure crystal, adorned with space;
it is declared to be the Kṣapa-sā, possessing a luster as red as vermilion.
O Six-faced One, this should always be employed for attraction and for divine enjoyments;
it is like the lotus situated within the colors, just as water is seen [within it].
One should know that Lord to be situated within, residing inside the lotus of the heart;
with whatever state of being the wise contemplate Him as being in the throat and lips.
O son of Kṛttikā, such indeed is his form to be known;
one should place [the syllable] entirely upon the throat, the lips, all the limbs, and the heart.
Having contemplated emptiness at the crown of the head, likewise [emptiness] for a moment at the crest-lock;
having placed the void-impurity in the two eyes, one should place the supreme void-impurity in the digits.
The internal [syllable] is situated in the middle of the mouth, while the partless (niṣkala) is outside;
it is pervaded by the fourteen vowels and joined with the sixth [consonant].
Having uttered the long *prasāda* [mantra] until one has reached the state of partlessness (*niṣkalatā*),
by this very practice one should install the partless [deity] everywhere.

One should perform the previously mentioned *aṅganyāsa*, ending with the weapon (*astra*) at the heart; having thus performed the ritual placement according to the rules, one should likewise perform the worship and the yoga.
Listen to how it should be performed by the lord of preceptors:
the sacrifice is declared to be as before, and the initiation is fully established.
Having performed the yoga of the equinox, that union is prescribed;
having recollected the grace established in the sound (nāda), which is within the range of the end of sound.
Having restrained the pair of powers within the equal [channel] for as long as possible,
one should release the sound (nāda) by means of Aurdhī, who is situated in the middle water.
The power known as Śivā, whose form is desire, abides at the end of the *nāda*;
she is the fourth, the eternal Supreme, the Great Goddess who transcends the *raudrī*.
Above that, however, stands the god Śiva, the supreme cause;
Maheśvara, with his face slightly turned upward, resides in the support of the void.
Having recollected [the deity], the teacher should cast the full oblation into the disciple;
thus, having understood the equinox, one is liberated from the bonds of the fettered soul (paśu).
Even one who is merely initiated [is purified] at the equinox, how much more so a man who knows the reality!
Therefore, with every effort, one should always remain situated during the equinox.
The placement (nyāsa) of the eight principles (tattvas) is the cause of success;
it is not [accomplished] through the yoga of the sacrifice of the self (ātmayāga), nor by means of the sequential division of the placement of phonemes (varṇanyāsa).
One should not visualize a seat in the heart as before;
rather, having placed the peak-syllable (kūṭa) in the center, one should contemplate that reality which is of the nature of Śiva.
One should place Sadāśiva in the east and Īśvara in the southeast;
having worshipped Vighna in the south, one should worship Māyā in the southwestern direction.
One should place Kāla in the western quarter, Niyati likewise in the north-west;
Puruṣa in the northern quarter, and Prakṛti in the domain of Īśvara (the north-east).

Having performed the rite of placement (*vinyāsa*) in this manner, one should proceed with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). One should perform the ritual actions beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) by means of this very mantra alone.
Having acted in this way, whatever reality a man who knows the mantra seeks to accomplish, that will be achieved through the eight realities; of this there is no doubt.
Or, even by means of the non-availability of physical substances, one should visualize them within the heart-lotus;
having thus visualized everything, one should then practice yoga.
Following the sequence of the transformations of the eight principles,
that which abides in the waking state is the *sakala* (with parts), while that which is within the *viṅghna* (obstacle) is based on the dreaming state.
In deep sleep it is the void, infinite; in the fourth state (turya), it is the sky adorned.
It is partless above the twelve, yet endowed with parts during the equinox.
The *kṣapaṇa* [sound] is for the destruction of suffering; it belongs to the throat and lips according to its true nature.
The Lord produces modifications within both pure and impure states of being.
One should know that the manifest (sakala) resides within the body (piṇḍastha), while the unmanifest (niṣkala) is based upon it;
the God who stands twelve finger-breadths above [the head] is the shatterer of the bonds of worldly existence.
The reality that lies between these two is proclaimed as "the Void" (śūnya);
it should be meditated upon with effort by practitioners who desire liberation.

When there occurs a separation between that which resides in the middle of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* and that which is established within the *suṣumṇā*, then I perceive that which is enriched with all its parts (*kalā*).
One should know that the reality which is proclaimed as the remainder of the active exhalation (recaka) resides there, as the pure void adorned with the principles (tattvas).
When yawning manifests in its own form as the sound "hā," know that this is declared to be the reality (tattva) called Kṣapaṇa, which bestows liberation.
When, having abandoned exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka) occurs, a slight state of nirvāṇa is attained; that which abides within destroys death.
O Six-faced One, those seven modifications which have been described are said to belong to the throat and the lips, yet they are the causes of the soul's departure.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Supreme Lord from the feet up to the head and so forth,
one should assume the lotus posture (padmāsana) or whatever posture is comfortable.
Having fixed the mind upon the crown of the head, one should mentally utter the supreme syllable;
having drawn it up very gradually, one remains established within the Brahma-nāḍī.
In front of the power of Rudra, one should cause the breath to enter the path of the uvula— which is non-dual in nature and has a reddish luster—
until it reaches that point, and then one should produce the *hikkā* sound.
O Skanda, one should fill [the mouth] completely and exhale the wind situated there;
having compressed it, one should direct it upward until it reaches the vicinity of the palate.
Above that is Sadāśiva, and above that is Bindu and Nāda;
having transcended Bindu and Nāda, one then proceeds in sequence to Śakti.
Having abandoned the power (śakti), one goes to the peaceful Śiva, the supreme cause;
having gone there, O dear son, they are not born again.
Thus, O observer of excellent vows, the *utkrānti-stava* has been briefly proclaimed;
it should be given constantly to one's own disciple who is endowed with devotion.
This knowledge is to be given to him alone whose devotion to the Guru is established as even weightier than [devotion] to Śiva, but never to anyone else.
Kārttikeya said:
"O Lord Maheśvara, you have described the eightfold division;
now I wish to hear about the *saṃkrānti* as well as the *viṣuva*."
Just as the Lord measures [time], so too is that which is known as the calculation of time.
Īśvara said: "O Six-faced One, sixty years are declared to be a single day and night for yogins who possess a lifespan of three hundred years plus sixty."
The *sādhaka* is said to be a *ghaṭikā*, and its number is proclaimed to be equal [to that].
In this way, the years are proclaimed, while that which is the *ghaṭikā* externally is likewise [reckoned].
O sinless one, it has been thus described by means of the internal movement:
the vital breath (prāṇa) constitutes a day and night, while the equinox (viṣuva) occurs at its two junctions.
When the Lord moves away from the equinox,
even when the deity has moved only slightly, it is traditionally recited as a *saṃkrānti*.
Kārttikeya said:
"O God, though I am sinless, I wander about, for my hope is fixed upon Viṣuva;
O Śaṅkara, explain that to me exactly as it is understood."
The Lord said:
That which has been described by me to you as a day and night is declared in the tantra known as Kālākhya to be a year.
Having divided that very [number] by thirty, one should take a twelfth part;
it is to be divided by six and reduced by three, thus being conceived as both supreme and non-supreme.
Remaining there, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti); indeed, by doing so without hesitation, one is liberated.
This is declared to be the bestower of liberation, for it grants release from calamities through its effortless power.
Those others which are called *viṣuva*, bestowing liberation and union (*sāyujya*),
should also be recognized by time through these various manifold distinctions.
Now, O Mahāsena, I shall describe the elements in brief:
that which was previously declared by me ends at twelve finger-breadths.
Above that, O observer of excellent vows, is Maheśāna at the end of the twelve;
he stands above as the cause that transcends all states of being.
The cause, however, would be the drop (bindu), as well as the dissolution of sound (nāda) and power (śakti);
and therein lies the supreme dissolution, which is indefinable and free from affliction.
Having gone to that all-pervading God, one does not return again;
for the God consists of all states of being within this entire universe of the moving and the unmoving.
The Great Lord, whose form is the universe, manifests as Time;
he should be known as the right and the left, designated as the left and the right.
Time is proclaimed according to its division into Saumya and others;
the solar eclipse is declared to be external, while the lunar eclipse is proclaimed to be internal and occurring at night.
The time previously mentioned is established as one ghaṭikā;
thirty such breaths are known as a month for yogis who understand time.
Twenty-one thousand and six hundred breaths are proclaimed as the number of external breaths in a single day and night.
O Six-faced One,
that number of breaths which has been declared for a single day and night should be understood as the number of *ghaṭikās* in a year.
Do not [rely] on external time at all; rather, unify it internally.
Abandoning external time, one should investigate the internal.
Internally, however, one should not undertake any [rites] at all except at the proper time;
for one desiring liberation, sacrifice during the equinox (viṣuva) is highly praised.
O Skanda, for the sake of pacifying the one who is gentle yet fierce, these [streams] flow toward Maheśvara; O handsome one, worship is ordained here directed toward you.
Knowing this, the knower of mantras is liberated from the ocean of existence;
and the knower of mantras also attains accomplishment, if he desires success.
"Otherwise, there can be no accomplishment or liberation; he does not know the time [of death].
Kārttikeya said:
Tell me, according to the proper method and in the sequence starting from the east, how indeed these obstacles do not truly arise for the yogi.
The Lord said: Having understood the true nature of that Great-Souled Supreme Lord, the God known as Haṃsa, one should then practice yoga.
Having first made oneself pure as previously described by me,
one must then practice yoga and not otherwise.
Having meditated upon the Pāśupata weapon, one should then commence the ritual action:
"Oṃ ślīṃ paśūṃ hūṃ phaṭ"—this indeed is the supreme weapon that destroys even the stars of destiny (tārakās).
This is proclaimed by the name Pāśupata; it is established for the purpose of protection, as well as for the removal of obstacles in the practice of yoga and the accomplishment of spiritual goals.
For the sake of palaces, water, or wealth, or even for the acquisition of land,
or when there is fear of Rākṣasas, serpents, gods, Asuras, or Guhyakas;
For the King of Weapons, when employed as a rampart and so forth, protects;
by mere remembrance, the King of Weapons destroys all obstacles.
O Six-faced One, listen now to the ritual of this sacrifice according to the rule and in its true essence:
having placed the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the heart, and likewise the syllable *ślīṃ* on the head.
The letter *ma* is its crest (*śikhā*), while *śū* is proclaimed as its armor (*varman*);
it is joined with the *huṃkāra* of the weapon and accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*.
Recalling the syllable *huṃ*, one should visualize the eye [of wisdom] in the two eyes;
having recited the mantra once, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body.
Thereafter, one should assign the limbs [of the mantra], beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *Namaḥ*;
then, one should perform the sacrifice (*yāga*) for the pacification of obstacles.
Having meditated upon a mental lotus with eight petals and a pericarp,
or else having drawn a mandala that fulfills all desires with colored powder.
Seated upon the seat of the *praṇava*, one should contemplate the mantra therein—
the great-souled one with ten arms and the mighty one with ten ears.
Endowed with fifteen eyes, throbbing and blazing with radiant splendor,
he made a "kara-kara" sound with his fangs, emitting a roar that was exceedingly difficult to overcome.
One should meditate upon the form of that Manu, which is exceedingly fierce with five heads, possessing the radiance of ten million suns, licking [with its tongues], and difficult to assail.
One should worship the Supreme Lord situated upon the peak of the pericarp;
by means of that which is joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, one should perform all rites.
First, one should place the Lord of Syllables (Akṣareśvara) on the Taijasa petal;
second, on the Īśa petal; and third, in the Nairṛta direction.
The fourth [syllable] is for Vāyu on the petal; *huṃ* is for the eyes of the deity;
and the weapon-mantra (*astra*) with the syllable *phaṭ* is established in the directions beginning with Indra.
One should install everything according to the prescribed rules, and then one should indeed commence this [rite];
once the *nala* has been consecrated with nine oblations for oneself.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), combined with curd mixed with ghee, honey, and other ingredients.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the rules with devotion and various offerings,
he [should place] a jar of unseasoned roots filled with water.
Having meditated on the form as before, the practitioner should consecrate the images with the Astra-mantra recited one hundred and eight times.
When this has been performed, those who act as his adversaries, the various Vināyakas, and all those established as obstacles, shall perish.
One should perform this sacrifice for them; they will perish, of this there is no doubt.
Or one may perform it for oneself when a calamity has indeed arisen.
"The King of Weapons destroys the fear of calamities and creation;
thus has the sacrifice of weapons been fully described by me to you."
Now, [I shall speak] of the supreme, most secret *piṇḍa* of Śiva, the Supreme Lord and the Supreme Self, which consists of all mantras.
By the mere utterance of which one is liberated from all sins and freed from various merits and demerits; of this there is no doubt.
By merely remembering this, one becomes initiated in an instant;
through effort, the mortal who is thus initiated is liberated according to the teaching of Śiva.
O Six-faced One, hear the true majesty of this god:
[it extends] through thousands of crores of births and hundreds of crores of births.
The cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is proclaimed to be infinite and immeasurable;
whatever sin has been accumulated therein by the measure of that saṃsāra—
O God, even that which is uttered but once destroys all of that;
I shall proclaim its extraction—listen as it is declared by me.
One should place beneath him a figure mounted upon a swan, situated above his own *tattva*, joined with a firmly held half-armed staff.
Then, having joined the twenty-first [letter] of the second group (the *āghna*) below that knot, one should place it upon the head of the immortal *kāla*.
Having joined the double-piṇḍa Amṛtāsana below the granthi,
one should place the Śoṣaka below Amṛta and situated above the base (tala).
One should place the drying [seed-syllable] joined with the seed-syllable of power (Śakti) below;
then, one should form Śiva above, conjoined with the Bindu.
One should contemplate the end of the resonance (nādānta) together with the crown of the syllable Oṃ;
this is the supreme reality that cuts away all sins.
The Lord of all principles, the peaceful Supreme Śiva who pervades the sky,
is proclaimed to be the heart of the deity of the thousand syllables.
By this being recited once by Śambhu, the God of gods,
seventy million mantras indeed become as if already recited.
It is remembered as the supreme seed of all seeds and the supreme among all principles;
it is for the practice of the transference of consciousness and for the purification of all sins.
This supreme [mantra] should be applied to the body by teachers who desire the welfare [of others];
now hear, O Skanda, the limbs of this deity in their proper order.
The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ), the male fire (puṃvahni), and movement (calana) joined with the second [vowel],
and pervaded by the complete tilaka— this is proclaimed as the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Thus, through the middle conjunction with fire and likewise again,
these limbs are joined with movement in due order.
Furthermore, the first [syllable] is adorned by the fourth, the sixth, and the twelfth;
the thirty-second is the second of the seventh.
The knower of mantras should first take that very [letter] and arrange it below; by joining it with the fifth letter of the first [group] and with the visarga, he should form the mantra.
The supreme and most secret Śiva-weapon, which destroys all sins and removes all obstacles, is a protector that is difficult to conquer even by the gods.
Enveloped in splendor by thousands of millions of suns, he remains standing;
one should employ this form of radiant energy, which is difficult to assail, for the purpose of protection.
By its mere remembrance, it destroys the many bonds of worldly existence;
such indeed is the weapon named Aghora, which brings fear to all spirits.
In the sacrifice, however, the knower of mantras, having joined the *praṇava* for the purpose of the month,
should apply "hāṃ" to the supreme Lord in relation to dharma and the other [puruṣārthas].
One should cause it to be performed by those who are capable in the left [hand];
having uttered Mahāśiva, one should [worship] the immutable Lord Piṇḍeśa.
When that [breath] is situated within the Suṣumṇā at the end of the sound (nāda) by means of the path of power (śaktimārga),
then one who desires the fruits of accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti) should perform the ritual of installation (saṃsthāpana).
Having placed the heart-mantra in the southeast and the head-mantra situated in the northeast,
one should place the crest-mantra in the southwest and the armor-mantra in the domain of the wind (the northwest).
One should place the syllable Aiṃ and worship the Supreme Lord as one's own self; this is known as the daily sacrifice (nityayāga). Now hear the specific ritual (vaiśeṣika) from me.
When the preceptors perform the consecration of sacrificial animals,
they do so starting from one cubit up to sixteen cubits.
The maṇḍala is square, adorned with four gates;
in its center is a full-blown lotus, radiant with its pericarp and filaments.
Having installed the Great Śiva as the deity within your heart,
worship Him according to the previously mentioned procedure, accompanied by the Heart-mantra and the Aghora-weapon mantra.
One should worship [the deities] in the petals starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, following the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions;
however, one should worship that which is established in the primary locus in the center of the petals.
In the midst of the purification, however, there are obstacles; it is endowed with a complete tilaka, peaceful yet mounted upon movement, destroying infinite evils through its great splendor.
At the beginning, however, the channels (nāḍīs), which are exceedingly beautiful with their hosts, are established within the seed-syllable;
they are pervaded by the second [vowel] up to the sixth face, starting from the divine [level].
The world-protectors [should be worshipped] with great missiles, beginning with Indra’s weapon, in due order;
[one should worship] the lords of the gods, Indra and the others, together with the weapons that destroy Rāghna.
The world-protectors have been described, holding their own weapons in their hands;
after the worship, the mudrās of these [deities] should be employed hereafter.
One should sequentially place the weapon-mudrās beginning with the vajra and ending with the trident;
for whatever [weapon] is prescribed here for a particular [deity], that mudrā is of its very nature.
One should join the Mahāmudrā salutation with the leaders of the hosts of obstacles,
and by name, one should join the Supreme Mudrā with Mahāśiva.
The characteristics of the mudrās for the king of mantras of Śiva are now described:
having placed the two hands palm-upward, the little fingers should be joined together on one side.
Likewise here, the ring fingers and the two middle fingers are extended upward;
the two thumbs are joined at the middle joints, and both index fingers are extended outward.
With the two hands joined together at the front and the middle fingers joined at the back—
this is the Mahāmudrā, which severs all bonds.
This is the Great Mistress of all mudrās and mantras;
one should employ her at the time of worship for Śiva, the King of Mantras.
For this [knowledge] fulfills the injunctions and destroys both merit and demerit;
it must be guarded with effort by the wise at all times, as they would their own lives.
One should perform the touching of the heart and the head of the disciple;
the ritual of the Śiva-hand and so forth is to be performed according to the rules with six *piṇḍas*.

The preceptor should perform the ritual action in its entirety using the "piṇḍa" known as the Heart-mantra, which is the essence of all; otherwise, it would be improper for the sake of the consecration.
The supreme teacher should purify the principles beginning with earth in the heart, head, crest-lock, and armor; however, he should not purify the ether-principle in Mahāśiva.
One should offer the rite of expiation and so forth with the *astrapiṇḍa* oblation;

at each and every level of reality (*tattva*), there should be a full offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the non-grasping of the fetters (*pāśa*). Or else, O Six-faced One, by means of a single oblation, [the fetters are dissolved] by the Supreme Lord.
One should unite [the breath] with that which stands at the equinox; thus one is released from the bondage of the fettered soul (paśu).
Upon the fall of the body, they go to Śiva, who is ineffable and free from all affliction;
[one should perform] the Gaṇayāga and the Vāstuyāga, and the Caṇḍīśa with the Hṛdaya mantra.
This entire procedure of the Supreme Lord has been fully explained;
however, due to its eightfold division, it cannot be described in any other way.
But the supreme power of Śiva, who eternally bestows grace—
whichever man she descends upon, he shall obtain the purificatory rite of the thread (Upanayana).
Otherwise, one would not attain initiation leading to the state of Mahāśiva.
Thus, O Ṣaṇmukha, this supreme knowledge has been told to you.
When a disciple has been thoroughly examined and is endowed with compassion, one should bestow what is to be given;
otherwise, one should not reveal the nectar to wicked mortals.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty [verse] section in the Kālottara.
The Two Hundred [Verses].
Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
Kārttikeya said:
But these mortals have short lifespans, little vigor and prowess,
meager strength and wealth, and are possessed by greed and delusion.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, for the sake of your grace toward me, you should speak that which is concise in words yet great in meaning, and which is filled with manifold subjects.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme true essence of the scripture,
extracted from the *Uttara-tantra* like butter from curd.
Thus, this supreme nectar has been extracted from all the scriptures;
like honey from a flower, this auspicious essence is the very quintessence of the essence.
O Mahāsena, having known that supreme seed called Nāda, which is established in all beings, the teacher becomes a destroyer of bonds.
From cowherds, women, children, and barbarians who speak vernacular tongues,
down to the sentient beings dwelling within the water— they all constantly recite it.
Having understood the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, one may perform action as desired.
The gross is said to be sound, while the subtle consists of thought.
That which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the supreme;
having understood this, the knower of mantras shall experience the destruction of all sins.
Having placed the eighth seed-syllable of whichever class [of consonants] with twelve mātrās,
and having interspersed it with other syllables, that six-limbed [mantra] becomes Śiva.
The first is the heart, which wards off obstacles; the second is remembered as Śiva;
the third is the goddess Śikhā; and the fourth shall be the armor (kavaca).
The fifth is Śiva [the heart], from the obstacle [the head] comes the sixth, the weapon [the eye] born of emission;
this six-limbed [mantra] has been taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Īśvara said:
I shall now describe its mudrā, by which practitioners attain success:
one should touch both feet with the two hands, extending them up to the head.
The Mahāmudrā of these is the accomplisher of all desires and aims;
having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), the wise one should display it.
Thus ends the first chapter in the two-hundred-verse *Kālottara*.
The Lord said:
I shall fully explain the sacrifice in its proper sequence:
the heart, the pericarp, the lotus, and likewise dharma, jñāna, and the rest.
One should likewise place detachment and sovereignty within the heart;
one should arrange the array of powers upon the filaments by means of the Heart-mantra.
The practitioner, knowing the mantras, should invoke the deity with the heart-mantra;
likewise, the knower of mantras should perform the installation, the offering of water for the feet, and the water for sipping.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing and the worship with the Heart-mantra;
indeed, whatever is enjoined by the ritual rules for anything whatsoever should be done with the Heart-mantra.
This is the single protective enclosure that accomplishes all desired aims;
it is common to all tantras and esteemed among all branches of knowledge.
Thus ends the second chapter on worship in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the fire-offering (agnikārya):
the tracing [of lines] is performed with the Weapon-mantra (astra), and sprinkling is prescribed with the Armor-mantra (kavaca).
Then the practitioner of mantras should perform the placement of power (śakti-nyāsa) with the Heart-mantra;
he should cast the fire into the womb of power by means of the Heart-mantra.
Having performed the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna) up to the final expiation (niṣkṛti),
the knower of reality should perform all rituals with the Heart-mantra.
Thereafter, one should visualize the previously mentioned Lotus-Vidyā;
one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) for Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas), which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
Thus ends the third chapter on the fire-ritual in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the mandala that fulfills all desires; having drawn it with a cord, making it square and equal on all sides.
Having established an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in the center,
measuring one cubit, two cubits, or even four or eight cubits.
This single enclosure, however, accomplishes all desired aims;
one who desires success, being composed in mind, should cause the door to be opened toward the west.

Then, one should cause a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit in size to be made level in the southeast; there, one should perform the ritual procedures for the fire sacrifice in a perfectly even manner within the two fires.
Having placed the heart-mantra in the southeast, one should place the head in the northeast;
one should place the crest-lock in the southwest and the armor in the northwest.
Having placed the weapon-mantra in the directions and Sadāśiva in the pericarp,
O Skanda, the ritual procedure has been succinctly proclaimed by me.
Whatever has not been stated by me, all that should rely upon the root [text].
Thus, a wise person who understands the rules and procedures should commence the ritual action.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Maṇḍala-paṭala, in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
Now I shall explain the candidate for initiation (dīkṣya), who is established within the five principles (tattvas):
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
The entire universe is pervaded by these five great principles (mahātatvas);
all other principles are situated therein and should be perceived by the best of the Śikottamas.
But he who, without knowing this, desires to perform initiation after having merely learned it, undergoes fruitless exertion; he shall not obtain its fruit in such a manner.
Cessation is to be known as earth, and support is said to be water;
knowledge is declared to consist of fire, and life is celebrated as peace.
Beyond Śānti is the supreme void, which is further than that—tranquil and imperishable.
Having known that, O Mahāsena, one may initiate even immobile beings.
Nivṛtti is established in the heart, while Pratiṣṭhā is in the head;
Vidyā is in the crest-lock (śikhā), and Śānti is indeed with the armor (kavaca).
One who causes that which transcends peace— the supreme tranquility— to arise through serenity,
should offer a hundred oblations for each [syllable] and indeed perform a hundred-fold homa.
O Six-faced One, afterwards,
for the sake of purification through atonement, one should offer the final oblation with a prayer of grace, followed by one oblation each in sequence.
The knower of mantras should perform the fire-oblation with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja), as previously described.
In this way, initiation (dīkṣā) is completed, being devoid of birth and other such processes.
Even when the oblation has been offered, practitioners are not released from the bondage of birth;
therefore, this sacrifice must not be disclosed, but kept secret with great effort.
This is the secret of all tantras, the supreme consecration;
for one thus purified by consecration, the state of Śiva arises with certainty.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord of Gods, abandon prolixity; speak to me in brief, so that by the mere understanding of it, one may liberate a bound soul (paśu) in an instant.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the truth by which liberation becomes certain,
through the subtle application observed in Yoga by one who knows the mantras.
He is impelled by his own power through the divine path of yoga;
having understood that life-force to be composed of wind, O Mahāsena, the wise man [proceeds].
One should deposit [the self] in the eternal state by means of the equinox-yoga;
for having attained the equinox-yoga, who is not liberated from bondage?
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
I shall now describe in due order this subtle system of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*).
Below the navel is the bulbous root (*kanda*), from which the channels emerge.
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated in the center of the navel;
they pervade everywhere—horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
Arranged like the spokes of a wheel, there are ten principal channels:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and likewise Yamā;
Alaṃbuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
These ten channels are indeed proclaimed as the carriers of the vital breaths:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
of these nine, Prāṇa is the first wind, and it is their lord.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the vital breaths, constantly fills [the body] from exhalation toward inhalation; it remains as the life-force of all living beings.
Because the life-force (prāṇa), which is dependent upon the individual soul (jīva), performs the act of departing through exhalation, inhalation, and coughing, it is therefore proclaimed as "prāṇa."
The apāna wind, however, carries down the food and drink;
because it carries semen and urine, it is celebrated as apāna.
The wind named Samāna brings to tranquility within the limbs the cold that has been consumed, smelled, or [otherwise ingested], as well as the states of rakta, pitta, kapha, and ānila.
The wind named Udāna causes the lower face to quiver, provokes only the eyes,
and agitates the vital points (marmas).
Vyāna destroys the limbs; Vyāna is the agitator of diseases.
It is said that pleasure is its destruction, and old age is called Vyāna.
The vital winds that destroy life have been described; now those that destroy the [five] serpents (nāgas) are being explained.
Nāga is said to be present during belching, while Kūrma resides during the opening of the eyes.
Kṛkara is present during hunger; Devadatta manifests as yawning;
Dhanañjaya resides in the sound of the breath and does not leave even when one has died.
This very collection of winds, established in the heart-lake and situated within the wheel of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*),

is constantly overcome by the one wind— from its state as a child, through youth, and even in the minds of those free from calamity— by means of exhalation, inhalation, coughing, panting, gasping, trembling, and reeling. It is ever-present, characterized by slight births, and devoid of affliction.
He plays with all sentient beings through the acts of shaking and scattering.
I shall explain to you in its entirety the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) according to its actual state,
so that this ten-spoked wheel may be understood in its proper divisions.
I shall tell you that; listen as I speak it.
The individual soul (jīva) revolves like a wheel through ten stations in succession.
That is the life-force of the world of living beings, yet those deluded by ignorance do not perceive it;
because it moves in ten ways, it is proclaimed as the "wheel" (*cakra*).
And he who indeed enters that which is known as the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra).
Kārttikeya said:
He is the life-force of the world of living beings, like a victorious sound;
O Mahādeva, I have a great doubt—be gracious and grant me [the answer].
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the vision of the individual soul (jīva) known as Puruṣa;
I shall describe it to you without doubt, especially out of affection for my son.
The transits and equinoxes, as well as the days, nights, and solstices;
the intercalary month, the debt, and likewise the subtracted night and the wealth.
The occurrence of a deficient night (ūnarātra) is the desire for food; the intercalary month (adhimāsa) is yawning.
Ashes become coughing, and exhalation is said to be wealth.
The right is to be known as the north, while the left is designated as the south;
in the middle, however, is declared the equinox, emerging from the two openings of the *mudrā*.
Furthermore, its transition occurs from the vehicle of the vowels (svarayāna) and from its very station;
it is endowed with Iḍā, Suṣumnā, and Pramā.
The Suṣumnā is indeed established in the middle limb;
the upward-moving breath (prāṇa) is day, and the downward-moving breath (apāna) is night.
He who knows through this division is wise and is called a knower.
I shall now describe to you briefly the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having filled the abdomen with air as much as can be seen, one should remain like a completely filled jar; that is the kumbhaka breath control.
Or is it joined with the wind? Then, when the exhalation has increased, one should exhale the wind that has increased while engaged in the yoga of exhalation (*niśvāsa-yoga*).
Known as Recaka, it causes danger to life;
that which is situated in the heart is established within the lotus.
One who is obstructed by the *padmakumbhaka* breath-retention will become one whose stream flows upward.
If not expelled during exhalation, the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes obstructed and life-destroying;
but once exhaled, it rises upward, piercing the knots in an instant.
Having pierced the door of the skull, the soul (jīva), thus exhaled, ascends above.
Having attained the state of Sadāśiva, one shall not undergo birth again;
for him alone is this span [of life] ordained, and never for anyone else.
I have thus briefly described that life-force (jīva) of the world of living beings,
from which Śiva, abiding in his own nature, spontaneously emerges.
Therefore, for those who know reality, that very [practice] is called *japa*:
ten thousand years, one thousand, and likewise six hundred.
In a single day and night, that lord of yogis completes his count of recitations.
Thus ends the seventh chapter on the Wheel of Channels in the two-hundred-verse *Kālajñāna*.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme true essence of the scripture,
by the mere knowledge of which one no longer takes up a physical body.

Abiding in the body, He is known as *sakala* (with parts); devoid of the body, He is *niṣkala* (without parts). He is to be reached through the instruction of a realized teacher; He exists everywhere as something indefinable.
Whoever should utter "Haṃsa, Haṃsa," the Haṃsa is the god Sadāśiva;
he is obtained directly from the mouth of the Guru as the one whose face is turned in every direction.
Just as oil exists in sesame seeds and fragrance is inherent in a flower,
so does that [Self] abide within and without this body of a person.
Just as someone with a torch in hand, having illuminated an object, might discard that torch;
so too, having illuminated the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should then relinquish that knowledge.
The flower is indeed the *sakala* (with parts), while its fragrance is the *niṣkala* (partless);
one should know that the tree is the *sakala*, while its shade is the *niṣkala*.
Established everywhere through both the manifest (sakala) and unmanifest (niṣkala) states,
he obstructs the manifest within the manifest, and likewise the unmanifest within the unmanifest.
It consists of three measures, two measures, and likewise one measure;
further, there is the subtle half-measure, and beyond even that, the supreme-non-supreme (parāpara).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself—
the entire [universe] is recited as having these five deities in its fivefold aspect.
Brahmā’s place is in the heart; Viṣṇu resides in the throat;
Rudra is situated in the middle of the palate; and Maheśvara is located in the forehead.
At the tip of the nose is Śiva; at its end is the supreme-non-supreme (parāpara).
There is nothing higher than the supreme—this is the firm conclusion of the scriptures.
Kārttikeya said: "O Mahādeva, how does his coming and going occur, or by whom is he led? I have a great doubt; tell me according to the truth."
Īśvara said:
"The individual soul (jīva) is led by Śakti; having reached its station, it returns.
I shall explain its state within her to you in truth; listen, O Ṣaṇmukha."
One should perceive that [Self], which transcends the body, twelve finger-breadths in extent, roaring within;
situated there, the Lord pervades all from the seed-syllable that resides therein.
Even though the impurity has been cast elsewhere and the gaze is directed elsewhere,
nevertheless, the yoga of yogis proceeds without interruption.
This indeed is the supreme secret; this indeed is the supreme state;
this is that supreme Brahman; for this is the supreme syllable.
"There is nothing higher than this, nothing more auspicious than this,
and no knowledge higher than this," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
The nectar of the knowledge of Śiva has been proclaimed in brief and not in detail; O Lord of the God of Gods, you have attained the definitive determination of the Supreme Imperishable.
For this, O Śiva, is the true nature of reality, issued from the mouth of Śiva;
it is a secret more secret than the secret, and must be grasped with diligent effort.
This must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor under any circumstances to one who is not a son;
it should be given only to one who is devoted to the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, who is peaceful, and who is an ascetic.
The nectar of Śiva has been fully explained by me to you; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Having understood this, O wise one, conduct yourself according to your pleasure.
Whether a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—
wherever situated, the man of knowledge is always a knower of the supreme syllable.

Even one who is attached to sense objects and immersed in worldly desires reaches the auspicious state at the end of the body through the knowledge of this scripture alone; so too does a human being, even if addicted to sin.
One is not tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin or the failure to perform the Ashvamedha sacrifice;
indeed, it is remembered as the supreme liberator through both water and the chariot.
Thus, these three types of teachers are to be known on the surface of the earth:
the instigator (codaka) shall show the path, and the awakener (bodhaka) shall point out the station.
But liberation is the supreme state, having gone to which one does not return.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
The Lord said:
In the midst of fire is the station of the sun; in the midst of the sun is the moon;
in its midst is the divine sprout, from which the creation proceeds.
One should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* there, as taught through the practice of repetition;
the best of practitioners should contemplate that [deity] as flowing, not as dead.

One who desires accomplishment and is composed in mind should contemplate the entire world— both stationary and moving— as consisting of Agni and Soma, yet as being their opposite within that [reality].
One should contemplate one's own body as entering a divine form beyond compare;
the wise person should contemplate whatever specific ritual action has been prescribed for that [deity].
Whoever should practice this nectar-like meditation, which faces in all directions,
shall in no long time become a partaker of the fruit of accomplishment.
