Without understanding the ritual placement (nyāsa) of emanation, how can practitioners apply it?
He is like one who strikes at the sky with his fist and shouts in vain for chaff.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Fire-Vyoma," in the two-hundred-verse *Kālottara*.
Īśvara said:
Henceforth I shall explain: if one, having aroused the *nāda* through grace, recites it constantly, perfection arises within six months for one engaged in yoga; of this there is no doubt.
Through the recitation of the *gamāgama* mantra, the destruction of all sins occurs;
within six months, one attains the sovereignty of the *aṇimā* and other supernatural powers—of this there is no doubt.
Becoming one with that reality, one attains perfection within six months;
the gross, the subtle, and the supreme have thus been described by me as grace.
Those by whom grace is perceived do not truly awaken to Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the two-hundred-verse [treatise] on the Knowledge of Time.
Īśvara said:
Henceforth I shall proclaim the characteristics of *prasāda*;
the knower of mantras should always discern it as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*).
The short [form] burns away sins; the long [form] bestows liberation;
and the prolated [form], endowed with a bindu upon its head, serves for nourishment.
Three gross divisions have been declared: subjugation (vaśya), eradication (uccāṭana), and killing (māraṇa).
By means of the *pluta* [vowel], one always effects subjugation; there is no doubt in this matter.
When joined with the syllable *phaṭ*, it quickly causes long-distance eradication;
and when the short *phaṭ* is placed at both the beginning and the end, it brings about violent death.
The Heart-mantra is prescribed for both the beginning and the end during the practice of attraction;
when properly employed, it will certainly attract even one situated hundreds of leagues away.
In this way one should attract the person to be accomplished, having understood their name according to reality;
it is taught that for the practitioner it should be numerous, while for the person to be accomplished it should be fewer.
Having understood this, the wise practitioner certainly performs the attraction;
without correctly understanding this, practitioners do not achieve success at all.
Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should cause the *argha* offering for the mantra to be presented.
Having offered the *argha*, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation (*japa*) for the deceased.
One should perform the recitation of five hundred thousand [mantras] while standing on the right side of the deity;
at the conclusion of the recitation, there should be a fire offering (*homa*) of ten thousand oblations.
Thus nourished, the mantra will thereafter become fit for ritual action;
and whatever rites have been taught by me will be accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
If one recites [the mantra] one million times, the people dwelling in their own places will indeed quickly come to him; this is the certainty of the scripture.
And by offering ten times ten lakhs [of oblations], those inhabitants of the ten villages come under one's control,
both in person and with their wealth.
With twenty-five hundred thousand recitations, one should bring the object of desire under control;
he who recites three million times shall become a sovereign ruler of a mandala.
With thirty-five hundred thousand [recitations], one shall bring the earth under one's control;
with forty hundred thousand, one beholds Hāṭakeśvara.
And by reciting another hundred thousand times over food, one becomes equal to a Vighnādharas;
there the mantra-practitioner rejoices until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord, O Master, even though I am free from sin, there remains a doubt regarding theoretical knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna).
How is that knowledge known, and how is the object of knowledge described?
The Lord said:

O Six-faced One, having first understood the support (ādhāra), one should subsequently discern that which is supported (ādheya); the wise person who knows the relationship between the support and the supported is competent in all actions.
The support (ādhāra) is called Muḍra, while that which is supported (ādheya) is called Īśa.
For he who rules over the Mistress (Īśinī) is traditionally known as Īśa.
Having realized the Lord, the wise man who always exults within himself,
though joined with the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka), moves both downward and upward.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, and ego—this is remembered as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
Until they are released by these means, how can they be liberated from bondage?
One should abandon sound and touch, O Brahmā; one should indeed abandon taste, O Keśava.
One should abandon form and smell in Rudra, the intellect and ego in Īśvara;
having abandoned the mind and the bindu in Śiva through these [stages], one becomes liberated as Śiva.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
I shall now explain the ritual procedure of Kālacakra according to the ancient tradition;
it is renowned as Kālacakra because by means of it one awakens to Time.
By the movement of the *iḍā* for three days and nights, he lives for three years;
by the movement of the *piṅgalā* for two days and nights, he lives for two years.
By moving for three days and nights, he lives for one year;
and likewise, by [moving] for one year, he lives for one *kāṣṭhā*.
Is it a proven fact of the scriptures that death occurs after six months?
By means of the movement of the two sacrifices, he lives for a day and night.
The Kālacakra has been fully explained out of affection for my son; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
Likewise, two paths lead forward;
people resort to them. One is joined with yoga, while the second leads to suffering.
"O blessed lady, tell me what happiness there is in union;
and I, O blessed lady, shall tell you what happiness truly prevails."
Seeing his return once more, she awaited him with eager longing; "That which was previously indicated by you, what is it that must now be recited?"
"O Aśva, this has been told to you... [for the sake of] happiness.
Then she said: 'What is this cry of distress? By you, who speak the truth.'"
Such and such indeed is the analogy, from which conviction arises. What is that yogic bliss which would be...
otherwise, for one who speaks differently, conviction does not arise at all.
Since it is indeed impossible to describe a happiness that is unmanifested?
In no long time, that happiness will be realized;
O blessed lady, there is no doubt that it will be exactly as you have described.
Whatever unpleasant thing has been said by me through the delusion of happiness born of ignorance—
thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the two-hundred-verse *Kālottara*.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord Śiva, O All-pervading One, you previously promised that there would be no division among the eight [forms].
O God, how can that be divided? Be gracious, O wielder of the trident!

Īśvara said: The eighth [letter] is remembered as *sakala*, *niṣkala*, *śūnya*, the destroyer of parts (*kalāghna*), the pure void (*khamala*), the act of creation (*kṛta*), the casting forth (*kṣepaṇa*), that which abides within destruction (*kṣayamantastha*), and that which is articulated with the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*).
The Śiva-tattva is proclaimed as being endowed with grace (prasāda), joined with the six [aspects], possessed of the six limbs, complete, and abiding in all beings.
The Lord himself departs, casting off the body like the wind;
one should know that to be the partless (niṣkala), which is Śiva, devoid of all color.
Having pierced through the body which stands like a log, devoid of inhalation and exhalation,
one should know it to be empty and contemplate it with the heart.
That reality which smokes on the earth with a kissing-like face, one should know that to be the first of the *kalās*; now hear from me concerning that which resides in space.
When the upward-sounding [vibration] has been exhausted, that which remains is proclaimed as the "A.
The knower of reality, situated therein, is adorned by the space of the feet.
But having heard that the Lord, the teacher of the world, had spoken the word "Kṣapaṇa" (the destroyer of suffering) with his face turned away,
he was remembered as Kṣapaṇa because of that destruction and because of his own exhaustion [of suffering].
In the beginning, when the sound has subsided, that which is proclaimed as the end of the word should be known as the semivowel (antastha); it is proclaimed as being unutterable.
The eighth of the eight groups is the peak; the second of the seventh;
that which transcends the groups is the sixth; and in the seventh, the third and fourth.
Furthermore, the first [letter] should be joined with the sixth of the first [group];
conjoined with Khaśekhara, it is known as the eighth, Kaṇṭhoṣṭha.
These varieties have been fully explained for the accomplishment of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*;
that which is beyond utterance and free from doubt is designated as liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
How is it pervasive— below, above, and across?
Tell me this true nature just as it was spoken in the past.
The Lord said:
As long as the living being remains within the body, it stays pervading [it];
having emerged, it pervades transversely; situated within, it is established everywhere.
The living being situated in the three paths is established within the entire body;
yet, by not knowing this, one is liberated, and even a killer would become like that [liberated] being.
He who knows this pervasion—the three paths and the three bases established throughout the entire body—is indeed all-pervading; of this there is no doubt.
They wander in saṃsāra as long as they do not find pervasiveness;
having known the all-pervading Lord, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Just as a grass-leech has reached the tip of a blade of grass and,
being unsupported, remains suspended above it, even so is the life-principle (jīva) situated.
Above is emptiness, below is emptiness, and in the middle is the stainless emptiness;
he who understands this triple emptiness is certainly liberated from the grasp of the planets.
And its pervasiveness has been declared by me in brief, but not in detail;
beyond this there is nothing that is more pervasive than the Pervasive One.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
Hereafter, I shall explain how the eightfold proof occurs:
namely, the blazing of fire without fuel, and likewise the climbing of a tree by one who is not a tree.
It is the paralyzing of nooses, the destruction of great sins,
the neutralization of poison, and likewise the rendering of [enemies] lifeless.
The destruction of fevers and planetary seizures is known through eightfold means;
having correctly understood this procedure, renown arises everywhere.
Oṃ hraṃ hrauṃ hrūṃ namaḥ. This should be employed in the fire-stream; this is the application for kindling the fire.
It blazes forth when joined with the *sahasvodghoma* [mantra]; of this there is no doubt. *Oṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hrūṃ namaḥ*.
This application is also proclaimed among the Agniśrotas;
when struck with five hundred blows, one certainly dies.
Furthermore, when the white [moon] is situated in the western [direction], there is its replenishment:
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hīṃ namaḥ.
That tree lives again, exactly as it was before.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ namaḥ.
(The application at the time of the equinox causes the paralysis of the fetters;
by five hundred upward breaths, one falls [into liberation]—of this there is no doubt.
Oṃ hyaṃ hrauṃ svaṃ namaḥ.
When grasping the jar, heaviness indeed arises;
Oṃ haṃ heṃ stheṃ namaḥ.
This is the practice of the Tulāpuruṣa sacrifice, performed ten thousand times along with its constituent elements.
Oṃ hyāṃ hyauṃ hyīṃ namaḥ. This application, indeed, for the removal of poison is by means of the Vāruṇa [mantra]. By exactly eight hundred recitations, one certainly removes the poison.
Just as it was taught regarding the blazing of the fire for the purpose of rendering it seedless,
so too here a distinction is prescribed by means of five hundred upward thrusts (*udghāta*).
Oṃ hraṃ hrauṃ hraṃ namaḥ.
This practice, established in the Vāruṇa [mantra], swiftly destroys the seizing spirits;
likewise, eight hundred udghātas are prescribed for the destruction of the grahas.
Oṃ huṃ phaṭ || Oṃ hroṃ phaṭ || Huṃ phaṭ ||
By means of the Vāruṇa stream, one quickly destroys fever;
indeed, this practice of eight hundred recitations with the *udghāta* is a destroyer of fever.
I have explained the application of the eight conditions.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
Of what nature is grace (prasāda) to be known, and of what nature is its pervasiveness? Of what nature is its manifestation? O Maheśvara, please tell me.
The Lord said:
He who does not know how to realize the great body of the five mantras,
which is endowed with thirty-eight kalās, is not called an Ācārya.
If a guru performs initiation without properly ascertaining the disciple's spiritual disposition (prasāda), he leads both the disciple and himself downward; of this there is no doubt.
The teacher who, abiding within the crest of grace (*prasāda*), performs initiation together with his disciples, shall go to union with Śiva.
The gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
as well as the siddhas and ṛṣis— all were born from the palace.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśa, Candra, Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati,
as well as Āditya, Śukra, Skanda, and Bhṛgu.
And whatever other hosts of planets there are, all of whom have arisen from the palace,
as well as these and many other sages of rigid vows.
They meditate upon the supreme Haṃsa, the temple known by various names.
I shall describe its division, knowing which one attains immortality.
They know the Sadyojāta to be born from the letter 'A' and endowed with eight digits;
the Vāmadeva is born from the letter 'U', while the Aghora is born from the letter 'Ma'.
The Puruṣa is to be known as born from the Bindu, while Īśāna is of the nature of the Śikhā;
thus these mantras arise, or they are produced from the Prāsāda.
By worshipping even one [deity] through grace, all mantras numbering hundreds of thousands of millions, possessing immeasurable power, are undoubtedly worshipped.
Those mantras proclaimed as destroyers of Māruta, Anala,
and Śakra all possess unfailing power, having arisen from the conclusion of the word "prasāda."
The Earth is to be known as Sadyojāta, and Water is proclaimed as Vāmadeva; Fire is said to be Aghora, and Wind is remembered as Tatpuruṣa.
Space, however, is the Lord; he himself is the god Maheśvara.
Sadyojāta is the Ṛgveda, and Vāmadeva is the Yajurveda.
The Sāmaveda is indeed Aghora, while the Atharvaveda is said to be Tatpuruṣa;
that which is the fifth, supreme, and subtle is Vyomavyāpī Maheśvara.
Sadyojāta is indeed Brahmā; Vāma is proclaimed as Viṣṇu;
Aghora is Devarudra; and Puruṣa is remembered as Īśvara.
Īśāna has Śiva as his presiding deity; these are remembered as the over-deities (adhidevas).
As for the sixth, which is the supreme principle (tattva), it exists with imperceptible qualities.
Having known the supreme ladder that leads to the fifth station, his body should not be described as being composed of the qualities born of material nature.
He by whom knowledge was known once, with an astonished inner self—
at that very moment he was liberated, for that state was indeed known.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the two-hundred-verse Kālottara.
May there be auspiciousness.
One hundred and fifty [stanzas]. Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
Kārttikeya said:
O Blessed One, God of gods, Lord of the world, Master of the universe! You have proclaimed the mantra, the tantra, and the detailed ritual practice for accomplishment.
But these mortals are short-lived, possessing little vigor or prowess;
they have little strength and little wealth, and are filled with greed and delusion.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, for the sake of favoring me, you should speak that which is concise in words yet vast in meaning, and filled with many explanations of the essential topics.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim this most rare scripture,
known by the name Vātula-tantra and designated as Kāla.
Having extracted the essence from everything, like clarified butter drawn from curd,
or as honey is the essence from flowers, this auspicious essence has been gathered.
That supreme seed-syllable called Nāda, which is established in all beings,
is the supreme giver of liberation, divine, and the bestower of all accomplishments.
Having known that, O Mahāsena, the teacher becomes a destroyer of bonds;
[he reaches] even cowherds, commoners, children, barbarians, and those who speak vernacular tongues.
Even those beings dwelling within the water always say this:
"Having understood [the object] whether it be gross, subtle, or supreme, one should perform the ritual action as desired."
"He is not defiled by evil, just as crystal is not [stained] by dust"— this is an additional reading found in another manuscript.
It is said that the gross [self] is sound, while the subtle consists of thought.
And that which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the Supreme.
Having understood this, the knower of mantras shall experience the destruction of all sins;
[he realizes] that which is peaceful, omnipresent, and empty, established through the twelve measures.
Having performed the interposition of syllables (*akṣarāntarita*), he becomes Śiva with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
(First, one should assign the Heart; know that the Eye is the fifth.
O Six-faced One, the short vowels are declared to be Brahmā, while the long ones are indeed the limbs (*aṅga*).
The "eye" (the letter *i*) with the *anusvāra* is situated above all [the letters];
that same [letter] with the *visarga*, devoid of the *anusvāra*, becomes the "weapon" (*astra*).
One should join the sixth with the end of the thirteenth in the fifth;
one should know that to be Śiva, Sadāśiva, whose form is the mantra.
But for the sixth [mantra], the second [syllable] is joined with the first of the fourth [group];
and in the second and fifth [positions], one should again join the first [syllable].
All obstacles are destroyed by the auspicious weapon (*śivāstra*); it is remembered as the bestower of liberation through the *śikhā*. This divine Pāśupata [mantra] severs all fetters.
The five Brahmans, Śiva with his limbs, the Netra, and the Pāśupata—
all this auspicious extraction of mantras has been told in brief.
I shall now describe its mudrā for the benefit of practitioners:
one should touch both feet with both hands, extending them up as far as the head.
The seal (*mudrā*) of these is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which accomplishes all desires and aims;
having first performed the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should then form the seal-binding.

One should purify the palms and the backs of the hands with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja). Beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb, one should perform the purification.
Just as with Brahmā, one should diligently install the Aiṅgas in their proper sequence (according to the *Mantroddhāra-pāṭha*).
Afterward, one should install Prasāda, which is all-pervading and faces in every direction.
O child, there is no doubt that this is the karanyāsa according to this tantra.
Thus ends the first chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
Īśvara said:

Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), as well as the arrangement of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vinyāsa) and the purification of the self (saṃbhūtaśuddhi), perform the placement of the internal organ thereafter.
One should always hold the seed-syllable of the heart conjoined with the earth element;
the head with water, the crest-fire with fire, and the armor with wind.
One should always hold the weapon-mantra conjoined with Śiva, directed toward the sky;
having pierced through the veil again and again with the word "phaṭ" at the end, one especially ascends upward.
At the time of initiation, one should perform the ritual procedure exactly as I shall describe it.
Then, for the sake of upward extraction (*uddhāta*), those two breaths (*praśva*) are unified into one.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone remains, empty and without any support.
Then, one should meditate on the nectar flowing from the letter *m* situated within the *prakṛti*.
By means of the syllable *oṃ*, there shall likewise be a lotus,
the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), resembling the solar disc, which indeed arises from the self through the letter *a*.
The principle of Vighna consists of the vowel *u*, while the principle of Śiva is born from the syllable *ma*.
(In one manuscript, the reading at the bottom of the page is: "Having pierced the enclosure with *hūṃ phaṭ* at the end, specifically as before.")

One should contemplate Sadāśiva, who is beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), consisting of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), as the supreme abode with his head pierced by the Suṣumṇā.
By that [water], one should contemplate oneself as being washed and filled;
whoever constantly practices this samādhi, which destroys death.
"Death does not arise for him"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
Afterwards, there shall be the grasping of the form by the teacher and the practitioners.
One should place [the mantras] beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta, starting from the head;
then, having assigned the eyes and invoked Sadāśiva, the God of gods.
The wise one should contemplate the measurement of omniscience,
as well as the heart, the head, the crest-lock, and the armor.
One who knows the mantras should employ the weapon-mantra according to its proper place;
or, according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the fire-oblation at the heart or at the navel.
One should meditate on Īśvara, the bestower of boons, facing in all directions, upon the forehead;
for as it is in the ritual worship, so indeed it is in the fire sacrifice and likewise in meditation.
O Six-faced One, having understood that this internal organ is just as [the deity] is in the divine body, and likewise in the fire and the oblation, one should thereafter attend to the external.
Having first established the outer and inner [circles], he should thereafter begin with the people of the western quarter.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Kālajñāna-vātula-tantra*, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme bath that removes sin:
the wise man, having taken earth with the Astra-mantra, [performs it] once.
Having first performed the ritual bath for removing impurities and having recited the Saṃhitā once,
O child, he should consecrate that very same clay by reciting the mantra over it once, one after another.
Then, having divided it into three parts, one should sprinkle the first with the Astra-mantra;
the second with the five Brahma-mantras; and the third, consecrated by Śiva, with the Śiva-mantra.
One should perform the binding of the directions with a portion consecrated by the Astra-mantra;
the sacred site (tīrtha) with one consecrated by the Śiva-mantra, and the self with one consecrated by the Brahma-mantra.
Then, having smeared himself, the wise one should bathe in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha,
contemplating that as it is with the deity, so it is with his own body.

Having first performed this internal [worship], O Six-faced One, one should afterwards perform the external worship with the ritual honors due to a universal monarch, using fragrant *āmalaka* fruits and other such items. (Alternative reading: *cakravarty-upacāreṇa*) (Note: The "top of page" mark indicates a textual break or transition.)
Having sipped water according to the rule, one should worship the Sandhyā in due order;
O child, one should perform the ritual salutation (upasthāna) once with all the mantras.
Having first performed the consecration (abhiṣeka), one should subsequently perform the twilight ritual (sandhyā).
The wise practitioner should apply the weapon-mantra (astra) to the body and cast it outward.
One should wither the body, O child, but one should not apply it to the self;
the wise should always employ it against obstacles and the snares of bondage.
Then, O Six-faced One, by the grace of that sacred site, the wise man should satisfy the ancestors and the gods with his heart, and [perform] the ritual withdrawal of that sacred site.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kālottara* consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, I shall now describe the procedure for the ash-rite in brief:
O child, having consecrated [the ashes] once with all the mantras in their proper order.
Having first performed the impurity-bath with the Astra-bīja, O Six-faced One,
one should thereafter perform the ritual bath and perform the placement (nyāsa) beginning from the head.
The knower of mantras should protect the head and face with the Īśāna mantra and the Cakra mantra;
the heart-limb with the Aghora mantra, and the private parts with the Guhyaka mantra.
O Six-faced One, the entire body should be consecrated by the Saṃgha with the five [waters]; thereafter, one should perform [the rite] with the water from the upper vessel.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Kālottara-vātula-tantra, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
I shall explain the ritual of sacrifice correctly and in due order:
first the seed-syllable and the sprout, then the primordial ground, and afterwards the infinite seat.
O Six-faced One, one should first perform the non-terminal [rite] in sequence:
the heart, the pericarp, the lotus, and likewise the dharma, jñāna, and so forth.
One should place detachment, sovereignty, the heart, and the source [in their respective positions];
one should arrange the array of powers with the filaments and perform the rite with the Heart-mantra.
Then the Six-faced One should invoke the deity with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
he should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in due order with all the mantras beginning with that of Śiva.
The knower of mantras should perform the ritual placement (sthāpana), as well as the offering of water for honor (argha), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
One should perform the ceremonial bathing and the worship with the Heart-mantra;
whatever has been mentioned or not mentioned, all that should be done with the Heart-mantra.
This is indeed the single protective covering that accomplishes all desires and aims;
it is common to all mantras and supreme among all forms of knowledge.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Vātula Tantra, within the Kālajñāna consisting of one hundred and fifty [verses].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya):
one should perform the digging with the Weapon-mantra (astra) and likewise the sprinkling with the Armor-mantra (kavaca).
Then the practitioner of mantra should perform the deposition of power (śakti-nyāsa) with the Heart-mantra;
indeed, he should cast the fire, which contains power within its womb, into the heart.
Having performed the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) up to the final one (nikṛti),
the knower of mantras should perform all ritual acts by means of the Heart-mantra.
Thereafter, one should arrange the previously described procedure for the lotus.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kālottara consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
Henceforth, I shall explain the mandala that fulfills all desires,
after having thoroughly purified the ground according to the ritual procedures seen in the scriptures.
Then, under an auspicious constellation,
the wise practitioner should perform the formal acceptance and draw the auspicious maṇḍala that bestows all accomplishments.
Having measured it out perfectly with a cord so that it is square on all sides,
he should establish an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in the center.
One should draw the enclosure as one cubit, two cubits, four, or even eight; it may consist of three layers, or be independent, according to the prescribed measurement.
The preceptor, well-composed, should open the outer gate in the west;
he should cause a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be made in the southeast, measuring one cubit in size.
One should perform the ritual procedure for the sacrifice upon a well-kindled sacrificial fire;
beginning from the east, one should then install the faces and other limbs in their proper sequence.
Then, one should place the purifying cities upon it as the limbs of Śiva;
having placed the heart in the southeast, one should place the head in the northeast.
It is circular and square, adorned with a moon-shaped girdle;
it is the destroyer of all desires and is declared to be the characteristic of the Āgneyī direction.
Having prepared the components of the sacrifice, one should perform the consecration of the seat upon the ground. (Bottom of page) p.
3b) (O Skanda, the ritual procedure has been proclaimed by me in brief.)
Whatever may remain unsaid, all of that [should be understood] by means of the heart.
Thus, one who knows the rules and procedures, having understood this, should commence the ritual action.
One should place the *śikhā* (topknot) in the southwest and the *kavaca* (armor) in the northwest;
having assigned the *astra* (weapon) to the cardinal directions, one should place Sadāśiva upon the pericarp.
This indeed is the procedure for the deposition of the womb (garbhanyāsa); now hear about the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa).
Beginning from the east, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) according to the prescribed rite.
In the third [verse], one should worship the guardians of the world (lokapālas) with a single weapon-mantra.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Kālottara-vātula-tantra*, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
Now I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā), which is established through the five principles:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
The entire world is pervaded by these five great principles;
all other principles are situated therein and should be perceived by the best of practitioners.
Having joined the nadīs through the yoga of union with the oblations in sequence, the universe (brahmāṇḍa) is indeed established by Nivṛtti; therein the hundred Rudras are situated.

In the stage of *pratiṣṭhā*, [the practice continues] from that point upward as far as the range of the unmanifest (*avyakta-gocara*). [The armor (*kavaca*) is likewise in *pratiṣṭhā* up to the range of the unmanifest; this is the external characteristic.]
Then one should apply the obstructions until reaching the presence of Vighneśvara.
Beyond that, one should worship Śiva, who is the path of Peace (śānti) and transcends peace (śāntyatīta);
having then attained Śiva, one shall never again undergo rebirths.
He who desires to undergo initiation without knowing these truths undergoes fruitless exertion; he shall certainly not obtain its fruit.
Cessation is to be known as earth, and support is said to be water;
obstacle is declared to consist of fire, and wind is celebrated as peace.
That which transcends peace is the void; it is supreme, peaceful, and undecaying.
Having known that, O Mahāsena, one should initiate both oneself and others.
One should establish cessation in the heart, indeed stability with the head-mantra,
obstacles in the crest-lock, and peace with the armor-mantra.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the *prasāda* [offering] into the supreme ether beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*);
one should offer one hundred oblations for each [deity], or indeed offer five hundred.
O Six-faced One, afterwards, for the sake of complete purification, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Prāsāda mantra;
as an expiation, one should offer eight oblations each in successive order.
The knower of mantras should perform the fire-oblation with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra), as previously understood;
thus the initiation is completed, having dispensed with [the rites of] birth and so forth.
Yet, even by performing this sacrifice, practitioners are not liberated from the bondage of birth;
therefore, this sacrifice must not be disclosed and should be guarded with great effort.
This is the secret of all tantras, the supreme consecration;
for one thus purified by consecration, the state of Śiva arises with certainty.
Kārtika said:
Skanda said:
"For all this that has been specified becomes partless (*niṣkala*) by means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Thus, O Maheśvara, he is united with that [deity] by means of the temple (*prāsāda*). This is an additional reading found in one manuscript.
O Lord, having performed the placement (nyāsa) beginning with the womb (yoni), and having also extracted the western [mantra],
please explain the sequence of purification according to the rule.
The Lord said:
O Guha, those seventeen who have been mentioned were indeed questioned by you;
I shall now describe, in due order, the seed that was assigned to each.
The womb-seed (yonibīja), the heart-mantra, and the kalpa-mantra, yellow in color, are to be applied in due order;
likewise, one should perform worship, sprinkling, and striking.
One should indeed perform the withdrawal and the union, as well as the placement,
and again perform the worship and the conception of the embryo.
O Six-faced One, birth, authority, enjoyment, and likewise dissolution [occur] within one's own principle through a hundred oblations performed with the heart-mantra.
Likewise, one should sever the bonds with the Astra-mantra and perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before;
thereafter, the opening of the door should be performed in due order with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *ṛ*, excluding the neuter vowels,
these vowels of the *ātmatattva* are proclaimed as five pairs.
O child, they should first be purified by means of the *bhūta* mantras and so forth, with permission;
likewise, the non-existence of the *bhūtas*, the *tattvas*, and the *gandha* [mantras] and others, in their proper order.
Smell, taste, form, touch, and sound as the fifth—
these, abiding in their respective subtle elements (tanmātras), one should offer into the fire in successive order.
O Six-faced One, the Gandharvas, the oblation, and the flavor are the manifestations of existence;
these are declared to be the fire-principles (tejas-tattva), and one should offer the seeds of touch as the oblation.
Having joined the word "śabda" with the word "śabda," they are encapsulated by the heart-mantra;
this is indeed prescribed for the extraction, the sprinkling, and likewise for the striking.

It should be performed in successive order, joined with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*; likewise, another [version] reads "and the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) as well. And the withdrawal of the principles (*tattvas*) must be performed according to the proper sequence.
In each and every reality, this is the ritual action; this indeed is the sequence of the rite.
Whatever seed is prescribed for whom, that very one is the sequence of the rite for him.
O child, when these are thoroughly purified, one attains the full ritual procedure;
otherwise, O Six-faced One, those who are devoid of the proper rite are not liberated at all.
The offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be performed accompanied by concentration (dhāraṇā);
O child, one should mentally contemplate the supreme nectar as it flows forth.
By him all those gods are nourished, for they have entered the mouth of Agni;
they all become bestowers of auspiciousness, being the applications of the Śiva-sacrifice. This [application] should indeed always be employed everywhere in the section on initiation.
But in the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga*, as well as in all purificatory rites, [this applies].
Kārttikeya said:
Regarding that liberation for the bound soul which you previously described to me:
where are my internal and external fetters situated?
In what place does that [state] which destroys the two-fold [bondage] exist, and of what nature is the departure of the soul (saghnotkrānti)?
What are the sacrificial animals (paśu) according to the instruction? O Maheśvara, please tell me.
Īśvara said:
Having grasped the first [syllable] with the second within oneself,
the wise one leads it to that location by means of a fist.
By means of the equinox, however, those two [movements] reach equality within a single day in the realm of Śiva; otherwise, they proceed separately.
Then, being abandoned by their own nature, they become applicable to him.
Whatever is performed that is inexpressible and devoid of conceptualization (or, according to another reading, "free from doubt") would be in vain; however,
an action performed with a specific purpose in mind undoubtedly bestows liberation.
Just as people perform rites for averting misfortune (kautukāghna) directed toward whatever they desire,
one enjoys the fruits accordingly; however, that which is not so specified bestows liberation.
O child, during a solar eclipse, when it is joined with the equinox (viṣuva) and severed at the end of the length, then one should certainly cause it to ascend.
By this, the snares are knotted together like clusters of jewels on a thread;
that lotus, which destroys the sins of the heart, has its stalk extended by the mind.
Having perceived that [object], one should effect its severance through the activity of the mind; one should cut off the mind with the mind.
When the mind is severed by the mind, the living being attains absolute isolation (kevalatā).
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord of Gods, abandon prolixity; speak in brief, so that by mere knowledge of it, one may liberate the bound soul (paśu) in an instant.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the truth by which liberation will certainly be attained through the subtle application perceived by yoga, for the knower of mantras.
O Mahāsena, having understood that the life-force consists of wind, it is impelled by the power of mantras through the divine path of yoga; thus should one know it, O wise one.
By means of the yoga of the equinox, one should deposit the eternal state;
having attained the yoga of the equinox, who would not be released from bondage?

The earth, water, fire, air, and ether do not indeed strike; rather, it is the knower, whose self is the deity presiding over the mind, who, having understood the qualities such as sound and the rest along with the winds, becomes the liberator and is liberated.
Indeed, connected to the openings of the channels, they extend upward from the nose and downward;
all are provided with two knots and joined at the interior of the gateway of *huṃ phaṭ*.
Then, impelled by the sound of the mantra, they ascend upwards;
at the time of initiation, the wise one should join them with the *udghāta*s as before.
With a mind focused on the worlds to be conquered by the earth, he should grasp [the elements] both externally and internally;
however, in each respective principle (tattva), they must be separated from the ego (ahaṃkāra).
O child, one should cause those who have slain a Brahmin to hear this; having practiced it twice with a focused mind, as uttered by the words of the mantra-lore, they shall not undergo rebirth again.
At the time of initiation,
having joined the individual soul (jīva), which rests upon all the pathways, to the extension of the sun at the tip of the nose, twelve finger-breadths [from the heart].
"O child, having struck [the heart] as before, the seizing should be as previously described.
Having pierced and entered, one should place the light; one should purify that reality by means of reality. Thus it is in one manuscript.
[The] reading:
Having pierced [the path], having gone to the end of the page), one should place the fire; one should then merge that reality (tatva) into reality (tatva).
Having encapsulated the *śakti* with the [mantra] ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should deposit it.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the section on Time (Kālākhyaprakaraṇa) within the Vātula Tantra, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
I shall proclaim the consecration in brief, and not in detail,
for the benefit of the foremost of practitioners, as it has issued forth from the mouth of Śiva.
O Lord, one should indeed have a single earthen jar smeared with sandalwood paste,
placed within a fold of *brahmapatra* leaves or a lotus leaf.
Having prepared it with all medicinal herbs and adorned with all fragrant incenses,
[he should place] a jar consisting of all jewels and embellished with all kinds of gems.
Having recited the Nināda mantra one hundred and eight times,
and having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should perform the consecration.
On an auspicious lunar mansion, day, and moment, accompanied by favorable omens,
amidst the sounds of many auspicious proclamations and the blaring of conchs and musical instruments.
With various sounds of the Veda accompanied by dance and song,
once permitted and consecrated, he becomes a teacher who severs the bonds [of worldly existence].
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Kālottara, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
I shall now explain this subtle wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra) in its proper sequence:
from below the navel arises the bulb (kanda), and from it the sprouts [of the channels] have emerged.
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated in the center of the navel;
by them, the body is pervaded on all sides—horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
For these ten principal channels are arranged like the spokes of a wheel, namely:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśas are recorded;
likewise Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī as the tenth.
These ten channels are proclaimed as the carriers of the vital breaths:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
Prāṇa is the first among these nine, and he is their lord as well.
Prāṇa is that which consists of breath; prāṇa is the emission toward filling. Abiding in the chest of living beings, it constantly fills [them].
For it is through this that exhalation and inhalation occur, and the life-force (jīva) is supported by it;
since it carries out the departure [from the body], it is therefore proclaimed as "prāṇa."
The *apāna* wind, however, carries food and drink downward;
because it conveys semen and urine, it is celebrated as *apāna*.
The wind named Samāna brings to equilibrium within the limbs the yellow, the consumed, the smelled, the red, the bile, phlegm, and wind.
The wind named Udāna causes the lower lip and the face to quiver, brings about agitation in the eyes and limbs, and afflicts the vital points (marmas).
Vyāna destroys the limbs; Vyāna is the agitator of diseases. It is said that the destruction of pleasure is old age, and it is called Vyāna.
The vital winds that do not destroy life have been described; now I shall tell you those that destroy the name.
Nāga is said to be present in belching, and Kūrma is situated in the opening of the eyes.
Kūrkara cries out when there is agitation, and Devadatta yawns; Dhanañjaya remains in the camp and does not leave even for one who is dead.
This very group of winds, situated heart to heart and established in the navel-cakra,

constantly breathes through inhalation, exhalation, and coughing; it is perpetually born in small measure from the chest and the lower body, and it is ever assailed by trembling and whirling, as well as by the animal-like state of one who has fallen into calamity due to the deficiency of youth.
The host of winds causes the atoms to tremble, and all beings play; I shall describe to you in its entirety the wheel exactly as it exists.
Just as this ten-spoked wheel is known through its division, so too is this [reality] understood.
The living being revolves like a wheel through the ten stations in successive order.
Deluded, they do not at all understand that he is the life-force of the world of the living;
because it moves in ten ways, it is proclaimed as the "wheel" (cakra).
It is renowned as the "wheel of channels" (nāḍīcakra), by which that [consciousness] indeed transmigrates;
it is an eight-petalled lotus in the center of the space of the heart, with a pericarp at its core.
In that [lotus] was indeed Uparicara, whose luster was like the sun, the moon, and gold, and who possessed power;
among those powers, Śakti was the first-born. That state of Śakti is a portion of Śiva, and within the lotus of Śiva’s satisfaction, there is the Puruṣa merged in penance.
It is empty on both sides, its nature as an instrument grasped by the pincers of the vital winds.
Like a dry leaf carried by the wind, he is led away from his station;
yet the digit (kalā) remains revolving within the lotus, bound to its own inherent portion.
Struck by the ball, it constantly performs leaping and falling;
through the yoga of the Lord, there is likewise a transition into the three directions by means of the connection with the left.
Due to the conjunction of the sun, there is the southern or northern course (ayana) resulting from the union with the [solar] birth-sign;
the two ayanas, left and right, are like two nostrils, and they call the equinox (viṣuva) that which occurs when they are joined in pairs.
The transition from here to there is described by those who know this;
the solar path is called *sabhya*, while the lunar path is known as the other.

Indeed, the Saura [Sun] yoga is auspicious for the performance of ablutions; it is also present when the fire is joined with the one called Viyu [Wind], situated as previously described, even in the case of a woman.
In the southeast direction, there arises the affliction of hunger for one who is radiant;
in the south is the southern portion, and in the southwest, the demonic portion is indicated.
When the leaf has gone to Varuṇa, it is established as Vāruṇa; when it has gone to the Maruts, it attains the state of the Maruts;
when it is in the Saumya [leaf], it is the Yakṣa-state; and in the Īśa [leaf], it is declared to be the state of Īśa.
In the realm of Brahmā, one attains the state of Brahmā; below that, O Lord of Serpents, is established the state of Viṣṇu.
Toward whichever direction one departs, one enters into the corresponding state of that [deity].
"Through the conjunction of the spaces between the petals, it appears as the self of the empty garland.
Thus, indeed, the movement of the person (*pudgala*) has been declared here as primary within the mandala of the movement of the channels (*nāḍī*).
Kārttikeya said:
He is the life-force of the world of living beings, by whom [all] know according to reality (or: as it should be known, according to another reading).
O Mahādeva, I have a doubt; be gracious, O wielder of the trident!
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the description of the individual soul known as Puruṣa;
I shall tell it to you without doubt, especially out of affection for my son.
The transits and the equinoxes, the days, nights, and years,
the intercalary month, the debt, as well as the night-credit and the wealth.
A deficient night (*ūnarātra*) is coughing; an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is yawning. Debt is a cough, while exhalation is said to be wealth.
The northern should be known as the right, designated as the left and the right;
in the middle, however, is declared the equinox (viṣuva), which issues forth from both nostrils.
Four equinoxes are proclaimed for yogins day after day:
at midday, at midnight, as well as at sunrise and sunset.
Furthermore, its transition, as well as its own place and non-place,
consists of the *iḍā*, the *suṣumṇā*, and the *amā* combined together.
The Suṣumṇā is established in the middle limb, the Iḍā in the left, and the Amā indeed in the right limb; this is called the Saṃkrānti.
The upward-moving breath is indeed the day, and the downward-moving breath is the night;
he who knows these ten divisions of the breath is a knower of the Veda.
The expansion situated within the body is considered a lunar eclipse;
however, when that [expansion] transcends the body, they know it as a solar eclipse due to the obstruction.
Since Śiva, residing within one's own body, utters [the mantra] spontaneously,
therefore that alone is called "japa" for those men who know the reality.
Indeed, the lord of yogis performs a recitation numbering twenty-two thousand six hundred in a single day and night.
I shall explain *prāṇāyāma* to you in its entirety in brief.
One who does not know this which has been stated— the *praṇava* with its vowel— is not a knower of yoga.
Having filled the abdomen with air to the desired extent, this is *prāṇāyāma*; in the *pūraka*, it is the filling of the body.
Having closed all the gates [of the body] and being free from inhalation and exhalation, one should remain like a completely filled jar; this is *kumbhaka*, the breath-retention of *prāṇāyāma*.
Then the knower of yoga should draw the breath upward with a single inhalation;
joined with the practice of exhalation, he should cause the upward-moving air to circulate.
This is known as recaka, the vital breath that causes doubt;
it is that which resides in the lotus situated at the heart with its face turned downwards.
That lotus indeed blossoms when filled by the *pūraka* [inhalation];
the lotus becomes an upward-flowing stream when restrained by the *kumbhaka* [retention].
Ejected by the *recaka* breath, which indeed severs life,
he leaves the heart-lotus and becomes established in the upward flow.
The exhaled breath indeed goes upward, piercing the knot in an instant;
having pierced the door of the skull, the life-force is exhaled upward.
Having attained the state of Sadāśiva, one shall not undergo birth again;
the expansion [of the breath] is performed for him alone, and never for anyone else.
That has been declared by me in brief as the life-force of the world of living beings.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the "Classification of Knowledge," in the Kālottara, consisting of one hundred and fifty [verses].
That Kuṇḍalinī which is joined with the Moon, Fire,
and Sun should be known as being situated in the region of the heart-lotus, abiding in the form of a sprout.
There, one should perform the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) as taught through the practice of repetition;
the best of practitioners should contemplate nectar flowing therein.
One who desires accomplishment and is composed in mind should contemplate the entire world, both moving and stationary, as consisting of Agni and Soma, yet in its opposite form.
The wise one should contemplate his own body as having two forms and being incomparable;
he should contemplate whatever action has been prescribed for whichever form.
The square, the half-moon, the circle consisting of three parts,
the void, the vajra-end, the triangle, and the dot-void are thus proclaimed.
Yellow, white, red, and black— this is the fulfiller of all desires (the *syāmavarṇa* reading is preferred).
O Six-faced One, he who knows this reality is a knower of reality.
O Guha, for one who practices samādhi in both its collective and individual aspects,
there is no doubt that the fruits of this world and the next will be attained without delay.
Having meditated upon her who exists in five states, who abides in her own reality, whose nature is endowed with splendor (or:
who is endowed with the splendor of existence),
one should proceed to the crown of the head and fix the mind there.
Stambhana, āpyāyana, utkarma, vidveṣa, uccāṭana, and so forth,
as well as the gentle rite that generates affection— these have been taught to you, O Six-faced One.
O Six-faced One, one who desires accomplishment should, with a concentrated mind, meditate upon the triad residing in the *bindu*, having unified oneself and the Lord.
One who practices this nectar-like meditation, which faces in all directions,
shall in no long time become a partaker of the fruit of perfection.
O Six-faced One, how can practitioners perform yoga without knowing the Sṛṣṭinyāsa? They are merely striking at empty space with their fists.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Kālottara consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
I shall now explain once more the process of emanation in detail and in its proper sequence,
according to how the Lord, who is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), is united.
The syllable *oṃ* is situated at the head and center of the month that produces the arts and sets all mantras in motion; the syllable *oṃ* pervades everywhere.
The syllable *oṃ* is the first line; the Lord creates the syllable *aṃ*.
That is indeed the digit (*kalā*) of the obstacles, established within every phoneme.
That which is seen as the *oṃkārābhā* kalā of the syllable *oṃ* should be known by the name *Pratiṣṭhā*, arising from the imperishable within the syllable *oṃ*.
But at his head shall be Ghanā, subtle in form and stainless.
The letter *ma* is its manifestation; that digit is named Nivṛtti.
The syllable *oṃ* conjoined with the *bindu* is the dissolution at the summit of the *oṃ*.
That line alone in the sky is the extinguished state; it is that digit, the supreme peace.
Through union, it shines forth clearly, abiding both in the partless and in the possessed-of-parts.
At the crown of the head is the syllable Oṃ; from the syllable Oṃ, the sound "Oṃ" arises.
That supreme, subtle peace arises together with the Bindu.
The light of a lamp and such shines forth, accompanied by sparks and flames;
that [light] invariably proceeds in three ways: toward Śiva, toward obstacles, or toward the ground.
Peace, obstacle-removal, establishment, and cessation—
this is that digit (kalā) which is the linear digit (rekhiṇī) fallen there together with the bindu.
He is declared to be the Lord of All, Śiva, the God of Gods, the Great Lord (Maheśvara);
that which is his primordial seed-syllable is celebrated as Bindu and Nāda.
One should not abandon the supreme state, which is eternal, fixed, and imperishable;
having cast the *bindu* into the belly, one protects it like a mother.
Above that, on the left side, the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu is proclaimed;
on its right side, the seed-syllable of Brahmā is proclaimed.
Situated in the left and right wombs, it is one and yet becomes threefold; the central line that stands between the two dots on either side is indeed that very [line].
Therein dwells the subtle Lord Śiva, the benefactor who remains hidden;
this is the supreme seed, O God, the Great Lord Maheśvara within the womb of Śakti.
From which proceeds the subtle mantra and tantra, including all that is moving and unmoving—
the unmanifest, supreme, and subtle, the stainless embodiment of power.
She who, having realized Śiva—who is without beginning or end—is not born again;
that which is the seed of the right side is indeed the supreme power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
That seed-syllable is the supreme Brahman, wherein He remains hidden;
it is the supreme Bindu residing in the left, for that indeed is the supreme Kriyā-śakti.
Therein Viṣṇu is hidden by his own seed-syllable, subtle and stainless;
this is the god established in emission, who was indeed emitted by Śambhu.
They do not perceive that hidden [reality] by which the moving and unmoving world was created;
from emission (visarga) creation is born, and he alone is the Lord, the Sovereign.
Because he has emitted the true seed, he is called Visarga;
or rather, by him the entire world, both stationary and moving, is filled.
By means of a multitude of rays, hundreds and thousands of times over,
Śakti creates and likewise devours, acting as both the uniter and the disuniter.
But by means of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the Blessed One does not grasp the embodied soul;
from the emission (visarga) creation is born, and together with the bindu comes dissolution.
The knowledge of the reality of nirvāṇa is not within the scope of extensive elaboration.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verses] on the Knowledge of Time.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, the withdrawal consists of the first [letter] placed within the enclosure at the end.
Having likewise offered oblations at the end of each *mātṛkā* letter, one by one and separately.
Kārttikeya said:
Both the dissolution and the creation of the All-pervading Lord have been fully described.
Tell me truly about the loss of their destination for those who have been initiated.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, listen now to the truth regarding the yoga that causes the ruin of one's state for those who are deceitful, dishonest, cruel, untruthful, and fond of quarreling.
O Six-faced One, when one attains the Nāda joined with the Bindu of the principles (tattvas),
then Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī swiftly enter into union.
Having placed [the breath] upon the head and contracted it by means of the expansion of Śiva,
and having visualized it with the mind as before, one's own course of existence ceases.
O Vatsa, the yoga that causes the loss of one's state has been described by you just as it is.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] section on the Knowledge of Time.
Īśvara said:
If one, having aroused the sound with clarity, recites the *saptaja* mantra, perfection arises within six months for one engaged in yoga; of this there is no doubt.
Through the recitation of the *gamāgama* mantra, the destruction of all sins shall occur;
within six months, the sovereign power of the qualities beginning with *aṇimā* will be attained—of this there is no doubt.
Having understood the coming and going, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having become identified with that very [reality] immediately, one shall attain perfection within six months.
The subtle, the gross, and the supreme have been described by me as *prasāda*;
those by whom *prasāda* is understood do not [need to] understand Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of *prasāda*;
the knower of mantras should always discern it as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*).
The short [form] burns away sins; the long [form] bestows liberation;
and the prolated [form], endowed with a bindu upon the head, effects nourishment.
Three gross divisions have been declared: subjugation (*vaśya*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*).
When [the syllable] is in the *pluta* (protracted) state, it always effects subjugation; there is no doubt in this matter.
When the long *uccāṭana* (expulsion) is proclaimed, it is joined with the syllable *phaṭ*;
joined with the syllable *phaṭ*, it shall cause death—of this there is no doubt.
The syllable *phaṭ* at the beginning and at the end of a short [mantra] is prescribed for killing.
At the beginning and at the end of the heart [mantra], it is prescribed for the application of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*). One should indeed summon [the target].
One who is properly engaged will certainly attract [the object] even from a distance of a hundred yojanas. (Pāda)
In this way, one should attract the object of practice after having truly understood its name;
the fires of the practitioner are said to be superior, while those of the object of practice are inferior.
Having understood this, the wise practitioner certainly performs the attraction;
however, without correctly understanding this, practitioners do not achieve success at all.
Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should cause the *argha* offering for the mantra to be presented;
having offered the *argha*, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra.
On the right side of the deity (or in the [right] part of the image), one should remain and recite five hundred thousand [times].
At the conclusion of the recitation, there should be a ghee oblation of ten thousand [offerings].
Thus nourished, the mantra becomes fit for ritual action;
then the mantras I have spoken will be accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
Whoever recites [the mantra] one million times, the knowledge-beings dwelling in that place will quickly come under their control; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Having recited [the mantra] three million five hundred thousand times, the inhabitants of ten villages come under one's control,
both in person and with their wealth.
By twenty-five hundred thousand recitations, one shall bring the sense objects under control;
by thirty hundred thousand recitations, even the lord of a mandala shall become submissive.
By reciting thirty-five hundred thousand times, one shall bring the earth under control;
by forty hundred thousand times, one beholds Maheśvara here in this world.
By fifty lakhs of recitations, one becomes equal to the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnādharasama);
there the mantra-practitioner rejoices until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the aeon.
Having recited it ten million times, the wise man certainly beholds Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Kālottara, the Knowledge of Time, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord, O Master, even though you are free from affliction, there remains a doubt regarding knowledge and realization:
how do they know that knowledge, and how is the object of knowledge described?
Īśvara said:
O Six-faced One, having first understood the support (*ādhāra*), one should thereafter perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
O wise one, a learned man who knows both the support and that which is supported (*ādhaya*) is competent in all ritual acts.

The support is called the city, and that which is supported is said to be the Lord (Īśa). For he who rules over the northeast is remembered here as the Lord (Īśa)— he who rules over something is the Lord of that.
The wise man who, having realized the Lord, always exults within himself,
moves both downward and upward, joined with the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, and ego— this is known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
As long as they are not liberated by these means, how can they be released from bondage?
One should renounce sound and touch for Brahmā, and one should indeed renounce taste for Keśava.
One should abandon form and smell in Rudra; the intellect and ego in Īśvara;
and having abandoned the mind and the bindu in Śiva, one who is liberated by these becomes Śiva himself.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Kālottara, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
I shall now explain, in due order, the ritual procedure of Kālacakra—
that which is renowned as Kālacakra, by which one awakens to time.
By the movement of one *iḍā* for a day and night, he lives for three years;
by the movement of two [channels] for a day and night, he lives for two years.
O Six-faced One, he who wanders for one day and night lives for one year; he who wanders for one day lives for one month.
"It is the certainty of the scripture that death occurs after six months;
however, by the practice of the two sacrifices for two months, he lives for one day and night."
Just as the left [channel] is, so too is the right, and the middle one likewise;
this is declared to be the Kālacakra, especially out of affection for my son.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [chapter] of the Kālajñāna.
Kārttikeya said:
O God, those who are liberated and established in a prowess equal to Śiva—
desire to hear from you in truth about their ultimate state.
The Lord said:
Just as two young maidens might affectionately consort with one another, yet when they are joined in union, one attains pleasure while the other (the second) experiences suffering.
"Tell me, what is that pleasure which arises from conjunction?
O blessed lady, I shall tell you of the pleasure that proceeds [from such union]:
having seen her returned once again, one embraces her with longing."
Tell me now that which was previously indicated by you.
"What you have asked cannot be told; it is impossible.
Then she spoke in anger: "Why [do you say this], O speaker of truth?"

Whether it be of such a kind or that kind, O auspicious lady, people do not know pleasure as it truly is—arising from the union of the senses with their objects—except through the medium of conceptualization; otherwise, they do not perceive it at all.
For one who speaks otherwise, no conviction whatsoever arises;
because that which is unmanifested cannot be described as happiness.
In no long time at all, that happiness was attained by me;
O auspicious lady, what you have told me is exactly so, there is no doubt.
O auspicious one, forgive that unpleasant thing which was spoken by me out of ignorance and delusion; please accept me as you did before.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
You have explained the knowledge of time (kāla-jñāna), having defined the characteristics of its own limbs and so forth.
That which is ordained by the Vedas as the true Self has the characteristic of being for the benefit of others.
"Speak according to what I know: that all beings are like oneself."
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the truth regarding the certain life of living beings:
one tooth withers away, while the remaining ones remain naturally moist by their very nature.
The lifespan of such a person is declared to be three years, without a doubt:
two years when two teeth fall out, and one year when three teeth fall out.
But with more [merit], he shall live for six months; there is no doubt in this matter.
It is said that during the five months, those with five tusks exist by their very nature.
When a man's entire row of teeth becomes parched, he has six months of life remaining,
with his body held together by only six teeth.
And one month is specified for his life; there is no doubt in this matter.
When two lines dry up, his life is reckoned at half that duration.
If the lower lip should wither, that very row of teeth [is the omen];
since his life is said to last for the number of directions (ten), that man [shall live] for five days.
The teeth and lips, the palate and tongue, and the mouth become parched;
death will occur immediately—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus, the knowledge of time has been briefly declared by me to you;
it is taught as a secret, a purification on the path to liberation.
Just as it is with oneself, so too should it be known with respect to others, following that sequence.
Kārttikeya said:
How is it pervasive below, above, and across? How so, O All-pervading Lord? Tell me this true nature out of compassion, O Supreme Lord.
Īśvara said:
As long as a living being remains within the body, [the breath] stays below;
once it has emerged, the Lord (pāda variant), residing within, pervades transversely and is established everywhere.
The living being situated on the three paths resides within all bodies;
without knowing [this], one is not liberated, even if one should attain absorption into that.
Having three paths and three bases, it exists within all bodies.
He who understands this pervasion in this way is undoubtedly a pervader;
O Lord, for him there is no birth from a womb, as it is thus revealed.
One wanders in saṃsāra as long as one does not find pervasiveness;
having known that all-pervading God, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Just as a grass-leech has gone as far as the tip of a blade of grass, remaining suspended above it without any further support, so does this living being remain.
O Guha, he who understands the threefold emptiness— the upper empty, the lower empty, and the middle empty which is free from affliction— is certainly liberated.
And its pervasion has been declared by me in brief, but not in detail;
therefore, there is nothing else whatsoever that could be the pervader even of the pervader.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall explain how the eightfold conviction arises:
namely, the blazing of fire without fuel, and likewise the climbing of trees.
It is the paralyzing of the fetters (prāṇas), the destruction of great sins,
the traversing of the sense-objects, and likewise the rendering [the senses] seedless.
It destroys the fever caused by planetary influences, and the eightfold nectar is the antidote;
knowing this, the knower of mantras attains renown everywhere.
Within the *praṇava*, there is the syllable *huṃ* situated in the midst of fire, as well as *hrau*;
it begins with *bahuṃ* and ends with *namaḥ*, impelled by the blazing of fire.
Oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ namaḥ.
The fire should be applied to the ear together with the simultaneous striking;
situated in the center of the circle of fire, it blazes through the application of the five syllables—of this there is no doubt.
The letter *u* is at the bottom of all, and the letter *ra* is joined above;
the letter *ru* is joined in the middle, illuminated by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) which destroys [all] sin.
This application, joined as before, is difficult to find on earth.
Oṃ hrauṃ uṃ namaḥ.
When the five empowered [arrows] are discharged upwards and strike, the tree is certainly felled;
furthermore, its nourishment occurs when the Vāruṇa [arrow] is stationed in the stream.
He remained established [in that state].
That tree lives again, exactly as it was before.
The letter *ū* is as before at the bottom, and the letter *ha* is situated above; such is the reading in another manuscript. (This line is at the bottom of the page)
And in such a case, it is not that [sound] for him; rather, it is [the sound] devoid of the letter *ra*.

Oṃ hauṃ oṃ, salutation! This is indeed the procedure for nourishment (*āpyāyana*), illuminated by five dots (*bindu*). It begins with the letter *ī*, with *haum* in the middle, and likewise again in the center of the fire (*vahnimadhya*).
The application at the time of the equinox causes the paralysis of the bonds:
*oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ namaḥ*.
By seven hundred upward breaths (*udghāta*), they fall; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, listen to how his departure occurs:
he is joined by the syllable *hrīṃ* and directed into the midst of what has been spoken.
In the *Prāṇānusvāra-dīpa*, it begins with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with *namaḥ*, and does not contain the seed-syllable of fire (*raṃ*).
It is: *oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ namaḥ*.
Should the knower of mantras employ [this rite] for the purpose of raising up all beings?
The seed-syllable is entered by the individual soul (jīva), situated at the end of the letter *ha*;
it stands in the middle as before, and its life-force consists of the two *namaḥ* syllables accompanied by the wind and the drop (*vāyu-bindu*).
Oṃ hrīṃ svāṃ hrīṃ namaḥ.
Just as weight arises when a jar is being lifted,
so too is the wind employed in the middle, while the beginning and the end are likewise joined.
For this brings about lightness; one should perform it with ten thousand [recitations].
The letter *sva* and the letter *ha* are illuminated by the vowel *ī*.
One should place the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and the end, and employ it in the middle;
by means of exactly eight hundred *udghātas*, the restraint of the sense objects is certainly achieved.
Just as it has been taught regarding the blazing of the fire for the purpose of rendering [the seed-syllables] seedless,
here a distinction is prescribed by means of five hundred *udghātas*.

Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, followed by the syllable *huṃ*, then *hrauṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *phaṭ*, and finally *namaḥ* at the end— this is the method of grasping [the mantra], which is beneficial for destroying [obstacles].
The application in the Varuna path is with eight hundred *udghātas*,
beginning with the *praṇava*, followed by *hrauṃ phaṭ*, then *phaṭ* again, and finally *hu hu phaṭ paṭ*.
Likewise, by means of the Vāruṇa [mantra], one quickly destroys fever in the ears;
indeed, the practice for the destruction of fever consists of exactly eight hundred recitations of the *udghāta*.
I have explained the application of the eight conditions.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Kālajñāna*, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The whole (sakala), the partless (niṣkala), the void (śūnya), the one consisting of parts (kalātman),
the pure ether (khamala), the destroyer (kṣapaṇa), that which abides within destruction (kṣayāntastha), and the throat-lip (kaṇṭhoṣṭha) are remembered as the eighth.
The Śiva-tattva is proclaimed as being endowed with grace (prasāda), joined with the group of six, accompanied by the end of the six, complete, and residing within all beings.
The Lord himself emerges, having cast off the body he had assumed;
one should know that Śiva to be partless and devoid of the six qualities.
Having pierced through the inhalation and exhalation, one should remain in the body like a piece of wood;
one should know that thread to be empty, yet cause it to be performed by means of the heart.
That reality which is heard on earth through the kissing mouth—one should know it to extend up to the path of the digits (kalādhvan); now listen to me regarding that which resides in space.
One should know that which is proclaimed as the end of the upward-sounding breath when it has ceased; it resides there in the sky, the void adorned with space.
Having heard that the Lord, the Teacher of the World, had turned away his face, he said, "It is a difficult penance";
thus it is remembered as the *kriyākṣapaṇa*.
One should know that which is proclaimed as the "lower" sound of the *kṣīṇa* [consonant] is the internal (*antastha*); it is traditionally remembered as being unpronounceable (*anuccārya*).
The eighth of the eight groups, the second of the seventh,
that which transcends the groups, the end of the six, and the fourth of the three in the seventh.
Furthermore, having joined the first with the sixth of the first, it is conjoined with Khaśekhara;
this is remembered as the eighth, consisting of gutturals and labials.
These divisions have been fully described as the means for attaining powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
that which is beyond utterance and free from doubt is designated as liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord Maheśvara, tell me: what is the nature of grace (prasāda), what is its pervasiveness (vyāpti), and what is its body?
The Lord said: He by whom [the disciples] do not understand grace, which has the five mantras as its great body and is endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, is not called an Ācārya.
If a guru performs initiation without correctly discerning the disciple's spiritual disposition (prasāda), he leads both the disciple and himself downward; of this there is no doubt.
The Guru who bestows initiation upon that [disciple] at the crest of the lotus of grace shall,
together with his disciples, attain union with Śiva.
The gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas, the kinnaras, apsarases, and siddhas— all these were produced from the palace.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; Candra, Indra, and Prajāpati;
Bṛhaspati, as well as Āditya, Śukra, Mandi, and Bhṛgu.
And whatever other living beings there are, all those produced within the palace,
as well as these and many other sages of firm vows—
They meditate upon the supreme Haṃsa, the grace that is beyond all names.
I shall describe its divisions, by knowing which one attains immortality.
They know that the eight obstructors (Saghna), joined with the [eight] digits (kalā), are born from the syllable *A*;
Vighna is born from the syllable *U*, while Vāma and Aghora are born from the syllable *M*.
The Puruṣa is to be known as born from the seed-syllable (bindu), while Īśāna is born from the crest (śikhā).
Thus, these five mantras are traditionally remembered as originating from the Prāsāda.
Ten thousand times ten million mantras of immeasurable power—by the grace of the sixth [deity], all of them become satisfied; of this there is no doubt.
Those mantras which are proclaimed as destroyers of the Maruts, Anala, and Śakra—
born from the lotus of the Prasāda— all possess unfailing power.
The obstructive [Sadyojāta] is to be known as earth; the left [Vāmadeva] is proclaimed as water;
the non-terrible [Aghora] is said to be fire; and the one-for-all (Tatpuruṣa) is remembered as air.
Space, however, is Īśa; he himself is the god Maheśvara.
From him was born Saghna, the Ṛgveda, and Vāmadeva, who possesses the Yajus.
The Sāmaveda is indeed Aghora, while Puruṣa is said to be the Atharvaveda;
that which is the fifth, supreme, subtle, all-pervading space is Sadāśiva.
Brahmā is indeed proclaimed as Saghna, Viṣṇu as Vāma,
Rudra as the deity of Aghora, and Īśvara is remembered as Puruṣa.
Īśāna is the deity of the gods, the primordial God who is firmly established;
he is the sixth, the supreme reality, situated beyond all similarities and qualities.
His body should not be described as being composed of the qualities born of material nature;
for he has ascended the supreme ladder that leads to the five purificatory rites.
When the object of knowledge was known all at once by him whose inner self was struck with wonder,
then he was thus liberated, for that very state had been realized.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Kālottara*, consisting of one hundred and fifty verses.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to this knowledge that is most difficult to attain;
I shall tell you that which has not been declared to anyone—that *Anākhyā* (the Unnameable) for your sake.
The manifest (sakala) is to be known as residing within the body, while the unmanifest (niṣkala) is devoid of the body;
this [reality], which exists as something indescribable everywhere, is accessible through the instruction of a Guru.
He who should utter "Haṃsa, Haṃsa"— the Haṃsa is the god Sadāśiva,
who is directly perceived everywhere through that which is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
Just as oil resides in sesame seeds and fragrance is inherent in a flower,
so does that [Self] abide within this body of a person, both externally and internally.
Just as someone with a torch in hand might discard it after seeing an object, so too,
having perceived the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should then abandon that knowledge.

The flower is indeed the manifest (sakala) form of the obstacle, while its fragrance is the unmanifest (niṣkala); the tree is indeed the manifest form of the obstacle, while its shade is the unmanifest.
Established thus everywhere through the state of both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*),
one perceives the manifest within the manifest and likewise the unmanifest within the unmanifest.
The three-mora, the two-mora, and likewise the one-mora;
the other is the subtle half-mora, and even half of that is the supreme-non-supreme (parāpara).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself—
the entire [deity] is recited as having five aspects and five deities.
