Brahmā has his station in the heart; Viṣṇu is established in the throat;
Rudra is situated in the middle of the palate; and Maheśvara resides in the forehead.
Śiva is at the tip of the nose; beyond that is the supreme-non-supreme (parāpara);
there is nothing higher than the supreme—this is the certainty of the scripture.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
Kārtikeya said: "O Mahādeva, how does his coming and going occur, or by whom is he led? I have a great doubt; please explain it to me according to the truth."
The Lord said:
The individual soul is led by Śakti; having reached that [state], it does not return.
O Ṣaṇmukha, I shall fully explain its end; listen to it according to the truth.
But having obstructed that [breath] which has transcended the body at the tip of the nose at a distance of twelve finger-breadths,
the Lord, stationed there, should cause it to pervade up to the end of that [universe].
Even when the mind is directed elsewhere and the gaze is cast elsewhere,
the yoga of practitioners nevertheless proceeds without interruption.
This is that supreme secret; this is that supreme state. This is the supreme Brahman; this is the supreme syllable.
"There is nothing higher than this, nothing more auspicious than this,
and nothing more to be known than this," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
This nectar of the knowledge of Śiva has indeed been declared by the God of gods in brief, rather than at length, as the definitive determination of the supreme syllable.
This true nature of Śiva has issued forth from the mouth of Śiva;
it is a secret more secret than the secret, a secret that must be guarded with great effort.
It must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has no son; however,
it may be given to one devoted to the gods, the sacred fire, and the guru, and to one intent upon the worship of the Śiva-scriptures.
This knowledge must never be given to others;
those who give it go to hell, and [the knowledge] will never attain success.
I have truly declared to you, my child, what is known as the nectar of Śiva;
having understood this, O wise one, conduct yourself according to your pleasure.
Whether a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—
wherever situated, the wise one (the yogi) who knows the supreme syllable is always [liberated].

One who is powerless against sense objects reaches the auspicious state near the end of the body through the knowledge of this very scripture; even a human being who is powerless against sin [attains it].
One is not tainted by the merit or sin of those rich in self-sacrifice, even the killing of a Brahmin;
the instigator and the awakener are indeed remembered as secondary to the one who liberates (the second).
Thus, these three types of teachers should be known on the surface of the earth:
the prompter (codaka) shall show the path, and the awakener (bodhaka) shall point out the station.
But the giver of liberation is that supreme state (or reality), knowing which one does not return.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
The Lord said:
The direct sacrifice is for the capable, and it is concise rather than elaborate;
by performing this sacrifice, men attain the eternal, immutable state.
Between the navel and the private parts, O Skanda, resides that which is called the syllable *oṃ*;
it is the support of all the channels and is joined with the *haṃsa*.
Of the seventy-two thousand channels that are extended and unceasingly established,
the great channel among them, O King, is renowned as the *rasanā*.
O Skanda, situated in its center are five downward-facing lotuses;
they are all joined by two knots and endowed with deities.
Having raised those lotuses upward, one should pierce them with the trident of Śiva;
having struck them with the trident of Śiva, one should exhale the upward-moving breath.
Accompanied by the exhalation (recaka), the individual soul indeed goes to Śiva.
All this has been fully explained in brief rather than in detail;
furthermore, the upward conjunction has been described by me as before.
But the embodied soul itself should perceive that four-part *bindu*;
one who knows the path always perceives it during the two solstices and the two equinoxes.
Having first performed yoga through pūraka, kumbhaka, and recaka breath-control,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa according to the rules with the limbs of Śiva, one becomes Śiva.
Having recited all the mantras and cast off the body, one shall be reborn;
for that supreme seed-syllable should be placed within the center of the body.
Having meditated upon the weapon-mantra (astra) as being located at the head, one should employ it there;
then, having deposited the causal reality (tattva), which is Śiva, one should worship it.
One should worship the one situated above with black and dark-red flowers;
thereby, an eternal performance of a hundred thousand worships is accomplished.
"O Lord, I and Śiva are indeed identical in all principles; of this there is no doubt.
[I am] the author of the entire collection of principles, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva."
Having thus performed the worship with perfumes, flowers,
and unhusked rice, Māyā— having reached the further shore of the teachings of Śiva— is declared to have completed the remaining rites.
Having uttered both [mantras] from the east, one should exhale in that sequence;
there is no other place for worship considered superior to this.
At the conclusion of yoga, one should cause [the disciple] to offer [the oblation] while supporting the head with a prostration;
O child, during a solar eclipse, the worship becomes manifest.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
In which [face], at what time, and in which mouth does the preceptor, the destroyer of the bonds of the bound soul, [attain] the five faces in the Śiva-fire, the supreme essence of Śiva?
In what does one perform formative actions? In what does one offer up sins?
In what does one perform sacrifice? In what is the final oblation said to reside?
Furthermore, O Blessed One, you ought to explain in brief all this: into which mouth [of the fire] should one offer oblations of sin, and how does one purify oneself?
Īśvara said:
The nooses are proclaimed for all the nooses as being the eastern face;
one should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) with the northern [face], but with the western [face] during the sacrifice.
O Mahāsena, the rule for expiation is prescribed for this southern face;
for that upper face, the offering of vital breaths (prāṇāhuti) is prescribed.
One should not cause the oblation to be offered upon the back of the hands or feet;
the preceptor who knows the reality of the purification of the mouth is the one who bestows liberation.
Thus, an ācārya who is himself bound by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) cannot bestow liberation;
they return once more to the state of conditioned existence—this is the truth, my dear, there is no doubt.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, I shall now declare the extraction of the *liṅga* for those who have taken a lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhika*).
Having observed either a five-night or a three-night fast, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
Having observed the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the renunciation;
there, one should install the *yonicakra* according to the rite prescribed by the rules.
Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel provided with two navels,
and having joined them in reverse order, one should generate the *naiṣṭhika* therein.
The wise one should offer five oblations at each of the five stages using curd, in due order,
bestowing them by means of the heart-mantra alone through the process of withdrawal.
Having done this, one should generate the ultimate [deity] there as before;
indeed, having performed the emission and reabsorption of the *kāskanda* for the ultimate [deity].
By worshipping according to the principle of emanation and reabsorption, the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) becomes pure;
even if he is attached to sense objects, he is not tainted by the defects of karma.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
The Lord said:
I shall now fully describe the funeral rite (anteṣṭi) as it was spoken in former times:
having generated the Śiva-fire, one should subsequently purify the Śiva [liṅga].
Having purified [the image] with water mixed with clay as before, one should bathe it with ashes;
then, having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should purify it with the *astra* seed-syllable.
Having performed the reabsorbing oblation (*iṣṭi*), one should cause [the deity] to enter with water;
having first spread a layer of darbha grass, one should place the weapon-mantra (*astra*) everywhere.
Being well-composed, one should kindle the fire on all sides with the Astra-mantra,
using sandalwood and agalloch wood, along with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
But when [the obstacle] is present, the other rites should be performed according to one's desire;
having meditated upon the *āgneyī* concentration, the knower of mantras should burn [the obstacle] with the *astra* mantra.
But if, after the time of initiation, one should transgress the rules of conduct (samaya),
it constitutes a great sin against both the deity and one's own guru.
O Guha, for those who have not yet abandoned their doubts and for others who are dominated by the quality of rajas, this Aṅgeṣṭi has been taught for the purpose of removing their sins.
If he should violate this convention— whether it be one with which he is personally acquainted or one that is not—
he incurs the status of being a giver of a maiden, as does one who violates a formal agreement.
Therefore, through union with the Unconscious (asaṃjñā), the grasping occurs as before.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
The Lord said:
I shall now describe, in due order, the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) which destroys defects,
on a previously mentioned pure ground smeared with cow dung.
One should place a jar filled with fragrant substances in the northeast direction; it shall be auspicious and free from obstacles.
Then, having drawn a lotus on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇṍila), one should worship it;
for there are many obstacles in colored powder (rajas), O Guha, but on a sacrificial mound there are no obstacles.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the weapon-sacrifice (astra-yāga) upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
according to the scriptures, this weapon-sacrifice is prescribed everywhere, though in some cases it may be performed elsewhere.
On the rampart are the Karṇikā-lotus, as well as Dharma, Jñāna, and the others;
likewise, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, and the Śaktis.
Then, the wise one should construct it provided with a surrounding wall.
One should place the divine Pāśupata weapon upon the pericarp,
joined with twenty-eight kalās.

Having arranged the directions starting from the east according to the scriptures, one should place the rampart in sequence using the intermediate directions; one should establish the weapon-mantra at the intermediate points as the all-fulfilling rampart.
This is the most excellent seat of weapons (*astrapīṭha*), which is supreme for making [the ritual] free of defects;
externally, [it is arranged] in all ten directions on every side.
The vajra, the staff, the sword, as well as the noose and the goad;
the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus, respectively.
One should not place it within the enclosure of the Pāśupata [temple];
it should be one cubit in size on all sides and provided with four navel-marks.
One should perform its purification with a surrounding wall;
one should carry out the rites of birth, atonement, and the ritual procedure according to the rules.
Then, having offered the oblation beginning with *vrajra* using the previously prepared portions,
the wise one [should recite] *huṃ phaṭ vauṣaṭ*... [and so forth].
Standing there, one should draw [the target] by means of that enclosure; of this there is no doubt.
In the homa of initiation and so forth, however, by means of the oblation,
she who brings about the state of Nirvāṇa is the supreme uniter with the Śiva-tattva.
From that, [there arises] the first form (*ākāra*) and the second line is like a half-moon.
The third is in the form of a hook, and the fourth arises from fire.
The ninth [state] is to be known as the Supreme Sovereign, wherein this entire world of the moving and the unmoving resides.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the one hundred and fifty [verse] Kālottara.
The Seven Hundred [Stanzas]. Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
Skanda said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Protector of the world, Master of the universe! You have explained in detail the mantra and tantra, as well as the actual means of accomplishment.
But these mortals have short lifespans, little vigor and prowess, meager strength, and scant wealth; they are possessed by greed and delusion. (2)
O Lord of Gods, O Master, for the sake of your grace toward me, you should speak that which is concise in words yet vast in meaning, and filled with many explanations of the essential topics.
Īśvara said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim this most difficult-to-attain scripture called Kāla, extracted from the Vāthula Tantra like butter from curd.
And just as honey is the essence extracted from the sap of flowers,
so too is this auspicious supreme seed called Nāda, which resides within all beings.
O Mahāsena, having known that which bestows liberation, which is supreme and divine, and which grants all perfections, the teacher becomes a destroyer of the bonds.
From cowherds, women, and children, down to the barbarians who speak non-Aryan tongues—
even the beings dwelling within the water— they too constantly proclaim it.
Having understood the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, one should perform action as desired.
The gross is said to consist of sound, while the subtle is composed of thought.
That which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the Supreme;
having known this, the knower of mantras shall experience the destruction of all sins.
Peaceful, all-pervading, and empty, established by means of the twelve mantras;
having interspersed the syllables [of the name], one who performs the six-limbed rite shall become Śiva. (10)
The first is its heart, the second is remembered as the head;
the third is indeed the crest-lock (śikhā), and the fourth shall be the armor (kavaca). || 11 ||
One should know the fifth to be Śiva and the sixth as born from the visarga of A-sva;
this sixfold limb has been declared by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
The true nature of the secret has been declared by the great-souled Sādākhyā;
it has now been told by me to you, bestowing immediate liberation.
The limb of Śiva joined with the long vowel is as it stands, beginning with the Heart-mantra;
likewise, by the sequential application of Sadyojāta and the others, that which is short is proclaimed when joined with a short vowel.
The "eye" (netra) consists of all [the preceding syllables] with the anusvāra placed above them;
the "weapon" (astra) consists of that same [syllable] with the visarga, conjoined with the anusvāra and the *vikharman*. 15.
One should know the Śiva-tattva as the supreme Śiva, whose form is mantra.
The second [syllable] of the sixth [group], joined again with the first of the fourth;
and in the second [position], one should join the fifth and then the first again. (17)
All obstacles are known to become bestowers of liberation when [struck] at the crest by the auspicious weapon;
thus is the divine Pāśupata, which severs all bonds. (18)
The five Brahmans, the limb of Śiva, and the Pāśupata [weapon]—all this auspicious extraction of mantras has been told in brief. (19)
I shall now describe its mudrā for the benefit of practitioners:
one should touch both feet with the two hands, and then place the two hands upon the head. (20)
The Mahāmudrā of these [deities] accomplishes all desired aims.
Having formed the hollowed hand-gesture (puṭa), the thumb is placed last.
One should diligently perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules using the limbs of Brahmā;
then, one should purify the forehead, hands, and back with the seed-syllable of the Weapon (astra).
Beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb,
one should diligently perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rule, using the two Brahma-limbs.

Thereafter, one should place the temple, all-pervading and facing in every direction; O child, this is the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa) according to this tantra—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, in the [tantra] called Mudā, one should not initiate either Śambhu or a bound soul (paśu);
rather, [one should do so] with nine crores of mantras and by the number of ten million mudrās.
Having performed every single sacrifice for you, I shall declare the reality of Śiva (śivatatva), including whatever action may arise through body, speech, and mind. (26)
Having seen the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), he shall become one of pure body;
and whatever other purities have been taught at length, O Mahāguha. (27)
He who possesses all three mudrās is distinguished above all others;
now listen to the procedure for the extraction of the mantra according to its true nature.
Thus ends the first chapter, the extraction of mantras, in the *Kālottara-mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Kārttikeya said:
The arrangement of the internal organ as well as the purification of the elements;
having first performed the purification of the elements, perform the arrangement of the internal organ afterwards.
Tell me truly how their nourishment is accomplished.
Īśvara said:
One should first apply consciousness, then burning, and thirdly nourishment;
these are remembered as the three types of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Burning is said to occur with a short vowel, while nourishment occurs with a protracted one;
with a long vowel, one should place the hard supports upon the lotus.
One should always bring the earthen element, conjoined with the heart-seeds, into the state of earth;
the fire-element, along with the first crest-mantra, should be placed on the head, and the armor-mantra together with the wind.
One should hold the weapon-mantra (astra) joined with the syllable for space (ākāśa) as Śiva does; having first diligently mastered this vidyā, one should strike with power at the end of "hūṃ phaṭ."
Regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should commence its practical application as I shall describe:
five *udghātas*, four, three, and two.
One should always contemplate consciousness alone, which is empty, entirely without support,
abiding within its own nature, and flowing with the nectar of immortality.
With the syllable *oṃ*, one should conceive the lotus as the yoga-seat,
which resembles the solar disc and is indeed the space born of the self.
The *vidyā-tattva* is the letter *u*, while the *śiva-tattva* is born from the letter *ma*.
The *puryaṣṭaka* consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and *sadāśiva* is beyond the fourth state (*turyātīta*).
One should contemplate the supreme dharma, with the head pierced by the *suṣumnā*;
by that, one should contemplate oneself being filled and nourished.
This concentration, which destroys death, should be practiced constantly;
for it is the certainty of the scriptures that death does not arise for such a person.
Then, the preceptor should perform the grasping by means of the forms for the practitioner;
beginning from the top, one should assign [the mantras] starting from Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
One should likewise offer the eye and the primordial [element] to Sadāśiva, the God of gods;
then the wise one should contemplate his own self as omniscience.
The knower of mantras should likewise apply the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the armor, and the weapon to the five locations in successive order.
Or rather, the procedure is performed in the heart; this [specific] fire-oblation is not prescribed.
One should indeed meditate upon the Lord on the forehead, the bestower of boons, facing in all directions.
Just as in worship, so too in the fire— specifically at the time of meditation—
one should first make this internal organ [pure], O Six-faced One, and only afterwards the external.
Having performed both the external and internal [purifications], he should thereafter commence the sacrifice.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Inner Organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*), in the *Kālottara-saptaśatika*.
Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme bath that removes all sins. Having taken earth while reciting the Astra-mantra seven times, the wise practitioner [should proceed].
Having first performed the ritual bath for removing impurities and having recited the Saṃhitā once,
O child, he should consecrate that very clay by chanting over it once each time.
Then, having divided it into three portions, one should consecrate the first with the Astra-mantra,
the second with the recited mantra, and the third with the Śiva-jaṣta mantra.
One should perform the binding of the directions with a portion consecrated by the Astra-mantra;
at a sacred site (tīrtha) with one consecrated by the Śiva-mantra, and within oneself with one consecrated by the Brahma-mantra.

Then, having smeared himself with [the paste], he should bathe in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha with the ritual honors due to a universal monarch (cakravartin), using fragrant myrobalan fruits and other such substances.
Having performed the ritual ablution according to the rules during the twilight worship in the proper sequence,
the wise one should perform the formal salutation (upasthāna) once with all the mantras.
Having first performed the consecration, one should subsequently perform the twilight ritual;
the wise practitioner should then apply the weapon-mantra to the body and cast it outward.
O Six-faced One, by that sound alone one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords;
O child, one should purify the body and thereby unite it with the Self.
He should apply that momentary [mantra] against obstacles and the snares of bondage;
then, with the heart-mantra, he should satisfy the deity and the ancestral deities.
"O Six-faced One, [this is] the withdrawal of all the sacred sites by means of the resonance.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kālottara* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Īśvara said:
O Six-faced One, I shall now explain the ash-bath in brief;
O wise one, having consecrated it once with all the mantras according to the proper sequence.

"O Six-faced One, having first performed the impurity-bath (*malasnāna*) with the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astrabīja*)," thus ends the fourth chapter on the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) in the *Kālottara*, consisting of seven powers (*saptaśaktika*).
The Lord said:
I shall now fully describe the sacrifice according to the traditional sequence:
first the seed-syllable and the sprout, and afterwards the infinite seat.
O Six-faced One, one should place Ananta within the center, and then in sequence:
the heart, the pericarp, the lotus, and likewise Dharma, Jñāna, and the others.
One should likewise place detachment and sovereignty in the heart;
one should then effect the manifestation of the powers within Keśava by means of the Heart-mantra.
Then, O Six-faced One, the knower of mantras should invoke the deity with the heart-mantra;
he should perform the installation, the preparation of the water-vessel for the guest-offering (arghya), and the ritual worship.
One should perform the bathing and the worship with the Heart mantra;
whatever has been mentioned or not mentioned, all that is done with the Heart mantra.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the ritual procedure for sacrifice, in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*, which possesses seven powers.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya) in its proper sequence:
one should perform the scraping with the weapon-mantra (astra), and sprinkling with darbha grass is prescribed.
Then the practitioner of mantra should perform the deposition of the powers (śaktinyāsa) with the heart-mantra;
he should cast the fire, which contains the power within its womb, into the heart.
Having performed the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and the final expiation (niṣkṛti),
the knower of mantras should perform all ritual acts with the heart-mantra.
Thereafter, one should arrange the lotus ritual as previously described;
then, for all the mantras beginning with Śiva, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) in successive order.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the ritual procedure for the fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*), in the *Kālottara-tantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the mandala that grants all desires,
after having diligently purified the ground according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Then, having given his consent under an auspicious constellation endowed with excellence,
the wise one should draw the beautiful maṇḍala that bestows all accomplishments.
Having marked out a square on all sides with a string,
one should establish a lotus in the center, complete with horse-leaf petals and a pericarp.
O Guha, it may be one cubit, two cubits, or even four cubits in size; it is known to be self-sustaining and endowed with three protective coverings.
One should cause the auspicious western door, as ordained by the Ācārya, to be opened;
one should prepare a *kuśa*-grass mat in the western direction, measuring one cubit in size.
One should perform the ritual procedure for the sacrifice when the sacrificial fire has been kindled;
one should then install the thunderbolt and other weapons at the eastern gates in their proper sequence.
Having first assigned the limbs of Brahmā to the city, one should then assign the limbs of Śiva;
having assigned the heart in the southeast, one should assign the head in the northeast.
Having placed the *śikhā* mantra in the southwest, one should place the *kavaca* in the northwest;
having assigned the *astra* to the cardinal directions, one should place Sadāśiva in the pericarp.
This is indeed the procedure for the deposition of the embryo; now hear the second enclosure:
one should worship the world-protector with the *hṛdinī* mantra at the eastern gate.
In the third [chapter], one should fill the weapon of the World-Protectors with a single ritual instrument.
Thus, O Skanda, the procedure has been proclaimed by me in brief.
O wise one, whatever may remain unsaid, all that should be understood from the heart;
thus, knowing the rules and procedures, one should commence the rites of Brahma.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all the gods who have approached— those deities have all been initiated by me in this supreme maṇḍala.
But when this maṇḍala, fashioned by the God of gods, is beheld,
they go to that supreme station, the stainless and auspicious state of Śiva.
Thus has the mandala been described, adorned by the Lord with a bindu;
there is nothing else whatsoever more secret or supreme than this.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the King of Mandalas, in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
Now I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā), which is established upon the five principles (pañcatattva):
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
By these five great principles (mahātattvas), the entire universe is pervaded;
all other principles are situated therein and should be perceived by the most excellent practitioners.
No other beings are to be joined with the yoga by means of oblations in succession;
having emerged from the Egg of Brahmā, they remain outside the Hundred Rudras.
Above that, however, one should establish [the deities] as far as the sphere of the Imperishable;
thereafter, one should apply the seed-syllables as far as the vicinity of Vidyeśvara.
One should place Śānti above that, and with Śānti, one should install Śiva;
he who endeavors to perform initiation without knowing this reality (tattva) [is at fault].
His exertion is in vain; he shall not obtain its fruit.
Cessation is to be known as the earth, and water is said to be the foundation.
Vidyā is said to consist of splendor, while Vāyu is proclaimed as Peace (Śānti).
Beyond Peace is the Supreme Ether (Vyoman), which is higher than that and supremely imperishable.
Having understood that, Mahāsena should initiate those who are steadfast;
for these five great elements constitute the body of the Sakala.
They perceive no conflict between the stationary and the moving;
nor is any other deity seen as distinct [from them].
By these [mantras], one becomes a sacrificer; by these, the sacrifice is performed, purified, and well-refined.
These five types of deities are well-established.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five principles (tattvas) abide [therein]; such is Nirvāṇa in its entirety.
One should place Nivṛtti in the heart and Pratiṣṭhā on the head;
Vidyā in the topknot and Śānti with the armor-mantra.
One should perform the homa with the *prāsāda* mantra into the supreme void that transcends tranquility;
one should offer a hundred oblations for each [syllable], or indeed offer five hundred oblations.
O Six-faced One, one should subsequently offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *Prāsāda* mantra;
for the sake of purification through expiation, one should offer eight oblations for each [mantra] in sequence.
The knower of mantras should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in due order with the seed-syllables of the weapons;
he should unify the self, the disciple, and Śiva—all three as one.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the wise one, remaining like emptiness within emptiness,
becomes one with the Supreme and attains a state of singular, equal flavor.
When it has perished, it is empty; likewise, it is empty everywhere. In that same way, one should lead both the self and the disciple to the state of Śiva, which is uniform and singular.
Thus the initiation is completed, devoid of birth and so forth;
by the very act of oblation, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of rebirth.
This secret is unmanifest and must be guarded with great effort;
it is the mystery of all mantras and the supreme consecration.
"In this way, the purification of the formative forces (saṃskāra) certainly arises just like that of Śiva.
Kārttikeya said:
O God, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from the beginning and having extracted the final [syllable], please explain the practice (sādhana) in due order according to the rule.
The Lord said:
O Guha, as you constantly inquire about the seventeen [yogas] that are to be mastered,
I shall explain to you, in due order, which seed is ordained for each.
One should likewise conceive of the heart as the seed-syllable of the womb, performing worship, sprinkling, and striking in due order.
Likewise, he indeed [taught] withdrawal, that very yoga, and also the ritual deposit.
Furthermore, one should perform worship (arcana), as well as conception (garbhadhāraṇa),
birth (janana), the rite of formation (kāra), enjoyment (bhoga), and likewise dissolution (laya).
O Six-faced One, one should perform the self-identification with the hundred oblations by means of the heart-mantra;
the severing of bonds with the weapon-mantra, and the full oblation as before.
Then, one should perform the heart-mantra in sequence,
as well as the extraction, sprinkling, and striking, exactly as prescribed.
It should be performed in successive order, joined with the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
The withdrawal of the principles (tattvas) must be performed in its proper manner;
this rite is to be carried out through each successive principle, and this is remembered as the prescribed procedure.
O child, one should perform this purification according to the complete procedure;
otherwise, O Six-faced One, those who lack the prescribed rite are not liberated at all.
One should perform the continuous stream of the final oblation accompanied by concentration;
O child, one should mentally contemplate that supreme nectar as it flows forth.
For this is the section on initiation (dīkṣā), which applies everywhere and at all times; however,
the procedure for the removal of the *liṅga* (liṅgoddhāra) pertains to all rites of purification (*saṃskāra*).
Kārttikeya said:
O sinless one, that which was previously declared regarding the seizing and releasing of the sacrificial animal—
Within or outside the two nooses, in what place and how does he abide?
In which region are they to be severed, and what is the nature of that which is said to be immediate?
O Maheśvara, please explain the specific instruction regarding the sacrificial animal as well.
The Lord said:
Addressing it with the second [mantra], the wise one should diligently grasp the self and lead it as far as the station of the sixtieth.
But through pure yoga, [the deities] from Brahmā down to Śiva reach a single commonality; otherwise, however, they remain distinct.

They should be cut with the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta), conjoined with the science of vowels; then they attain the state of being fit for sacrifice, free from all defects. However, that which is performed without specifying the name [of the deity] becomes futile.
An action performed with that [deity] in mind grants liberation; of this there is no doubt.
O child, when a solar eclipse occurs and one is endowed with purity, whatever vow (āyāma) is undertaken at that time will certainly be said to be fixed.
By this [mantra], the nooses are bound together like clusters of gems on a thread,
extending from the heart-lotus as far as the [supreme] lotus, including the mind-weapon and the sons.
Having seen that, one should effect its severance; the mind's activity is the mind, and Śiva is the mind.
When the mind is severed by the mind, the individual soul (jīva) attains absolute isolation (kevalatā).
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord of Gods, abandon elaboration and tell me in brief that which,
upon mere understanding, liberates the bound soul (paśu) in an instant.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the truth: through this practice, a practitioner of mantras who perceives yoga with subtle application shall certainly attain liberation through yoga.
O Mahāsena, once the wise one has recognized that the individual soul (jīva) consists of wind, it is impelled by Śakti through the divine path of yoga.
One should join oneself to the eternal state through the yoga of the equinox;
for having attained the yoga of the equinox, who would not be released from bondage?
Having known that [the self] which arises from earth and so forth, from birth and so forth, which possesses qualities such as sound through the winds,
and whose nature is the deity of the mantras and so forth, one is liberated from bondage.
The channels, which have the nature of hollows, are like upward-pointing stalks with their openings facing downward;
they are all provided with two knots and are animated by the syllables *haṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Then, O Guha, the wise one, having observed the earth and other elements with his mind, performs the two upward movements (udghāta) as before, proceeding upwards toward the external and internal.
In each and every reality (tattva), however, those who are liberated, free from egoism, and whose abode is Brahman— like a bird that has left its nest, my son— shall not undergo rebirth again.
Having repeated these twice, one should join the mantra uttered by the word "nāda" at the time of initiation with the breath-restraint (āyāma) of the Sun.
O child, having struck him as before, his capture shall occur as previously described;
having pierced through his blameworthy faults, one should lead him to reality by means of reality itself.
Having encapsulated [the disciple] with the Śakti-mantras and ending with *vauṣaṭ*, one should cast [the initiation];
this initiation, in brief, is the means of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Mahāsena, in which [the Lord] reside the mantras, initiations, and the splendors of mudrās and maṇḍalas; as well as the pure powers (śaktis) and the worlds.
O Maheśvara, this very being, when purified, is the giver of liberation.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the section on initiation, in the *Kālottara Mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
One who knows the self through the moment (*muhūrta*) should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the pure deity.
And by the blows of the Vajraparāla [mudrā], he who is unknown to others attains consecration in the sky of his own speech; the Ācārya is the destroyer of the bonds of the bound souls (paśu).
Thus ends the ninth chapter on consecration in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
I shall now explain this subtle wheel of channels in their proper sequence.
That which is subtle below the navel, [there one should perform...]
(At the top of the page) Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the consecration (abhiṣeka), both in brief and in detail,
for the benefit of the foremost of practitioners— [teachings] issued forth from the mouth of Śiva.
Thus, having consecrated an earthen pitcher purified by Candrasena,
endowed with all medicinal herbs and adorned with all fragrances,
one should recite the *Sarvatomukha* mantra one hundred and eight times over it.
Those garments are seventy-two in number, while you yourself are formless.
Extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards, pervading everywhere,
these ten principal channels are indeed situated like a wheel, originating from the Pradhāna.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third;
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and likewise Yaśas.
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth;
these ten channels (nāḍīs) are proclaimed to be the carriers of the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
And the first wind is Prāṇa; he is the lord of all nine.
Through the exhaustion of Prāṇa, one becomes breathless, [and thus] the exhalations [are directed] toward filling [the internal channels].
Abiding in the chest of living beings, this [wind] constantly fills [the body];
the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the basis of inhalation and exhalation, is dependent upon the individual soul (jīva).
Because it moves forward (prayāṇa), it is therefore proclaimed as prāṇa;
O wise ones, the apāna, however, carries away the food, O younger brothers.
The wind that carries semen and urine is proclaimed as apāna;
it conveys what is drunk, eaten, smelled, and blood, bile, phlegm, and wind.
It carries [the breath] equally through the limbs; it is known by the name Samāna.
It causes the lower lip to quiver and provokes agitation in the eyes and the body.
The vital air named udāna agitates the vital points (marmas);
vyāna destroys the limbs, and vyāna provokes diseases.
That which causes the destruction of pleasure and manifests as disease is called Vyāna;
the vital airs beginning with Prāṇa have been described, and now those beginning with Nāga are being described.
Udgāra is said to be Nāga; she remains in the opening of the tortoise (kūrma);
and Devadatta yawns when Kṛkara and Kūrmila are agitated.
Dhanañjaya remains in the throat and does not leave even when one is dead;
thus these [five winds] reside within the cluster of channels (nāḍicakra) placed in the heart-joy, manifesting through inhalation,
exhalation, and coughing, and by the shaking and whirling of the breath from the mouth downward.

Though his births are eternal yet few, he is struck down by calamities in youth and even in old age; though he is but a single wind, he is toyed with by all beings through lightning, disease, and death.
I shall describe the entire wheel of channels exactly as it exists,
so that this ten-spoked wheel may be understood through its various functions.
The living being revolves like a wheel through the ten states in succession;
though he is the life-force of the world of beings, those deluded by ignorance do not perceive him at all.
Because it moves in ten ways, it is proclaimed as the "wheel" (cakra);
and because it indeed traverses [the body], it is renowned as the "channel-wheel" (nāḍīcakra).

In the center of the sky of the heart is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp; within its middle, at the center, are the powers (śaktis) possessing a luster like that of lightning, fire, and gold. Above that, indeed, is the power of the powers, which is the primordial state of Śiva himself—the lotus of the fourfold power.
In the middle, the persons are dissolved; having grasped the void with the tongs of the desert,
the one whose nature is the instrument (the senses) surely does not cause [them] to rest on either side, nor does he ever make them into withered leaves.
Within the lotus, the binding of the noose of the four arts will be stolen away.
As if struck by the play of a ball, it rises up and then descends; through union with Īśvara, it attains both the equinox and the solstice.
Without assignment, there is no rising on the right during the movement; there is no conjunction with the north.
The two solstices are the left and the right, while the equinoxes are the two pairs of nostrils.
They say that "transference" (*saṃkrānti*) refers to that which moves from here and there; this has been declared by the wise. It is proclaimed as belonging to the Sun, Soma, Garga, and the Moon.
Indeed, the essence of the sun-god (Saura) is auspicious when it is joined with the fire-essence (Agni-sattva).
In the eastern petal, there is pride toward kings;

one is radiant yet agitated in soul. In the southeast, there is yellowish luster and victory. In the south, the disposition is that of a Yama-like being; and in the southwest, there are indeed Rākṣasas.

In the Vāruṇa [element], one attains the state of Varuṇa; in the Marutpattraka, the state born of the Maruts; in the Soma, the state of the Sādhyas; in the Īśa, the state known as Īśa; in the Brahma, the state of Brahma; and in the Uraga, the state of the Lord of Serpents. Whichever [element] one approaches, at its conclusion one attains that state.
Due to the union with the interior of the vessel, she shines forth as the Equal One (Samā) within the void.

Thus, indeed, the mandala of the movement of the channels and the course of the individual (pudgala) has been explained here in its primary form; it should be understood with effort as the cause of accomplishment once [the practice] is perfected.
Kārttikeya said:
That living soul is not truly [identical] to the world of living beings as it is to anything else.
O Mahādeva, by your grace, O wielder of the trident, my doubt has been dispelled.
Īśvara said:
"O Skanda, you who are full of idle chatter, you who have cast out your own self and are empty!
I shall speak; in the knowledge of the cloth, it bestows [the fruit] again and again."
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the vision of the living soul called Puruṣa;
I shall describe it to you without doubt, especially out of affection for my son.
The transits, the equinoxes, the days and nights, the solstices,
the intercalary month, and the debt— [these are the afflictions].
Anarātra becomes *śikhā*, and the intercalary month is *vijṛmbhikā*.
Debt should be understood as the upward breath (cakāśa), while exhalation is called wealth (dhana).
The northern [channel] is to be known as the right, and the left is designated as the right [in this context].
That which issues from both nostrils is declared to be the equinox (viṣuva) in the middle.
Furthermore, its transference is to its own place and indeed to the very station;
it is endowed with the iḍā, the suṣumnā, and the amā.
The Suṣumnā is established in the right limb, and the Iḍā in the left;
in the middle limb is Amā—this is called the transition (saṃkrānti).
The upward movement of the breath is indeed the *prāṇa*, while the downward movement is the *apāna*; this is called "night.
He who knows such a division of the tenfold breath is a knower of the Veda.
The expansion at the center of the body is desired as the lunar eclipse (*somagrahaṇa*).
But they know that the grasping of the sun, which transcends the body,
consists of twenty-two thousand six hundred [breaths].
In a single day and night, he performs the recitation count for yogis.
Kārttikeya said:

O Maheśvara, [I have described] inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), exhalation (recaka), and the state of perfect stillness (praśāntaka), as well as the practice (karaṇa) according to the proper rule.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to that which is truly difficult to obtain in knowledge;
it has not been told by me to anyone, but shall now be spoken, O Śikhivāhana.
p. 9a) I shall explain the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) in its entirety in brief:
the knower of yoga should utter the Praṇava with a single tone.
Having filled the abdomen with air to the desired extent,
this becomes prāṇāyāma known as pūraka, which fills the body.

Having closed all the gates [of the senses] and being devoid of inhalation and exhalation, the breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) is indeed like a full pitcher; it is called "kumbhaka" because it is like a water-pot.
Then the knower of yoga should release the upward-moving breath with a single exhalation;
one engaged in yoga should exhale the upward-moving air through the out-breath.
This is known as *recaka*, which causes the cessation of breath;
it is that [wind] which [reverses] the lotus situated in the heart, which was previously positioned with its face downward.
That lotus indeed blossoms when filled by the pūraka;
however, the half-mātrā is restrained by the padma-kumbhaka.
But when it is forcefully expelled by that which instantly takes away life,
having pierced the lotus of the heart, it becomes established in the upward current.
The *recaka* indeed goes upward, having sequentially knotted [the breath];
having pierced the door of the skull, the life-force (*jīva*) is exhaled upward.
Having attained the state of Sadāśiva, one shall not undergo birth again.
The measurement is performed for that [specific part] and never for any other;
one should withdraw the thought from there, in the middle where it is excluded.
The foodless one, dissolved in the state [of the Self], is the "Tranquil One" because of his perfect stillness;
he is the life-force of the world of living beings—this I have declared in brief.
He who knows that Śiva, who abides within his own body and utters [the mantra] by himself,
is eternally called a "victorious god" (devajaya).
Twelve thousand, one thousand, and six hundred;
such is the number of recitations that yogins perform in a single day and night.
For him, no obstacle arises; there is neither the need for a rosary nor any restriction.
There is no fixed time, nor even the attainment of the goal through ritual means.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the movement of the channels, in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*, which possesses seven powers.
Īśvara said:
Through the union of the moon and fire, that which is the Kuṇḍalinī nāḍī is to be known as situated in the region of the heart, established like the source of a sprout.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) there according to the method of emanation (sṛṣṭi), repeating it twice as prescribed for the feet;
for the best of practitioners should contemplate the nectar flowing [from them].
One who is concentrated and desirous of attaining supernatural powers should contemplate the entire world— both stationary and moving— as being composed of fire and moon, yet as being reversed.
The wise one should contemplate within his own body a divine form beyond compare;
the learned man should contemplate whatever specific action has been prescribed for him.
Whoever should practice this immortal knowledge which faces all directions,
shall, in a very short time, attain perfection and become a partaker of the true fruit.
"Without knowing the Sṛṣṭinyāsa, how can practitioners apply it? It is like striking the sky with one's fist or threshing husks.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, concerning the nature of Fire and Moon, in the seven-hundred-verse Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Furthermore, I shall explain the creation again in detail and in due order,
how the manifest [sakala] is endowed with the unmanifest [niṣkala] within the God.
He brought forth the *kalās* that are excluded from all tantras;
the syllable *U*, situated in the middle of the preceding [syllable], pervading everywhere as the syllable *Ū*.
The letter *U* is the first line; the Lord creates the worlds.
It is established in the principle (*tattva*) of knowledge (*vidyā*), and it is likewise established in the phoneme (*varṇa*).
The appearance of the letter *a* within the syllable *uṃ* is seen as the *kala*;
it should be known by the name *pūti*, arising from the letter *ā*.
At his head, during the watches of the night, there exists a subtle form, stainless;
born from the letter *Ma*, that digit is named Nirvṛti.
The syllable *uṃ* conjoined with the *bindu* reaches dissolution at the crest of the *uṃ*;
the line, however, is extinguished in space—that is called the digit of peace (*śānti*).
He, who exists both as the partless (niṣkala) and the whole (sakala), reveals this yoga;
having ascended to the head [of the central channel], he gives rise to the sound "oṃ."
That peace is supremely subtle, situated in the state together with the *bindu*;
by its nature, it is like a lamp from which another lamp arises, accompanied by sparks.
The unborn *kalās* fall and proceed in three ways, ending with that which is like Śiva:
namely, Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti—that is the *kalā*.
As soon as she was struck by the arrow, she fell down, crying out in distress.
He is proclaimed as the Lord of Knowledge, Śiva, the God of Gods, the Great Lord (Maheśvara);
his first seed-syllable is celebrated as being composed of the Bindu and the Nāda.
One should not abandon the supreme state, which is eternal, fixed, and imperishable;
for having cast the *bindu* into the belly, it is thoroughly examined by means of the mantra.
Above that, on the left side, the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu is proclaimed. The right [side] is situated within the left womb; thus, though being one, it becomes threefold.
On both sides there are two dots (bindus), and the line stands in the middle.
Therein dwells the god Śiva, the subtle, hidden, and auspicious Śaṅkara;
he is the supreme deity who is the seed, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) whose womb is power (Śakti).
From which the Swan proceeds, the unmoving and the moving, together with the enemy;
it is unmanifest, supreme, subtle, the body of power, and stainless.
Śiva is without beginning or end, from whom Vidhātṛ is born;
that seed which resides in the south is indeed the supreme power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
That seed is the supreme Brahman, wherein he remains hidden;
that which is the highest seed within the head is indeed the supreme power of action.
Therein, by means of the Viṣṇu-seed-syllable, this god is hidden, subtle, and stainless; he is indeed the emission (visarga), the sixth, born from the womb.
There they perceive that which is unmanifest, by means of which the creation of all things mobile and immobile occurs;
from the creative emission (visarga) arises both the creation and the Lord, the Sovereign himself.
That seed which is emitted is called "visarga" (emission) because it ends in emission;
by that, the entire world, both stationary and moving, is filled.
By means of a multitude of rays of power, hundreds and even thousands at a time,
he emits and withdraws them, and likewise joins them together and separates them.
The Lord, abiding in the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), bestows grace upon embodied beings;
from emission (visarga) comes creation, and together with the bindu, there is withdrawal (saṃhāra).
The knowledge of the reality of nirvāṇa is not, however, within the scope of extensive elaboration.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, concerning emanation and reabsorption, in the Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord, you have indeed explained everything regarding both dissolution and creation;
now tell me truly this matter concerning the loss of the goal for those who have been initiated.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, listen now to the truth regarding the yoga that causes the loss of one's state: it makes one deceitful, dishonest, cruel, and always fond of quarreling.
Having pierced all the gates and likewise drawn the moon toward the bowstring,
no one in the world can turn back his course.
O Six-faced One, having performed the *saṃpuṭa* by means of the *saṃhāra*, one should likewise offer the *mātṛkā*s at the beginning and the end for each [syllable] individually.
Just as the yoga that causes the loss of one's state has been illustrated by the example of the calf.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Destroyer of the Transmigrations," in the *Kālottara Mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses. The Lord said:
If one performs the recitation constantly after having established it upon a palace, perfection is attained within six months by one engaged in yoga; of this there is no doubt.
By meeting [the deity] through recitation, the destruction of all sins shall occur;
the sovereign power of qualities such as *aṇimā* will be attained within six months, without a doubt.
Having understood the coming and going [of the breath], one is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
By making the mind focused on that and becoming absorbed in that, one shall attain perfection within six months.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, one who is agitated and overwhelmed by fear will,
even when death is imminent, spontaneously set that [meditation] in motion.
When the deity proceeds through effortless play with spontaneous movement,
that recitation is indeed mindless, unarisen, and free from affliction.
I have explained the grace (prasāda) that is gross, subtle, and supreme;
by means of that through which they understand Prasāda, they understand Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Clarification," in the Kālottara.
The Lord said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the temple;
the knower of mantras should always observe whether it is short, long, or protracted.
The short [vowel] burns away sins; the long one becomes the bestower of liberation;
and the prolated one, when endowed with a bindu upon its head, provides nourishment.

The three gross divisions are declared to be subjugation (*vaśya*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*). By means of the *pluta* [vowel], one always effects subjugation; there is no doubt in this matter.
When combined with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, it swiftly eradicates even long-standing [afflictions].
The syllable *phaṭ* at the beginning and end of a short mantra is prescribed for killing;
the heart-mantra at the beginning and end is prescribed for the practice of summoning.
If all the attraction is performed without knowing the reality of the name, it will result in a defect for the practitioner; such a practice is declared to be deficient in its accomplishment.
Having instructed thus, the wise one certainly performs the summoning;
if this is not correctly understood, the practitioner will not succeed at all.
Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should offer half of the mantra;
having offered half of the mantra, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation (japa).
Having performed the consecration of Manu for the practitioners with a concentrated mind,
one should remain engaged in recitation for five hundred thousand times at the right image of the deity.
By means of a hundred thousand burnt offerings in the fire-pit, the mantra becomes ten-thousand-fold;
thus nourished, the mantra then becomes fit for ritual action.
Those rites which have been described will succeed without any doubt;
he who recites [the mantra] one million times will [bring relief] to people, whether they are healthy or not.
They indeed quickly come under one's control, either by means of oneself or by wealth,
after reciting three times five hundred thousand [mantras] ten times for those dwelling in the numberless [realms].
"They indeed come under control quickly; such is the certainty of the scripture.
By twenty-five hundred thousand [recitations], one shall bring the object of desire under control."
He who recites it three million times shall bring even the inhabitants of the celestial realms under his control;
with twenty-five million recitations, he shall bring the entire earth under his control.
With forty lakhs [of recitations], one beholds Hāṭakeśvara;
having recited fifty lakhs, one becomes equal to an Avidyādhara.
Therein, the mantra-practitioner rejoices in this manner until the dissolution of the offering.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Temple," in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*.
Kārttikeya said:
O Maheśvara, tell me what kind of palace it is, what its knowledge is like, what its pervasiveness is like, and what that body is like.
The Lord said:
He by whom the five great mantras are not realized through clarity,
nor that which is endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, is not called an Ācārya.
But if you perform this initiation without knowing the state of [the disciple's] faith, the disciple and yourself will both be led downward; of this there is no doubt.
The teacher who performs initiation while stationed within the heart-lotus of the temple spire shall attain union with Śiva, together with his disciple.
The gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, along with the yakṣas,
uragas, and rākṣasas, the kinnaras, apsarases, and siddhas— all were produced from the palace.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, as well as Candra, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, the Ādityas, Śukra, Skanda, and Guru,
as well as all other living beings— these are all produced from the temple.
These and many other sages of rigid vows meditate upon the supreme Haṃsa, the temple (Prāsāda) that is beyond all names.
I shall explain its division, by knowing which one attains immortality:
they know it as being produced from the syllable 'A', joined with the eight kalās.
One should know that the Vāma face is born from the syllable *ukāra*, the Aghora face is born from the syllable *makāra*,
the Puruṣa face is to be known as born from the *bindu*, and Īśāna is of the nature of Śiva.
In this way, these five mantras are all produced from the Prāsāda;
they possess the splendor of even hundreds of thousands of millions of mantras.
When a temple (prāsāda) has been worshipped, there is no doubt that all have been worshipped—
namely, Māruta, Nala, Śakra, and others, whichever deities were not specifically mentioned by name in the mantra.
All those born from the lotus of the palace possess unfailing power;
the Earth is to be known as the right [side], while Water is proclaimed to be the left.
They say that Aghora is splendor; Vāyu is remembered as Tatpuruṣa;
Ākāśa is Īśa, who is himself the god Sadāśiva.
The one born immediately is the seer Dōvāmadeva, who is remembered as the Yajurveda;
Aghora is indeed the Sāmaveda, while Puruṣa is called the Atharvaveda.
The fifth is that which is supreme, subtle, all-pervading like space, and stainless;
it is the syllable *U*, situated at the crown of the head, possessing the form of Śakti and endowed with the Bindu.
In this very way, I have declared that which the wise know as the supreme Śivatattva; Sadyojāta is indeed Brahmā, and Vāma is proclaimed to be Viṣṇu.
Aghora has Rudra as its presiding deity, and Puruṣa is remembered as Īśvara;
Īśāna has Śiva as its deity, established as the presiding divinity.
The sixth is that supreme seed, endowed with qualities beyond comparison;
its body must not be described as arising from the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having known the supreme ladder that ascends through the five stages,
O Lord, he for whom knowledge and the object of knowledge are never forgotten even for a moment— indeed, such a one is truly wise.
At that very moment he is liberated; that which was ignorance becomes the state [of liberation].
Skanda said:
When some, having heard [the teaching], do not awaken to the meaning even after knowing it through lack of wisdom,
those deluded ones, infatuated with sense objects, will commit sins.
Alternatively, out of the fault of attachment, he praises animal-like knowledge;
for what state of existence does one who reviles the supreme knowledge attain?
Īśvara said:
When indeed the man of knowledge, having ascertained that to be certain, does not turn back from his purpose,
he should repeatedly hold fast to what has been abandoned and again take up what has been censured.
Then, when that blissful one is liberated from the body through diligent effort,
he possesses neither merit nor sin, whether past or yet to come.
At the first stage, however, knowledge, mind, ego, and intellect each dissolve into their respective sources;
they do not perceive themselves as being bound.
When all the vital points have been pierced and the life-breaths have reached the throat,
and supreme knowledge has been released, how can one maintain mindfulness of this?
The Lord said:
Henceforth I shall speak; listen now with a one-pointed mind.
Even when all my vital breaths have been severed, or when they have reached the throat.
Then that supreme sound itself sets forth as knowledge;
one neither grieves nor is overwhelmed by both states, whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking.
Even when death is imminent, this [rite] proceeds of its own accord;
whether one has been initiated or not initiated, the embodied soul performs whatever action is necessary for purification.
Those who are not burned when the Vedas are consumed by fire are not truly burned; however, one who is burned by them is burned again.
Likewise, the fool who acts contrary to this, being immersed in the objects of the senses, is likewise consumed.
That initiated one shall not be defiled by action, nor by sin, whether through speech, mind, or body; thus is action said to be threefold.
It is not obstructed by that, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Analysis of the Temple," in the Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
Even now, O Lord, O Master, there remains a doubt regarding knowledge and realization:
how is that knowledge known, and how is the object of knowledge described?
Īśvara said:
O Six-faced One, having first understood the support (ādhāra), one should subsequently [understand] that which is to be abandoned (heya).
A wise man who understands the relationship between the support and the supported is competent in all ritual actions.
The support has been described; now that which is supported by it is being told:
He who is the Lord by means of Īśa is known, O gentle one, as Īśa.
Having realized the Lord, the wise man always attains liberation;
endowed with the eightfold powers, he moves both downward and upward.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
the remaining ones are intellect and ego—these are remembered as the eight rays of the Sun.
As long as they are released by him, how can they be said to be liberated from bondage?
One should abandon sound and touch for Brahmā; indeed, one should abandon taste for Keśava.
Rudra indeed [abandons] form and smell; the Lord [abandons] intellect and ego; Śiva [abandons] mind and the bindu. By abandoning these, one becomes Śiva when united with them.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Examination of the Support and the Supported," in the Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
How is it pervasive, both below and above, and how indeed does it become divided?
Tell me this true nature, O Maheśvara, out of your compassion.
The Lord said:
As long as a living being remains within the body, [the Self] is situated within every body;
once it has emerged, it is pervasive, remaining everywhere and abiding in all things.
A living being situated on the three paths remains established in the upper state;
as long as they do not know [the truth], they are not liberated, even if their dissolution should occur.
For those who have entered by the three paths, this all-pervading pervasion of the primordial source (sarvādi) is established;
there is no doubt that he who possesses this pervasion is all-pervasive.
O Lord, it is declared that for such a one, there is no further rebirth from a womb.
They wander in saṃsāra as long as they do not find pervasiveness;
having known the all-pervading God, one is released from terrible bondage.
Just as a leech on the tip of a blade of grass remains extended until it reaches the top,
being without support above, even so is the individual soul (jīva) situated.
The upper is empty, the lower is empty, and the middle is the stainless emptiness.
He who thoroughly understands the triple emptiness is liberated from the bonds of qualities;
his pervasiveness has been declared by me both in brief and in detail.
"There is nothing higher than this, for it is the pervader of the all-pervading.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Pervasiveness," in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
Kārttikeya said:
O God of gods, Maheśvara, how is it that the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala),
as well as the supreme state beyond the mind (amanaska), are to be understood?
The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, to this knowledge that is extremely difficult to obtain in its true essence;
it has not been told to anyone, being the ineffable [truth] for one who has transcended worldly existence.
The differentiated (sakala) is to be known as residing within the body, while the undifferentiated (niṣkala) is devoid of the body;
this [reality] is accessible through the instruction of a realized teacher and exists as something indefinable everywhere.
He who says "Haṃsa, Haṃsa"— the *haṃsa* is the god Sadāśiva,
pure, awakened, supportless, eternal, subtle, and ever-inexhaustible.
But it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru as something manifest and all-encompassing,
just as oil resides in sesame seeds and fragrance is inherent in flowers.
Within this body of a person, he resides both externally and internally;
it is like when someone with a torch in hand approaches a substance to reveal it.
Having illuminated the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should then abandon that [instrumental] ignorance.
The manifest (sakala) is to be known as the flower, while the unmanifest (niṣkala) is its very fragrance.

One should know the bull to be the *sakala* (with parts), while its shadow is the *niṣkala* (partless); the essence (*rasa*) is to be known as the *sakala*, while its savor (*āsvāda*) is the *niṣkala*.
The manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala) are established throughout all tantras;
one should know that within the manifest is the manifest, while the unmanifest is said to be the Bindu.
Three measures, two measures, and likewise one measure;
further, half a measure, which is subtle, and even half of that, which is beyond the beyond.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva—
these five deities are proclaimed as the totality in their fivefold aspect.
O Lord of the gods, the Gāyatrī for the propitiation of Śiva consists of five measures; it is not, however, the complete form endowed with all its manifestations.

Śiva is to be known as fivefold: as Sakala (with parts), Niṣkala (without parts), and likewise Sakalaniṣkala (partially with parts); as Sūkṣma (subtle), Abhinna-kalā (undivided by parts), and Abhinna (undivided).
The deity who possesses phonemes is Sakala, while he who is joined with phonemes is Niṣkala.
The deity with parts (sakala) possesses syllables, while the partless (niṣkala) is without syllables;
he is both united and separated, having pierced through the head and the forehead.
It proceeds as a subtle process; it leads one to the eternal state. Therefore, it is called "subtle" here.
When that light proceeds, possessing a luster like the color of cut gold, the yogi is liberated upon seeing it; by what [means] and what is called "gold"?
Brahmā has his place in the heart; Viṣṇu is stationed in the throat;
Rudra is situated in the middle of the palate, and Maheśvara is in the forehead.
One should know Śiva to be at the tip of the nose, and at its end, the supreme-non-supreme (parāpara).
There is nothing higher than the Supreme; this is the certainty of the scripture.
Kārttikeya said:
What kind of dissolution (laya) is to be understood by those who know the truth regarding him?
How does his union [with the supreme] occur, and by what is he led?
I have a doubt, O Mahādeva; tell it to me according to the truth.
Īśvara said:
It is led away by the nature of Māyā and goes to dissolution into Brahmā;
Brahmā also dissolves into Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is dissolved into Indra.
I alone shall dissolve, yet I shall go to dissolution in the Lord;
O Six-faced One, the Lord as well shall thereafter dissolve into her.
In whichever principle (tattva) one proceeds, that is said to be the Śiva-tattva;
the practitioner who possesses full knowledge of the Śiva-tattva merges into it.
There is no distinction from Śiva alone regarding the established state of the void and the non-void;
this, O child, has been told to you as the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
The individual soul is led by Śakti; having reached that [state], it does not return.
O Six-faced One, I shall describe its end to you; listen to it according to the truth.

One should know that [state] as transcending the body, twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose; one should recognize it as the end of sound (nādānta). Residing there, the Lord pervades all, even while the mind is cast elsewhere and the eyes are directed elsewhere.
Nevertheless, the practice of praise proceeds without interruption.
This is the supreme secret; this is the supreme state;
this is the supreme Brahman; for this is the supreme nectar.
For this indeed is the entire deity; this indeed is the supreme syllable.
There is no knowledge higher than this, and there is no auspiciousness higher than this.
"Therefore, there is nothing higher than this," said the Blessed Lord Śiva;
"the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva has been proclaimed both in brief and in detail."
The determination of the supreme syllable has been declared by the God of gods.
For this is the true essence of Śiva, issued forth from the mouth of Śiva;
it is a secret more secret than the secret, a mystery that must be guarded with great effort.
It must never be given to a disciple, nor ever to a son.
This scripture should be given to one who is devoted to the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, and who seeks the welfare of all living beings; however, it should not be given to others.
The givers go to hell and never attain accomplishment;
this which is called the nectar of Śiva is the truth, the absolute truth, as told by me to you.
Knowing this, O wise one, conduct yourself as you please—
whether as a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant.
Wherever the practitioner of mantra may stand, if he is always a knower of the supreme syllable,
then— whether as a subject or an object, or even while attached— he attains Śiva at the end of the body.
Having purchased [the scripture] as desired and having enjoyed its pleasures as one wishes,
that person who has conquered sin through the knowledge of this scripture of the Lord is not tainted by merit or sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin or the horse sacrifice.
The reviver, the awakener, and the liberator is remembered as the highest.
Thus, these three types of teachers are to be known on this great earth:
one who impels should show the path, and one who awakens should instruct.
But Mokṣaka is the supreme reality, knowing which one does not return;
Codaka is indeed I, the Lord, while Bodhaka is Sadāśiva.
But the liberator is the supreme reality, knowing which one does not return;
thus these three have been declared, who are to be saluted in their proper order.
The Lord himself accepts from all sides that which is worthy of worship at the three locations;
indeed, even one who stands outside accepts what is worthy of worship. Śiva, having assumed the form of the Preceptor (deśika), will speak of that glory.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Reality," in the *Kālottara-mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Kārttikeya said:
It was previously understood that the division of Śiva is eightfold;
O Lord, tell me truly how one may know that God.
The Lord said:
That reality is divided within the Śaiva tradition; here, the differentiation of the powers (śakti) is explained.
O dear son, I shall tell you this regarding this matter, of which there is no doubt.
The whole (sakala), the partless (niṣkala), the void (śūnya), that which begins with the kalās, the sky adorned [with the vowels],
the destructive (kṣapaṇa), the non-destructive (akṣapa), that which stands within (antaḥstha), and the eighth is remembered as the throat-lip (kaṇṭhoṣṭha).
The Prāsāda mantra, as taught by Śaṅkara, is endowed with the six endings;
it is proclaimed as the Śivatattva, which is complete and resides within all bodies.
The Lord himself departs, casting off the body like the wind;
one should know him to be partless, Śiva devoid of the six qualities.
Having abandoned inhalation and exhalation, one should know that state which remains in the bodies like a piece of wood as "void," and one should contemplate it with the heart.
That which is heard on earth with a mouth shaped like a kiss (cuṃbākāra) should be known as kalāḍhya; now hear from me about that which resides in space (ākāśastha).
One should know that which is proclaimed as the end of the upward-moving nāda when it has been exhausted; situated there, it is endowed with space (ākāśa).
Having heard this with his face turned away, the Lord, the Teacher of the World, said, "Suffering lasts but a moment"; thus he is remembered as the one who brings about its destruction.
That which is proclaimed as the end of what has been diminished below the *nāda* should be known as *antastha*; it is proclaimed as that which is not to be recited (*anucārya*).
The eighth of the eight groups, the second of the seventh group,
that which transcends the groups, the end of the six, and the fourth of the seven.
Furthermore, one should join the first with the sixth and the sixth with the first;
conjoined with the crest of space (the letter *ha*), it is known as the eighth, the throat-lip (*kaṇṭhoṣṭha*).
This object of knowledge is exceedingly vast, adorned with the ornaments of the *kalās*.
Indeed, an excessive burden of the *tattvas* is established within that body. These divisions have been fully explained in the practice of the *siddhis*, beginning with *aṇimā*.
The state of being led [to the goal] and so forth is designated as liberation. Thus,
having [attained] such knowledge, one should initiate even immobile beings.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Eightfold Divisions," in the *Kālottara* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Īśvara said:
Just as the wind moves within an opening,
so too is the letter *U* [manifested] by means of the body, which is the color of a swan, and by the foot.
When the *iḍā* is joined with the *suṣumṇā* and flows within the body,
it is conjoined with the *bindu* and resides in all living beings.
The *haṃsa* is to be known as the individual soul (*jīva*) present in all living beings;
residing within the body as mere vital breath (*vāyu*), it is likewise perceived through the inner sounds (*nāda*).
All that is to be known flows [through it], and here the seed-syllable unfolds.
But the transition of the whole is Śiva, devoid of the six letters.
I shall further describe the *haṃsa* within the body of all embodied beings as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).
Furthermore, I shall describe Śiva as being partless (*niṣkala*) and devoid of the six syllables.
When they carry the letter *u* conjoined with the *bindu* while remaining at the place of the knot, she should be known as the Kuṇḍalinī, coiled like a serpent.
Joined with the *iḍā* and *suṣumṇā*, yet devoid of *bindu* and *nāda*,
it should always be understood as being without parts (*niṣkalā*) both in oneself and in the disciple.
But the transition of the partless [Śiva] is devoid of the six phonemes;
I shall further explain the knowledge of the Haṃsa, wherein this Void is born.
When there is the sound of clouds and thunder, or even the sound produced by [other] noises,
amidst the cries of elephants and horses and the clamor of various sounds—
if one perceives emptiness therein while remaining in the body like a log, one should know that state.
Wood, clods of earth, and stone are said to be insentient;
they remain motionless where they are and do not breathe again.
Now, when sound enters the ear, that is proclaimed as "the void" (śūnya).
One should indicate the transition of that void as being Hayagrīva.
Standing eternally on one foot, it is proclaimed as "Kalāḍhya";
when situated at the station of Suṣumnā, there is no doubt that the cause is the syllable *Huṃ*.
Likewise, here among the fires, situated in the crooked and the curved,
he repeatedly increases and consumes while remaining in the ether.
It constantly drinks the space that is the form of all embodied beings;
one should point out that the transition of Hayagrīva is indeed the sky, rich in its digits (kalās).
Wherein their own nature (*svabhāva*) arises—
[this is] the division of the animal-mantra (*paśu-mantra*), accompanied by the *bindu*.
When the auspicious [breaths] fill the empty wood,
it should be known that the void has been purified and they are always situated in the region of the throat.
But at the time of the great departure, no one knows the Lord of the World as he breathes out, stationed in space.
One should point out the transmission of the *Khamalam-kṛta* as Hayagrīva;
furthermore, this division of Hayagrīva is that which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Those people who do not perceive [the truth] through direct experience do not know reality.
Having heard of the Lord, the Teacher of the World, from whom all conceptual proliferation has ceased, he is called a "deva-kṣapaṇa";
because of that cessation, he is known as a kṣapaṇa.
There was a great sound of the Kṣapaṇakas and the hymns of Mahādeva; whenever anyone among the living beings raised a cry, "Mātrā! Mātrā! they would shout it out.
Where Mahākāla acts as the great leader,
he laughs, sings, and likewise utters cries of "Hāhā!"
Vedāraṇya is to be known as having Mahākāla and other deities;
wherever there is a great sound, there indeed Kṣapaṇa is traditionally taught to reside.
One should indicate the transference of Kṣapaṇa as belonging to Hayagrīva.
Now I shall describe what kind of transference occurs for that Kṣapaṇa.
Alas! Wherever a mendicant takes a knot and places it around his neck, or between his tongue and palate, or within his chest—where in that body is it produced?
One should know that the middle [state] is in the abdomen; it is always born from sound (nāda).
Therein occurs the transition of decay; decay is the exhaustion of the essence of saṃsāra.
One situated at the knot awakens everything; one situated at the knot is within the circle of enemies.
It is written in all the scriptures that it arises as being situated right within the body.
That which is the upward-moving resonance (nāda) is likewise the nature of Hayagrīva;
it is where the triangle-headed [vowel] resides, and where the letter A is produced.
In the middle of the night, he should always consume and drink from the palate and lips of Hayagrīva; he should withdraw [the essence] below by means of the resonance.
