The *iḍā* ascends for him, and through the *suṣumṇā*, the nectar-eaters are known;
or else, they are situated below, having entered the lower half of the *suṣumṇā*.
Beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), incomparable and yet possessing similarity, both supreme and inferior;
furthermore, O Goddess, those of Suṣumnā are proclaimed to be dark-complexioned.
In the Gaṅgā, however, the goddess Iḍā is proclaimed as the swift Gaṅgā;
its further division is the circular Koṭideśa.
The transverse channel (tiryaṅnāḍī) is at the center of the jewel; from it, creation arises instantly.
It is the immediate seed, Śiva, the Haṃsa, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) for all embodied beings.
Without knowing the reality of Śiva, one who has been initiated will not practice;
likewise, the individual soul [does not attain] devotion to Śiva or Śiva himself, [without knowing that reality].
Nirmitā, Jvalanī, Dhūmrā, Kṛṣṇā, and likewise Vidyutā;
Śarkarī, Bālamitrā, Sumati, and Prati-bodhanī.
The emanated [mantra] is to be known as having six syllables; in the Jvalinī [mantra], it should be doubled.
Dhūmrā is said to possess three qualities, while Kṛṣṇā should be known as having four;
Vidyā has five qualities, and Sarkarī should be known as having six.
Bālā possesses seven qualities, while Mitrā becomes eightfold;
Sumitrā is known to have nine qualities, and Bodhanī shall be the tenth.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Determination of Transitions, in the *Kālottara* consisting of seven powers.
The Lord said:
The transference should be known as eightfold, and again it should be known as thousandfold;
furthermore, it should be known in that same way by the number of one hundred and eight.
Having known that through its many divisions, one is indeed liberated from saṃsāra;
for the Haṃsa, abiding in the power of the peak (kūṭa-śakti), liberates when uttered with mastery.
For she is indeed consecrated at that time; otherwise, it is not ordained. By means of this, O Haṃsa, they truly perceive the knowledge of the body in its essential reality.
For them, there is no attainment of perfection by means of liberation; the Haṃsa remains bound within the knot. One should declare that it is only when liberated that it moves.
The transition at the tip of the nose is the power (śakti) whose essence is Śiva expressed through speech;
however, the Peak Power (kūṭaśakti) is to be known as being in Hayagrīva and Saṃkampa.
When one utters some mantra while exhaling,
the *haṃsa* accompanied by the *śaktis* becomes one with the *śakti* in a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*).
When the vital air flows joined with the *iḍā* and *suṣumnā*, it should be known as "equal flavor" (*samarasa*); thus the wise understand it at the tip of the nose.

One should know that there are seventy-seven [states]; among these, the waking-within-waking (jāgrājāgra) is intended. Furthermore, the "divider" (chedaka) is to be understood as that which is called reality (tattva), consisting of the nature of the Lord (īśvara).
Rudra is the uniter, and likewise the Śiva-tattva;
the Lord whose body is the axle is called Śrīkaṇṭha, the thrower.
He is indeed called the King of Devis, the one who performs infinite attraction;
the severing of the noose, however, is to be understood as coming from the Teacher, the knower of the Śiva-tattva.
One who knows the reality of Śiva is terrified by the well-spoken teachings on the knowledge of Haṃsa;
[therefore] one should understand the knowledge of Haṃsa, for the teacher will surely grant liberation.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Union of Powers," in the *Kālottara* consisting of seven powers.
Īśvara said:
Just as [pleasure] arises between two people through mutual affection, as in the case of a young maiden and her lover, I shall explain how that bliss is fully attained; of this there is no doubt.
When the two join with one another, yoga arises and happiness is born;
when they are separated from one another, human suffering proceeds.
Seeing you have returned once more, she embraces you with longing; tell me now what was previously indicated by you.
Since you have asked that which was spoken out of mere suspicion, why do those enraged ones say to you, "Are you one who speaks the truth?"
O auspicious lady, such and similar signs consisting of conviction regarding the recitation arise for the sake of union and happiness; otherwise, one would not know them at all.
For one who speaks otherwise, no conviction whatsoever arises;
even if one were to concede his happiness, it would be impossible to explain it.
The happiness that you have attained in a very short time—what you have said, O blessed lady, is exactly so; there is no doubt about it.
Out of ignorance, pleasure, and delusion, I have indeed spoken words that were pleasing;
forgive me, O dear and auspicious lady, and when the time comes, accept me as your lover.
O auspicious lady, through union there is happiness, the meeting with the knowledge of the yogi; he who is joined to that abides in happiness characterized by bliss.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Section on the Virgin," in the *Kālottara Mahātantra* consisting of seven powers.
19a) Īśvara said:
I shall now explain the ritual procedure of Kālacakra in due order;
it is renowned as Kālacakra because by means of it one awakens to time (kāla).
By the movement [of the breath] through the *iḍā* for one day and night, he lives for three years;
by the movement for two days and nights, he lives for two years.
By moving for three days and nights, he lives for one year;
by moving for four days and nights, he lives for six months.
By a movement of five days and nights, he lives for three months;
by a movement of six days and nights, he lives for two months.
By moving for seven days and nights, he lives for one month;
by moving for eight days and nights, he lives for half a month.
By moving for nine days and nights, he lives for ten days;
by moving for ten days and nights, he lives for five days.
With eleven days and nights, he lives for three days;
with twelve days and nights, he lives for two days.
With thirteen days and nights he lives for one day;
with fourteen days and nights he lives for half a day.
He lives for fifteen muhūrtas;
he may practice the vow for one day and likewise for half a night.
"It is the certainty of the scriptures that death will occur after six months;
by the movement of two watches [of the breath], he lives for one day and night."
Just as there are the *yāma* [hours], so too should the *cāma* and the *madhyamā* be;
this is declared to be the *Kālacakra*, especially out of affection for my son.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the Kālacakra, in the seven-hundred-verse Kālottara.
The Lord said:
I shall describe direct worship both concisely and in detail;
by seeing which, men attain the eternal, imperishable state.
That which is called the syllable *U* resides within the center of the navel.
It is the support of all the channels, and it is joined with the *haṃsa*;
seventy-two thousand channels are proclaimed to be there.
In their midst, O Skanda, is the great channel known as the *rājanāḍī*;
situated within it are five lotuses facing downwards.
All [the lotuses] are joined with two knots and endowed with the deities of the gods;
having placed those lotuses upright, one should pierce them with the root-mantra of Śiva.
Having made the gross root of Śiva [the object of focus], one should exhale the upward-moving breath;
indeed, joined with this exhalation, the individual soul goes to Śiva.
All this has been fully explained both in brief and in detail;
the upward progression of sentient beings has also been described by me from the beginning.
But the embodied soul itself should behold that fourfold universe;
the knower of the path always beholds the two solstices and the two equinoxes.
O child, having first performed the yoga of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka),
one should worship in due order, uttering the syllable *bhaya* at the beginning.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should cause [the disciple] to offer [the oblation] while placing it upon the head with a salutation;
O child, for during an eclipse of the sun, worship is indeed considered to be performed directly before the deity.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Direct Sacrifice," in the Kālottara.
Kārttikeya said:
In which of the five faces of the Śiva-fire does the supreme essence of Śiva reside?
O Teacher, destroyer of the bonds of the bound souls (paśu), [tell me] in which face that resides.
In what manner and how does one offer the formative forces (saṃskāra) into which fire?
In what does one perform the sacrifice, and in what is the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) traditionally taught to reside?
In which face, moreover, does one purify both sin and the self?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this in brief.
Īśvara said:
That which is declared as the noose among the nooses is proclaimed as the eastern face;
purification is in the northern face, while birth is in the western one.
The procedure for expiation is prescribed for this southern face;
O Mahāsena, for that upper face, a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is prescribed.
One should not cause the oblation to be offered upon the hands, feet, or back;
for the teachers who know the reality of the purification of the mouth are the ones who grant liberation.
Thus, when there is doubt regarding the sacraments, the teacher himself has not been consecrated;
yet the sacraments must be performed again—this is the truth, my child, that I tell you.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Consecration by the Fire of Śiva," in the Kālottara.
Hereafter, I shall explain the eightfold sign as it occurs:
namely, the blazing of fire and the touching of trees.
It is the strengthening of the wings, the destruction of great sins,
the transference of poison, and likewise the rendering [of it] seedless.
The destruction of fevers and seizing spirits is said to have eight types of signs;
having understood this according to the prescribed rule, renown arises everywhere.

The syllable *ha* is preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and situated in the middle of the fire (*ra*), thus forming *hrau*; likewise again, the beginning and the end are joined at the conclusion, which is beneficial as the blazing of the fire without [the initial] *ā*.
Having joined the fire with the stream and combined it with a thousand upward thrusts, through the application of the five-syllable mantra, it blazes forth; of this there is no doubt.
The letter *u* is at the very bottom and the letter *o* is situated halfway up;
joined with the letter *ha* in the middle, it is pressed between the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) at the beginning and the end.
As before, it should be applied; those who practice this yoga are rare to find. Slowly, with seventy breaths, the tree of the throat is made to dissolve.
Furthermore, his nourishment is established in the ear of Varuṇa;
he lives once again, just as that tree was before.
Furthermore, for him, that same [procedure] is performed again, but with one [element] excluded;
for this is the method of nourishment, fivefold and illuminated by the Bindu.
O Śambhu, Īśa is at the beginning with the letter *ha*, while Vahni and Parā are in the middle.
The application [of this] is at the time of the equinox for the purpose of paralyzing the fetters;
by seventy-one upward breaths, they are certainly severed—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, listen to how its reawakening occurs:
it is indeed joined with that which begins and ends with the letter *i*, while being placed in the middle of *e*.
The knower of reality should employ the mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), joined with the *bindu*, and ending with *namaḥ*, for the purpose of rousing all beings in the watery element.
It is established with the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, situated between the letters *ha* and *kṣa*;
as before, it is positioned in the center, endowed with the wind and the bindu.
It is said that by ascending Dadasi, one becomes like a cowherd.
I shall indeed explain that by which lightness arises:
the syllable *ukāra*, *sahakāra*, *aikāra*, and likewise *haṃ namaḥ*.
This is the Tulāpuruṣa yoga; it is joined with the udghāta, and the letter ya together with the letter ka is illuminated by the vowel ī.
The wise one, using the mantra *hro hro* in the middle and *hrīḥ* at the end, together with the Varuṇa [mantra],
certainly effects the transference of poison by means of this very eighth *udghāta*.
Just as the seedless state is achieved by seeing the blazing of the fire,
so too is a specific distinction prescribed here through the five gradual upward thrusts (udghātas).
Having placed the syllable *uṃ* at the beginning and the syllable *hūṃ* immediately thereafter,
with *hrauṃ hraṃ* first and *namaḥ* at the end, this is beneficial for the destruction of the planets.
Furthermore, at the time of the equinox, when eight hundred *udghātas* have passed,
one should then [recite] the *praṇava* and so forth, followed by *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, *hauṃ*, and again *phaṭ*.
By performing eight hundred suppressions (udghāta) with "hūṃ phaṭ," and then again "phaṭ" and "phaṭ phaṭ" in the western [direction], one swiftly destroys fever.
I have explained the application of the eight conditions;
having understood this, the wise man should perform his actions as he desires.
Śiva, the Lord of the World, is worshipped and shall always become manifest;
indeed, there is no conviction [of truth] without this, for knowing this one attains liberation, and not otherwise.
Success in this world is achieved, and with the body cast off, one shall go to Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Eightfold Realization," in the *Kālottara* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Kārttikeya said:
O Maheśvara, tell me the rule for all those who have taken lifelong vows;
explain to me truly how their withdrawal from such a state occurs.
Īśvara said:
O Six-faced One, I shall now proclaim the extraction of the *liṅga* for those who are lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*);
indeed, I shall explain their renunciation to you in brief.
Having spent either three nights or five nights, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa);
having performed the previously mentioned rite, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) and the withdrawal (nivartana).
One should place the yoni-cakra there according to the ritual procedure seen in the injunctions;
having drawn an eight-spoked wheel provided with two navels.
Having applied the reversal, one should recite the mantra for the final rite;
one should offer five oblations for each [syllable] in the final rite according to the sequence.
The wise one should offer [the oblation] with the heart-mantra, using the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Having performed it in this manner, as previously described, the worship there becomes final and complete.
The withdrawal of the desired [elements] indeed belongs to the ultimate [yogi] who has abandoned the aggregates;
having performed the emanation of the continuum, the ultimate yogis attain perfection.
Whether attached or a seeker of sense-objects, he is not tainted by the defects of karma;
this, my son, is what has been told to you regarding the specific nature of renunciation.
And for those others who have approached [for refuge], there is likewise their turning back from it.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the rite of initiation, in the *Kālottara Mahātantra*.
The Lord said:
I shall explain the *ucchiṣṭika* rite correctly and in due order:
having caused the Śiva-fire to flow [with water], one should subsequently purify the Śiva [fire].
Having purified the horn with water, one should perform the ash-bath as before;
having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should purify it with the *astra* seed-syllable.
Having performed the withdrawal of the desired [deity], one should place the feet upward;
having first prepared a layer of darbha grass, one should deploy the weapon-mantra everywhere.
With great concentration, one should cause the fire to blaze on all sides with a mantra,
using wood of sandalwood and agallochum, combined with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
Having meditated upon the Āgneyī Dhāraṇā within his own body, the knower of mantras, using whatever is at hand among all these [substances], may act as he desires with the Astra-mantra.
But after having been initiated, if one should transgress the rules (samaya),
that is indeed a great sin against either the deity or the guru.
O Guha, this has been declared as the means for removing the sins of those who are not liberated, those still possessed of doubt, and others whose natures are defiled.
I shall enter the abode of my own perception when there is a transgression of the commitments.
Their designations and conjunctions, as well as their grasping, should be understood as before;
thus, for one who performs the final sacrifice here according to the prescribed ritual.

"Completely liberated from all evil, he goes to Śiva like one who is purified. Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, on the funeral rite, in the *Kālottara-mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Henceforth, I shall explain the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) in brief;
indeed, I shall describe the weapon-sacrifice, which destroys defects, in its proper sequence.
On the previously mentioned pure ground, which has been smeared with cow dung,
one should place a water-filled jar provided with the mantra and the ritual substances.
One should place auspicious offerings in the directions starting from the northeast to ward off obstacles;
then, having drawn a lotus, one should worship it either on that [lotus] or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
O Guha, there are many obstacles on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
therefore, with every effort, perform the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) upon the mound without impediment.
Everywhere, the supreme sacrifice is ordained as peaceful upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
there is the enclosure wall, the pericarp in the lotus, and likewise the [petals] beginning with Dharma and Jñāna.
Likewise, dispassion, sovereignty,
and the powers [should be worshipped] at all times by the devotee according to the rules with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and other articles.
With that, the wise one, well-prepared, should construct a rampart;
he should place the divine Pāśupata weapon upon the pericarp,
having first fashioned it with the thirty-eight kalās and then installed it.
Having placed the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions and the enclosure in the intermediate directions in sequence,
this is the supreme and excellent seat of the weapon-mantra, which renders [the area] completely free of gaps.
One should place the vajra and the others externally in all ten directions:
the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, and likewise the noose in their proper sequence.
One should place the mace, trident, discus, and lotus in their proper sequence; indeed,
in the Pāśupata [rite], one should place them all around with a surrounding wall.
The worship and the fire-rite (agnikārya) are proclaimed as belonging to the eastern quarter;
one should make the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) circular, with its height being four finger-breadths.
It should be square, measuring one cubit on all sides;
it is the performer of all rites, especially for the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga).
On the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or when applying colored powders (rajas), one should construct the pit (kuṇḍa) according to its defining characteristics.
O Six-faced One, one should perform its purification by means of a wall;
one should carry out the rites of birth, expiation, and the ritual procedure in their proper sequence.
The wise one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the ritual procedures seen in the scriptures,
[offering] the divine Mahāpāśupata and the merit that serves as a protective wall.
Then, having offered oblations beginning with Vajra into the previously prepared vulva,
one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) ending with "HŪM PHAṬ VAUṢAṬ."
The wise one should place the womb (yoni) born of the enclosure within the station of the bindu;
situated there, it is drawn forth by the enclosure—of this there is no doubt.
For the initiation and other rites, however, one should perform the homa with twenty or thirty oblations;
for the full [initiation], one hundred and eight, and one should cast [the final oblation] with the Great Weapon mantra.
The initiation of the weapon (astra-dīkṣā) shall be completed; it cuts through all defects and is intent upon bringing about the liberation of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
Then one should perform the consecration with the jars prepared as previously described;
Vināyakas, planetary afflictions, and other obstacles are destroyed—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the Astra-yāga, in the *Kālottara-mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
The square, the half-moon, the three-part circle,
as well as the void marked with a vajra, the triangle (śṛṅgāṭa), and the void itself are thus proclaimed.
He who knows these principles in their proper order— as yellow, red, white, and black— is a knower of reality among the most excellent of those who know reality.
O Guha, for one who practices samādhi through both the combined and individual methods,
there is no doubt that its fruit will manifest here in this very life before long.
Those who know the true reality of the five states possess a nature endowed with brilliance;
having meditated upon these [states] as being within the head, one should offer the mind into that [state].
[The results are] paralyzing, causing affliction, increasing, creating enmity, and expulsion.
O Six-faced One, that which is gentle and generates joy—
one should meditate, with a mind concentrated on the rites for accomplishment, upon the triad situated within the Bindu.
O Six-faced One, having unified the five vowels of the Self with the Lord (Īśa),
there are those beginning with 'A' and ending with 'U', excluding the neuter vowels.
These indeed are the lords of the principle of the self (ātmatattva), proclaimed as the five pairs;
O child, having first purified the four beginning with the element of earth (bhūta).
The state of being, likewise reality, and the seed in their proper order;
as well as smell, form, taste, sound, and touch as the fifth.
Indeed, one should offer these together with their respective subtle elements (tanmātras) in successive order;
the fragrances and the elements should be offered as the essence of taste, O Six-faced One.
The principles of fire (tejas-tattvas) have been fully described; one should offer the seed-syllables of touch (sparśa-bījas) into the fire.
Having produced sound within sound and enclosed it within the cavity of the heart, one should offer the various principles of one's own mind into the fire in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, there are the elements beginning with earth, the qualities beginning with dharma, the forms beginning with shape, and likewise the vowels.
This supreme consecration is prescribed in all tantras.
One should purify with *hrāṃ hrīṃ*,
and cleanse with *hrīṃ hram*.
With *hrūṃ hrīṃ*, one should cause [it] to overflow; with *hyaiṃ hlāṃ*, it becomes firm.

Having thus brought about the separation of friends among these very [beings], one should sequentially resolve the fragmentation of the knots of karma; having performed the conjunction with Vāmā, one performs the disjunction through Jyeṣṭhā.
One should raise the fierce [element] upward and place it in successive order.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Kālottara-mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Kārttikeya said:
How does the movement of the *haṃsa* abide within the center of the body?
Tell me all this in brief, according to the truth.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Skanda, I shall explain the sequential procedure for the movement of the *haṃsa*.
Indeed, the *iḍā* is the left eye, while the *suṣumnā* is on the right.
Piṅgalā is said to reside in the ears, nose, teeth, bones, and skull;
as well as in the hands, feet, heart, shanks, breasts, soles of the feet, and the two arms.
Gāndhārī always performs [worship] on both [the testicles],
Hastinī on the testicles and the penis, and Pūṣā on the belly and the anus.
Yaśas resides in all the nails, Alambuṣā in all the pores of the skin, Kūrma in the hips and back, Dhuvini in the nape of the neck, Kaṅkaṇī in the bones and marrow, and Śaṅkhinī dwells at the end.
For one who is awake in the *iḍā*, the teacher explains the vast [dreams];
one who relies on the right eye sees a dream in the *suṣumnā*.
Gāndhārī discharges semen, Hastinī likewise urine, and Pūṣan discharges feces; each finds pleasure at the appropriate time, just as it is.
Alambuṣā and Kuhū are thirsty for the faces;
Śaṅkhinī drinks the water immediately from the very source, for all [these channels] are indeed so.
Iḍā is in Karṣaṇa, while Piṅgalā is in Koya;
Suṣumnā is in Viśāda, and Gāndhārī has taken refuge in Bhaya.
Hastinī laughs, and Pūṣā is based on sound; Yaśasī perceives, and Alambuṣā perceives taste.
The Marudvaktra channel carries feces, and the Śaṅkhinī smells odors;
the Iḍā channel is situated in the prāṇa, and the Piṅgalā in the apāna.
In the *samāna* [vāyu], however, is *suṣumnā*; *gāndhārī* is born from the *udāna*. In the *vyāna*, there is the one named *hastinī*, and *pūṣā* is situated in the *nāga* [vāyu].
Kūrma is Kuhū, while Alaṃbuṣā is in Kṛkara;
Devadatta is Marudvaktra, and Dhanañjaya is Śaṅkhinī.
At the time of death, one indeed gasps repeatedly;
the *devadatta* wind expands with a long, rattling sound.
Dhanañjaya stands in the body even after death and does not leave it;
thus this host of winds is established within the heart of every being.
The lower channel, however, is situated in the form of pus;
the world of the ancestors is in the *iḍā*, while the moon is in the *piṅgalā*.
In Suṣumnā is the world of all beings; Gāndhārī is the source of worms and insects; in Hastinī is the world of the Rākṣasas; and in Pūṣā is certainly hell.
And indeed, donkeys and camels are born when the sun [is obscured];
but the movement of the swan on the trident grants the door to liberation.
The fires of the letter *ha* blaze forth, and by the thunderbolt, the swan proceeds.
The army of the Śailas and Kālāgniratha was like a forest fire.
One may shake the three worlds again from the bondage of worldly power;
Suṣumnā is the vehicle of the deity, while Piṅgalā is the city of the Asuras.
In the *iḍā* [channel], there is the human world; in the *gāndhārī*, birth as a worm;
in the *hastinī*, the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*); and in the *plavācana*, certainly hell.
Thus, their state of being and the state of liberation are one and the same.
Beyond this, no [other] gates are found; therefore, this gate is praised.
The wise one who performs the rites for the goddesses, beginning with the *ajā* (goat) sacrifice,
shall not experience birth again.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Practice of the Haṃsa," in the *Kālottara-mahātantra* consisting of seven hundred verses.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva!
The omniscient Śiva, eternally satisfied, endowed with awakening and sovereignty,
whose glory is never diminished and who possesses infinite power, reigns supreme.
Now, I shall briefly describe the daily rites and so forth, for the benefit of those of limited intellect.
Having risen in the morning and meditated upon Maheśvara in the heart, [one should proceed].
Having gone outside to a clean place on ground covered with grass,
one should void excrement, urine, and so forth, without facing toward the Guru or other venerable persons.
During the night, he remained silent with his face turned toward the north; during the day, his face was turned toward the south.
His sacred thread rested upon his right ear, and his eyes were fixed intently on the tip of his nose.
Having evacuated the anus, one should perform purification with earth and water using clods of earth and the like;
one application of earth is for the penis, five for the anus, and ten for the left hand.
Having joined the seven [limbs] of both hands once each on the feet and hands,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should cleanse the teeth with prescribed tooth-sticks.
That [staff] for liberation should be eight finger-breadths long, while for worldly enjoyment it should be nine finger-breadths;
or else, [the lengths] for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of low birth [should be determined accordingly].

Men should avoid brushing their teeth on the new moon day, the eighth, the fourteenth, the full moon, and the sixth lunar days, as well as on the days of the sun’s entry into a zodiac sign and on the days when the moon is eclipsed.
One should not do so while facing the sun or while bowing down.
Alternatively, having purified his mouth with mouthfuls of water from the sun, he should perform his bath;
and that [bath] is likewise of four kinds: Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Māhendra, and Māruta.
The earthly [weight] is in the mantra; that which is approved by Kapila is mental.
Now, the one hundred and ten-fold [measure]. (p.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord of Pārvatī, O Master, you have spoken to me a mere aphorism (sūtra) that is concise in words yet vast in meaning, and which is crowded with manifold categories of existence.
O Lord, that reality known as Time has not been understood in its true essence;
it is concise in its textual form yet possesses great significance, being established as an extreme secret.
O Supreme Lord, for the benefit of mankind, speak to me concerning those overwhelmed by great delusion and submerged in hunger and thirst.
O Śambhu, do not open the eyes of the Lord of the Earth for those deluded beasts who are [merely] infatuated by a mere name; do not do so regarding the true reality.
And the meaning of the mantra, according to its actual state and according to those who abide in their respective places,
is deposited along with the principles (tattva), distinguished by vowels and prosodic measures.
O Śambhu, tell me the truth: in what place does reality reside?
Yet again, you have described the God as omnipresent and all-pervading.

O Supreme Lord, you have described [the deity] as residing in Brahmā, residing in the limbs of Śiva, residing in the elements, and residing in the weapon; yet what was spoken has not been fully comprehended by me.
Peaceful, omnipresent, empty, all-pervading, and existing in many ways—
the one Lord, the Reality, has been described as manifold, O God.
O Śambhu, you have described the five types of pride as being distinct;
O Supreme Lord, purification must be performed regarding those elements.
Five, four, and one, and also two—everything is empty and without support; consciousness alone remains.
O God, O Supreme Lord, this meaning of the question causes delusion;
O All-Knowing One, clarify for us—whose minds are bewildered—the meaning of these few words.
O Lord, how can that which is empty and without support abide within consciousness?
It is taught that consciousness is everything; this is my great doubt.
How should one contemplate the nectar flowing within the *prakṛti*?
That nectar is established wherever it resides within the process of *prakṛti*.
O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord, which of these two natures is it,
at the end of which that [state] is situated— namely, the immortal state that destroys death?
And how many types of death, O Supreme Lord, are established?
And what is it that the Lord, the Master who abides within the end of nature, destroys, O God?
O Lord of Gods, make it flow; it should be contemplated by practitioners.
O Śambhu, out of your grace, please tell me this most secret [teaching].
O Supreme Lord, O Lord of Gods, the placement of the heart-lotus has been indicated by you through various designations, established within the syllable *oṃ*.
O Maheśvara, was this distinction between the various types of breath-control not known to you? O Sūta, [it is established] by means of the purification rite and the regulation of the breath.
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M,
as well as the eightfold primordial group (pūryaṣṭaka) and the subtle elements (tanmātra), have been differentiated but not revealed.
O Maheśvara, how many aspects should the syllable *a* be known to have?
And the syllable *u*, O Lord of Umā—tell me truly of the syllable *m* according to each of its states.
Beyond the fourth state, the supreme deity who is proclaimed as the Fourth (Turya),
there resides the peaceful Sadāśiva in the form of Sound (Nāda).
O Lord of the World, tell me this distinction among them,
O Śambhu, so that I may understand the meditative absorption that destroys death.
Tell me of the apprehension of form; the poetic form is recited [as follows]:
the gross, the subtle, and the supreme deity were previously described as the means of reasoning.
Sound is said to be gross, while that which consists of thought is subtle;
the God who is free from thought is declared to be both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara).
Tell me, how many kinds of gross sound (*śabda*) are to be known?
O Lord, how many kinds of thought (*cintā*) are there, and what is the nature of that reality (*tattva*)?
How can that which is devoid of form and characteristics be grasped through thought?
O Lord, how can that which is devoid of thought be known as anything else? O Sovereign of the Gods, all this is like a great ocean for one seeking the meaning of the categories of existence.
O Supreme Lord, speak in detail to me, your devotee;
O Master, you have already taught the chapter on bathing and the application of ash and camphor.
O Lord of the Lords of the World, what was spoken by me has been understood;
the worship of the God of Gods has indeed been described in brief.
O Devatānanda, the supreme and infinite lotus of Śambhu, supported by Dharma and the other [qualities], has been described to you specifically according to the ritual procedure.
O Lord of the Gods, explain to me the array of powers (śaktivyūha) with clear meaning;
how do all these principles reside within the heart?
O Supreme Lord, they worship this secret; tell it to me:
first the seed and sprout through Śakti, then the infinite lotus.
O Lord of Gods, what is that primordial power (pūrva-śakti) to be known as, which spreads from the seed to the sprout? O Lord, may I create an infinite lotus.
Those people who are experts in the sūtras recite the sūtra here as follows:
"In the beginning, through the power of the seed-syllable, the infinite lotus comes into being."
O Lord of Gods, O Master, tell me the definitive conclusion regarding these two feet; and at the end, O Lord, you have explained how one should perform the Anantaka rite in due order.
Of what nature is the Anantaka-sūtra, and how is it performed in sequence?
Furthermore, the ritual procedure for the fire-offering (agnikārya) has been described in brief.
The ritual acts beginning with scraping, as well as the sprinkling again,
and the birth starting from the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) and so forth, have been described in brief.

The application of oblations is established in many ways; however, because it has been described very briefly, it is not fully understood. Therefore, the Lord is the one who performs the manifold rites.
He also taught the procedure for nourishment (*āpyāyana*),
as well as specifically for the purposes of nourishing (*puṣṭi*), killing (*māraṇa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and bewildering (*mohana*).
Regarding the paralyzing of those to be subdued, the possession by spirits, and the seating [of the disciple],
as well as at the time of initiation for the fetters— how do the mantras function in these cases?
"O Lord, O Master, how does the division of mantras occur— namely, illumination, awakening, striking, and the destruction of impurities?"
Because they are so few, the various classes of mantras and their many purposes were not fully understood; nevertheless,
practitioners and others perform sacrifices with them through various types of rites.
O Śambhu, how is it that those who are of a single form bestow the fruits of desire? Furthermore, what is the measurement of the mandala, including its gates and enclosures?
The womb, the lotus, the city, and the sky— [what is] the determination of the filaments, from the petal-tip to the sub-petal-tip, for the two-faced one?
How are they situated according to the measurement of the pericarp? What is the measurement for the other rites, and what is the characteristic of the colored powders?
O God, when the lines are inferior, the [mandala] should be especially large for the purpose of nourishment, while it should be subtle for pacification or killing.
O Supreme Lord, what merit or fault would there be for him in this case?
And how should initiation be performed by teachers for the practitioners and others?
The five principles, beginning with the earthly, are indeed established within a single principle;
yet they were not understood by you, O Mahādeva, when the time for initiation had arrived.
Which among the principles is that of the earth, and likewise of water and the north?
Among the forms of fire, air, and space, which are proclaimed to be the seed-syllables?
O Lord of Umā, due to this confusion, I do not understand how all the principles (tattvas) are indeed situated within them. Please explain the regions.
O Śaṅkara, how are those to be accomplished (sādhya) at the time of initiation when they reside within one principle after another? And how does the power of the principles (tattva-bala) come to be?
All are said to be omnipresent; all are permeated by omniscience.
They are pervasive, stainless, and pure; how then can there be any purification of them?
O Maheśvara, you have declared that [beings] are designated as impure or pure;
yet you have described [the Self] as all-pervading, reaching even down to cowherds and women.
O Lord, how is the Supreme Deity situated within the end of sound (nādānta), or how is He established in purity?
O Lord, tell me the meaning of this question, for it causes me confusion.
How is there purity and impurity, and what constitutes the nature of mantra? How might this be so, by which I may understand initiation that bestows the fruit of nirvāṇa?
All those principles (tattvas) have been declared pure, for they are the lords of the lords of reality;
how then could they, being impure, be joined in the sacrificial rite?
Cessation is declared to be the earth; she is proclaimed as that which is called the primary element (bhūta).
It is said that he was born as Saghna, established in the state of Brahman.
Or how is it said to be pure? The Goddess Maheśvarī is pure;
she is declared to be the heart of the Great Lord.
O Lord of Gods, how is the purification of the Brahman-principle prescribed?
O Lord, the Brahman would be the short seed-syllable, having a short form through that [purification].
O Maheśvara, how is the earth the seed for the sake of the liberation of the world?
O God, best among the gods, what distinction exists among seeds?
Cessation is proclaimed as the earth, and likewise as the principle of the Self;
O Lord of the Gods, that differentiation of principles has been described by you in many ways.
Water becomes the foundation, and the power of the elements is firmly established;
that [power] must be offered with the head, O Supreme Lord—so it has been declared.
One should know Vāmadeva as the short vowel situated in the letter *ī*.
How, then, is he to be purified? The pure deity is stainless (*nirañjana*).
Therefore, it is pierced by me; it is proclaimed as established through the arising of the *kalās*.
Know that the fifth is Aghora, which is to be offered together with the group of six.
O Lord of Pārvatī, you have spoken of that Supreme Goddess Śikhā;
how indeed should she be purified when the time for one's own initiation has arrived?
The pacification of the wind is fully described as being established in the pacification of the elements;
one should know that person to be situated in the single syllable *ekāra*.
O Supreme Lord, it has been declared that one must never offer oblations into the *kavaca*;
the supreme void beyond the *śāntyatīta* is proclaimed as the *ākāśa*.
Nevertheless, it was perceived by Devatānandana:
"O Lord, what kind of grace is this? You are the omniscient Supreme Lord."
It is pervasive, all-encompassing, pure, and known as the Great Purity.
You have described it in many ways through its various divisions and numerous syllables.
O Śambhu, I have not understood the definitive meaning of that deity;
O Lord of Gods, what is intended by the address "be gracious" (prasīda) for the sake of recognition?
O Supreme Lord, what need is there for names for the Nameless God? O Kevala, what purpose do the various colors serve for the cuckoos dwelling therein?
What are the forms of these [deities] that arise when the time for initiation has arrived—
the all-pervading Lord of the universe, the supreme reality in its entirety?
O Great Lord, Supreme Sovereign, for the sake of the liberation of the world, You have spoken of the bound soul (paśu), the principles (tattva), and the counter-principles (pratitattva), O Śaṅkara.
"O God, these words are supremely bewildering and difficult to penetrate.
O Supreme Lord, one hundred seeds of each kind must be offered as oblation."
The sevenfold group of the four [elements], excluding birth and so forth,
and the fifth itself, should be offered with devotion as described.
Thus, O Śaṅkara, five hundred [verses] were spoken of old by the God of gods through his knowledge to the Teacher, the Lord.
O Dakṣa, how does the expiation for that come about?
Always enlighten me on this most wonderful question.
"O Lord of Gods, let it be that one performs the oblation with the seed-syllable (bīja) in due order;
how indeed does the application proceed within these mantras?"
Since it contains few syllables yet great meaning, how was its existence maintained? One should offer a hundred oblations for each [syllable], or one should perform five hundred oblations.
Thereafter, O Maheśvara, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with a gracious mind;
for the sake of purification through expiation, one should offer eight oblations each in due order.
One should perform the fire-oblation in the proper sequence, conjoined with the seed-syllable;
in this way, initiation is completed, free from [the cycle of] birth and so forth.
Yet, even when the oblation has been performed, practitioners are not released from the bondage of birth;
O Lord, this statement which you have uttered is truly marvelous.
"But when there is knowledge, O Lord of Gods, in the pervasive Śiva who is grace itself,
no expiations arise; tell me this, O Śaṅkara."
O Maheśvara, how are they joined through the application of the seed-syllables and weapons?
O Maheśāna, O Great Lord, [explain] that which resides in the elements and that which resides in Brahmā.
O Lord, all these [elements] residing in the limbs are employed in the Śiva-sacrifice;
O Maheśvara, these seventeen have indeed been declared by you as those to be purified.
O Mahādeva, you do not know how those who are sacrificed in the ritual are liberated;
for practitioners are not liberated from their bonds merely by the offering being made.
O Supreme Lord, the entire secret of mantras has been told,
because it establishes the state of Śiva for one who is purified by all purificatory rites.
Nevertheless, purity shall not come to pass as long as one does not find yoga;
when the supreme yoga is known, then liberation is attained.
Thus indeed my mind is agitated and my senses impaired by this question;
therefore, O Lord, speak to me in such a way that I may become free from doubt.
O Śaṅkara, the seed-syllables for the seventeen Sādhyas have been proclaimed; by means of these, purification occurs for those who have practiced them.
O Devatānanda, the purification of each individual mantra has been described by the Lord in many ways, yet it has not been understood by me in its true essence.
O Maheśvara, [the rites] are indeed worship, sprinkling, striking, as well as withdrawal, union, and deposition.
O Mahādeva, Lord of Pārvatī, the extraction of even a single noose has been proclaimed by me; it has been told to you by means of the Heart-mantra.
Nevertheless, O Supreme Lord, there would be no manifestation [of the result] in the purification through that initiation;
therefore, a hundred oblations in one's own essential nature (svatatva) have been taught to you.
O Lord of Umā, my own true nature is not known by me; for there is doubt regarding the matter of that [oblation] which, O God, must be offered a hundred times in the Śiva-sacrifice.
The extraction from the *Hṛdaya* has been told according to the sequence of Manu;
O Lord, tell me that very sequence so that I may understand it.
According to the ritual procedure of Śiva’s sacrifice, there is the severing of the bonds of the bound soul (paśu),
as well as the extraction, the sprinkling, and especially the striking.
This yoga, joined with the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra), has been described in its proper sequence;
yet this cause of delusion was not fully grasped by me.
First, the Heart-mantra of the Lord, which performs all rites, was taught;
then his grace was declared, and immediately after that, the syllable *phaṭ*.
The seventeen mantras of the Lord consist of both the indivisible and the divisible;
by means of which that purity belonging to the Supreme Lord is truly known.
Action abiding in each respective reality has been explained, yet it was not fully grasped;
those of small intellect have not all purified the meaning of the reality of everything.
O Supreme Lord, it has not been understood due to delusion and the limited nature of one's cognition;
how so, when the five elements are conjoined with the practice of dhāraṇā?
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered by me with the differentiation of the syllables of Brahman and endowed with the meaning of grace; thus is liberation ordained.
O Lord, since such is the established state of existence within this world of transmigration,
how may I understand, O Śambhu, the conceptualization of the reality of the seed-syllables?
Those beings who are the supports are indeed the *kalās* residing within the mouth;
O Śaṅkara, how then does their state of Brahmanhood come to be?
The pure Brahmas have been fully described, as well as the impure classes of beings;
these were previously declared by you alone, O Supreme Lord.
Those *kalās* are known as "manifested" (*vyakta*); how can their purification be achieved?
For you have not yet explained the complete purification by means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
The limbs (aṅgas) are said to be complete, while the digits (kalās) are subtle and stainless;
thus has this been explained in reverse order for the sake of those with limited intelligence.
O Śambhu, those digits (kalās) which have been described as bestowing liberation upon all castes—
by means of them, O God, the all-pervading Sadāśiva exists as the ultimate reality (tattva).
O Lord, this entire universe has the elements as its support, and those elements,
O Maheśvara, are declared in the *Pūrvatant*ra to be of two kinds: gross and subtle.
Earth, which sustains itself, is declared to have five forms;
water is said to possess four qualities, and fire, O Lord, has three qualities.
They say that wind is twofold, and space possesses a single form;
these are declared to be the gross elements, the lords of the sounds of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
The subtle parts situated within the [five] kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti and ending with Śānti, have been pointed out;
those illustrious ones residing therein are indeed said to be immutable and imperishable.
Those fourteen [evolutes] that are predominant in qualities undergo destruction in their gross form;
however, the subtle ones, having transcended [the gross], are to be known as omniscient, all-pervading, and supreme.
The Great Pure Ones, the Beings, the Final, and the Ultimate Reality—this is declared to be Nirvāṇa; this group of four is indeed Sadāśiva.
O Maheśvara, its purification has been prescribed by means of the heart;
for this reason, O Lord, one has transcended the great delusion.
Awaken me, O Mahādeva, through your instruction that makes the meaning clearly known;
for you yourself have declared that the yoga of Madhu is the cutter of bonds.
Whoever attains the equinox and the great yoga is liberated;
by the mere knowledge of which, the destruction of the bonds of the bound soul (paśu) occurs.

Having known the earth and the others, the ointments and the rest, as well as sound and the other qualities along with the winds, the presiding deity of the mantra, and the Self, one is liberated from bondage.
The mantras, known as the *dhāraṇās*, begin with Śakra and end with Vāyu;
these are declared to be the gross *kalās* pertaining to the deities (*adhidaiva*).
It was fully explained in the *Āditantra*, but in this tantra it is otherwise;
because of this absence of delusion, O Supreme Lord, [the reality] is indeed known.
Having beheld the earth with a universal disposition, one becomes purified;
why then has it been further urged by means of the yoga that is free from egoism?
Having joined the conscious and unconscious together, it was uttered twice by the feet [of the Teacher] at the time of initiation,
O Mahādeva, during the expansion of the sun.
"It liberates; there is no doubt in this, O Supreme Lord, as you have said.
The mind does not recognize the mind, nor likewise the state of double practice."
O Lord Bhāskara of great splendor,
please grant me your grace, so that there may quickly be liberation for me, and all that is auspicious may be pacified.
O Lord Śaṅkara, how does the eclipse of the sun occur?
It is joined with poison, consisting of illusory flesh, and situated at the feet.
And then the thread ascends if it is properly applied;
this must be performed with effort by the Lord for the sake of perfect attainment.

The snares bound by the mind are like clusters of jewels upon a son; they arise from the heart-lotus and other such sources. But that mind, accompanied by the son—having given all this away, O Pārvatī, [attains] liberation.
The lotus situated at the heart and so forth, which is surrounded by a lotus, is thus prescribed;
O Lord, all of this is a cause of delusion.
But by means of subtle practice, O God Śaṅkara,
he is impelled through the divine path of yoga by that manifest [power].
Having known him, who consists of wind...
But by means of the equinox yoga... [text missing] ...||
If this is so for you, then indeed the purpose [of your inquiry] is out of a desire to exhaust all directions.
O God, there are three methods for the initiation of the fire;
[how can] their liberation occur without knowing the procedure according to the rules? (p.
The ritual procedure is said to be of many kinds and is explained at great length in the Siddhānta.
O Lord, it was understood by me that the great tradition which causes delusion consists of the conceptualization of mandalas through the various divisions of sacrificial sessions (satra-yāga).
O Supreme Lord, it has been taught that [the disciple] possesses various forms and qualities;
having performed the supreme initiation, one should subsequently establish him in the reality (tattva).
O Śambhu, when this has been spoken by you, what then follows from that application?
If initiation does not bring about purification, how can it be the destroyer of birth?
O Lord of Gods, why then is that [reality] not employed first?
For it is all-pervading, subtle, partless, and resides within the heart.
O Lord of Pārvatī, the all-pervading God who bestows liberation has been described;
without the essential reality (tattva), there is no liberation, and without the essential reality, there is no higher goal.
O Lord of practitioners, one does not attain reality without reality;
therefore, everything that has arisen, whether moving or unmoving, is composed of reality.
O Lord of Sūras, why would one not perform that very initiation at the outset,
by which the purification of the reality of mantras was taught to you, O Mahādeva?
One should undertake re-initiation (punardīkṣā) in the sacrifice of the path of the kalās, which arises from yoga;
for having attained the equinox of yoga, who would not be liberated from bondage?

Having pierced and entered, one should deposit the womb; one should then join principle (tattva) with principle. Having encapsulated it with Śakti, one should cast it out with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
"O Lord, thus the entire initiation consists of five principles;
please explain the specific details by which no confusion may arise."
O Supreme Lord, grant me awakening through a clear scripture, by which I may know that reality; for initiations are recorded as being of many kinds.
O sinless one, regarding what you previously stated concerning the seizing and releasing of the bound soul (paśu):
where exactly are the internal and external fetters (pāśas) firmly established?
O Maheśvara, tell me in which place those [channels] are to be severed, what kind of sudden departure (*sadyotkrānti*) it is, and how the animals (*paśu*) may be rendered free from defect.
"O Lord of Gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, this has not been understood by me through mere names alone. Therefore,
O Protector, explain it to me so that full conviction may arise."

the principle of Time (*kālatattva*) exists in two states, while Niyati assumes a single form.
The letter *ma* is thus fully explained as the *śivatattva* characterized by tamas.
I shall now describe the syllable *U*, which is established as the Rajasic Viṣṇu;
its principle is said to be Vidyā—listen to its sequence as well.
The Puruṣa, Prakṛti, the Manifested, and the qualities produced by me— O son of Śaṅkara, that principle of Puruṣa has been described as threefold.
One should know that the unmanifest is twofold, conjoined with the manifest; the subtle elements (tanmātras) are to be understood as being of one kind. Now hear concerning the support.
The seat of the three measures (trimātrāsana) has been described; the second is the support of the ear.
Furthermore, the pentad beginning with earth is proclaimed as being of one kind.
O observer of excellent vows, the *ātmatattva* is declared to be *sāttvika*.
One who is established in the *ātmatattva* immediately becomes one born in reverse order within the *vidyātattva*.
Aghora resides in the principle of Śiva, while Sadāśiva resides in the principle of Bindu;
beyond Sadāśiva is the supreme deity Nāda, which is most difficult to attain.
That which is called the nectar (amṛta) situated at the end of the sound (nāda) is declared to be emanation (sṛṣṭi), and this is the process (prakriyā), O fair-faced one.
O auspicious one, it has been declared that [this practice] abiding in the five principles destroys death;
furthermore, O sinless one, I shall explain it again in brief.
Established with nine principles and facing in all directions are Prakṛti,
Puruṣa, Niyati, and Kāla.
The five elements, ending with Māyā, are fully contained within the syllable A;
established in the principle of Īśvara and Vidyā, he is both with parts and without parts.
Sadāśiva and Śivā are established, as is the partless (niṣkala) Śiva;
these nine principles have been declared, and they are remembered as the three principles.
Furthermore, there shall be one reality, the reality of Śiva, which is the great flood;
I shall explain its division so that it may exist in its various states of measure (mātrā).
But the *mātrā*, my child, consists of a quarter-part added [to the preceding];
now listen as to how the division of the syllable comes to be for you.
The syllable has been described as being first; it consists of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.
O child Guha, listen attentively to their division.
The head, the crescent moon, and the staff—these three parts indeed arise from the letter *A*.
That which is the other, consisting of two humps, is the fourth part within the division of reality (*tattva*).
In the midst of that, however, the established principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is to be joined;
it is to be understood as Pratiṣṭhā, and it is described as consisting of a single digit (kalā).
These have indeed been described in brief as beginning with the letter *a* and ending with *sa*;
now, O Lord of Putra, I shall tell you the fourth part concerning the letter *u*.
The head-staff, the wheel, and that which is joined with the remaining portion.
From the mouth [of the letter *ma*], above and below that wise one,
I shall describe the head of the letter *śa*, which is half-tiryaṅga (diagonally inclined).
I shall describe the upper portion as Śaka and the head as half-tiryaga;
likewise, the upper portion and the tiryaga portion are situated upon the head.
Know that state of Śiva to be established beyond the two measures (mātrās); it is called the half-measure (ardhamātra), a station transcending the eighteen.
Below that is the Bindu, which is knowledge; it is the all-pervading Maheśvara. O observer of noble vows, situated above those is the union of the Mātrās.
That which is described as the subtle, partless (niṣkalā) [reality] above the Bindu is that [state].
And Dhanañjaya, the omniscient one, together with the wise Śiva—these are indeed established in one place; thus they should be understood by those who contemplate pervasion.
O Grasper, that place where they go to dissolution is the immortal state;
I shall explain its practice by which death is no longer found.
O Six-faced One, one should contemplate that thread flowing from the upper part;
make the Great Reality face downward, situated within the Suṣumṇā.
One should always contemplate [the deity] flowing with thousands of streams of milk above him,
O wise one, as he remains within the space of the heart.
Reflecting thus, a man who is always intent on the true nature of reality lives as one truly lived; he is truly possessed of a son, even though this [body] has been led to the abode of death.
How much more so, then, for the supreme master of practitioners who, by the power of thorough knowledge,
meditates upon the Supreme Lord— how could he ever enter into death?
The yogi quickly becomes omniscient and a Great Lord (Maheśvara),
and he shall always be the creator of the two-fold arrangement and of the cosmic eggs (aṇḍas).
And he who performs this rite in such a manner becomes a destroyer of the nooses.
This nectar that destroys death has been told to you, O blessed one.
Thus ends the second section on the classification of sūtras within the *Kālajñāna* consisting of one thousand three hundred verses.
O Guha, I shall further explain to you the grasping of the embodied form.
Listen to how it should be for both the practitioner and the preceptor.
O Guha, the form (mūrti) is seen to be of two kinds: the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).
That which is known as the supreme, subtle sixteenth digit (kalā) is that by which the form, initially endowed with consciousness, is conceptualized.
Consciousness is designated as the state; therein the reality is established.
Through the union with that reality-consciousness, the cage of the body comes to be.
But he [is that] supreme body of the process previously described,
which has arisen from the unmanifest and is manifest, having Śiva as its essence.
From that very [Self], space arose; from space, the Lord Wind;
from Wind, Fire was produced; and from Fire, Water was born.
Water, however, was born from earth, and it is traditionally held to possess five qualities;
it is deficient by one quality compared to the others, while the remaining four are those previously mentioned.
From that portion of the primordial tattva, a form (mūrti) was produced;
from it, the five elements previously mentioned are born.
The supreme form is declared to be that which resides within all living beings;
the lower one, known as "become" (bhūta), is said to be designated as Brahman.
From that, there arises the remainder, which is the domain of the collection of the sense organs;
it is conjoined with the garland of principles (tattvamālā) and is proclaimed as the triple essence (tritatva).
Pervaded at all times by that [consciousness] through its various forms and divisions,
the aggregate of the elements, which is the domain of the collection of one's own senses, is completely consumed.
O mighty-armed one, O observer of excellent vows, having consecrated [himself] with consciousness established in the five-fold upward stroke within the nectar, as previously proclaimed.
Then, O Mahāguha, one should take up the auspicious form consisting of the essence of the five Brahmans; it is declared to be the "Aparā" (the Lower) and is known as the "Elemental" (bhūtākhyā).
One should place Īśāna on the portion of the head, Tatpuruṣa on the face,
Mahāghora on the heart, and one should assign Vāmadeva to the private parts.
One should place Sadyojāta on the feet; one should place the Lord Ādisṛṣṭi upon all the limbs, and for the others, beginning with Sadyojāta.
One should perform the Brahma-installation from the feet up to the crown of the head.
One should install Vāmadeva in the secret place and Bahurūpa in the heart.
One should join the god Tatpuruṣa to the mouth and Īśāna to the head;
having first performed the Brahma-nyāsa, one should subsequently arrange the limbs (aṅgas).
Having first placed the eye, one should likewise place [the other limbs] from the heart to the end;
for those mantras characterized by Brahman which have been declared in the extraction of mantras (mantroddhāra).

O observer of noble vows, one should perform their placement (nyāsa) upon the locations of the limbs; having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place those [mantras] on the head after having placed them there.
One should place the *śikhā* on the crest-lock, and the *netra*, as previously envisioned, upon the eyes;
the *kavaca*, which protects the body, should be applied to all the limbs.
One should place the weapon-mantra in the hand, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions;
this form is declared to be established as both supreme and non-supreme.
O Mahāsena, by means of that [knowledge] one should worship the Lord, both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala);
having worshipped by that means, O Mahāsena, one does not take on a body again.
Alternatively, having purified his state of being with a mind that is focused,
he should first perform the internal and external [purifications] and thereafter begin the sacrifice.

The elements are declared to exist externally; the wise know them to exist within the three principles (tattvas). O Skanda, as you have asked, this has been explained to you regarding both the external and the internal.
O knower of the ritual procedures, having first performed the purification of the body with mantra-water mixed with earth according to the rules, one should thereafter commence the preceding [rite].
Having purified himself with pure ashes consecrated by all the mantras,
the knower of mantras should smear them upon his own body, including the limbs and sub-limbs.
The limbs beginning with Brahmā have been fully described from the head down to the feet;
I shall now explain their respective locations in due order.
Having rubbed [the ashes] on the head with Īśāna, the face with Tatpuruṣa,
the heart with Aghora, and the private parts with Guhyaka;
O Lord of Vatsa, these feet are [formed] by the *sadya* [mudrā]; indeed, O dear one, this is the conceptualization of the limbs (*aṅga*).
Now hear from me the division of the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) in their proper order.
The heart is not [placed] in the heart, nor indeed the head in the head.

One should dust [the deity] as proclaimed by the Great One; likewise, one should dust the crest with the crest-mantra, the eyes and the mouth with the eye-mantra, and the entire body with the armor-mantra.
One should rub the hands with the Astra-mantra and perform the *tāla* gestures within the eyes;
O son of Kṛttikā, the arrangement of the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) has thus been described.
However, when directed toward the Brahmans, they become the Upāṅgas;
otherwise, one who knows the mantras will not find the Aṅgas in any of the scriptures.
Thus, having performed the smearing with holy ashes along with the limbs, the secondary limbs, and the male limbs together with the Brahma-mantras,
I perform the Sandhyā worship with the purifiers (pavitrakas).
O best of brahmins, when the twilight has arrived, apply that very rite previously ordained by which you worship Śiva.
Thus, O son of Pārvatī, it has been told both separately and in its entirety;
O highly fortunate one, out of affection for my son, it cannot be withheld from you.
I shall now declare the worship of one who possesses affection and whose consciousness is cultivated through meditative development; herein the fivefold purity is established.
The ten purificatory rites (saṃskāra) must be performed by all preceptors;
likewise, the purification of the temple, of oneself, of the ritual materials, of the mantra, and of Śiva.
These purifications have been proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
the purification of the self is fully described as being established through the expulsion of the elements and so forth.
O Six-faced One, the purification of the temple must be performed;
having placed the eyes [of the deity] within it, one should gaze upon that temple as the God.
From that, the purification of the temple shall occur; there is no doubt about this.
However, the purification of the materials themselves is not accomplished by the temple alone.
Whatever implements for sacrifice there are, that substance is proclaimed as such;
having consecrated it with water by means of mantras, one should prescribe purification by that.
O sinless one, the purification of mantras has already been explained to you previously;
however, my child, it is when they are joined with the reality (tattva) that those things called mantras become purified.
Otherwise, O fair-faced one, those devoid of reality are never purified at all.
Know that reality is omnipresent, established within every caste.
O Guha, that god is to be known by the best of practitioners through the oral tradition; otherwise, they do not know him at all without such application.
Just as the ghee residing in milk cannot be churned out by people without the application of effort,
O auspicious one, so too is the stainless God.
The application of that milk is indeed a great austerity;
it reaches the state of curd when joined with the binding of the rope.
Just as clarified butter is produced from the churning-stick itself,
so too does that which resides in Śiva arise for the ignorant through the sphere of reality.
O child, by means of the union of the seed and the churning-stick, together with the qualities of transformation, the twenty-fifth principle, Puruṣa, causes Prakṛti to come forth.
O observer of noble vows, some phonemes are conjoined and others are disjoined, situated in relation to one another through a fourfold yoga throughout the entire class of letters.
In this way, one should understand that reality as being joined with the churner and the act of churning;
indeed, there is one [syllable] in excess of the five, situated at the head of that which ends in the Visarga.
One should know that as the second; the third is that which is continuous.
Thus, reality as it truly exists is difficult to comprehend even for the gods.
The first is the principle of Rudra, the second is the partless Śiva,
and the third, O Mahāsena, is endowed with existence at the summit of Time.
One should understand Time as the Bindu situated within the reality of existence;
in this way, that reality becomes the purifier of all mantras.
Those phonemes which are devoid of vowels and stripped of even the nasal bindu should be rendered pure by their very nature; they are then known as partless (niṣkala).
In each and every reality, this yoga should be understood by those intent on attaining perfection;
[the mantras] beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, joined with worship, ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and so forth.
In the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should employ [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā;
and in rites for nourishment and growth, they should be made to end with Vauṣaṭ.
Endowed with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, perform the severing of the bonds by means of the Vāyavya, Āgneya, Māhendra, Vāruṇa, and Vāruṇātman [mantras].
One who knows the ritual injunctions should perform these rites according to the proper rule for the sake of the task at hand—
whether in acts of subjugation and attraction, or in paralyzing, immobilizing, and so forth, including killing.
In rites of eradication, in incantations for causing hatred, in matters of inquiry, and in rites of pacification;
in the attainment of the fruit of liberation, and in the accomplishment of both desired and undesired goals.
If these high-souled ones perform [the rites] while being disciplined, they lead to satisfaction;
one should quickly draw out blood, for blood is proclaimed to be fire.
Vāyu conjoined with Varuṇa is thus beneficial for attraction;
but for paralyzing, it is Vāyu devoid of Bindu and conjoined with Agni.
It performs the rite of stimulation (stobhana); furthermore, even for a woman who has been struck down, she shall be aroused.
One should perform the rite of paralysis (stambhana) joined with Śakra, endowed with a yellow form.
O Mahāsena, if it is joined with the wind, it shall cause [the enemy] to be uprooted,
their movement becoming as unstable as the cotton-wool of a śālmalī tree.
The supreme rite of eradication (uccāṭana) is beneficial when performed with the smoke-colored [mantra];
however, for the sake of pacification (śānti) and especially for the sake of nourishment (puṣṭi), it should be performed with the water[-colored] mantra.
For the rite of killing, the wise one [should visualize] the color black, ending with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*;
at that time, the words of the victim become blood-red.
And these six endings should always be employed in the rite of nourishment;
these indeed are to be known as the dhāraṇās that bestow the fruit of all accomplishments.
These ten mantras, joined with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
are to be employed at the time of initiation for the purpose of severing the bonds (*pāśas*).
O Śāṅkarī, this purification of reality has been told to you;
now I shall explain the purification of the *liṅga* for the benefit of practitioners.
By means of that very purity, it swiftly bestows the accomplishment of mantra.
Three kinds of assemblies have been described, which exist by relying upon the *liṅga*.
One should perform their expulsion so that purity may indeed be attained;
for they are of two kinds: those whose bodies consist of mantras born of the elements (*bhūtajā*), and likewise those who are liberated from the body (*muktadeha*).
Those hosts abide in three places, relying upon the *liṅga*:
the elemental beings reside in the temple, and those whose bodies are composed of mantra reside in the *piṇḍaka*.
Those who have indeed been liberated from the body depend upon Śaṅkara through the Liṅga; having performed their expulsion, they are not appointed to the office of attendants by his grace.
Then the obstacles and the obstructing teachers will perish;
thereafter, one should perform the worship consecrated by the ten purificatory rites.
O highly fortunate one, by means of this practice, the newborn deity should intensely assume the form of Śiva, with [the mantra] residing upon his head.
Otherwise, O Śaṅkara, there can be no worship for one who is devoid of a physical form;
therefore, having meditated upon Vāmadeva, one should seat him upon the Yoga-pīṭha.
One should effect the presence [of the deity] by means of the Bahurūpa mantra;
through that, Maheśvara, whose form is the mantra, attains a state of presence.
One should follow [the mantra] with the heart-mantra; one should fashion the head with the half-[mantra];
with the crest-mantra there should be the water for the feet (pādya); and with the armor-mantra one should veil [the deity].
One should perform the rite of immortality with the Astra-mantra, as well as the rinsing of the mouth with the Vaktṛ-mantra;
then, one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) at the Īśāna direction, located at the position of the head.
Thus, my dear child, these ten types of purificatory rites have been described to you;
having performed the ritual in this very manner, one should then arrange the worship.
The five purities have been declared; at their conclusion, the procedure is traditionally taught:
the fourfold [powers] consisting of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
O Mahāsena, the knower of the ritual procedure should briefly place the filaments and the pericarp of the lotus in the intermediate directions with the heart-mantra.
One should place the deity Prasāda, whose form is space, upon the pericarp;
one should fashion the array of powers (śakti-vyūha) with the filaments by means of the Heart-mantra.
One should first place the seed-syllable, the sprout, and the infinite lotus by means of power (*śakti*).
What was previously described as grace (*prasāda*) is the supreme seed-syllable of power and the sprout.
And one should place "Anantaka" at the beginning, which is that which has abandoned an end;
this purity of the ten formative factors (saṃskāra) has been taught by me for the sake of recollection.
One should perform that [rite] in brief with the heart-mantra of the Great-Souled One:
the invocation, the installation, the presence, and the confinement.
Sprinkling with water, worship, incense, and unguents;
food, water for the feet, and the water of honor—these are performed with the heart-mantra, as is the ritual dismissal.
The Heart has been explained first; the Śiva-tattva follows it. It should be provided with the Bindu, and by means of that, one should perform everything.
This has indeed been fully described as the worship; now hear the procedure for the fire-ritual.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kālottara* consisting of one thousand three hundred verses.
When [the deities] are satisfied, the wise one should perform the rite of the sky-path (khanādi) and likewise the sprinkling again,
using either the Astra-mantra or the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Or else, O best of Brahmins, one should cause it to fall into the womb of Śakti with the Varman mantra;
and by that very [mantra], one should perform the heart-rite for the divine Śikhin.
One should perform the oblation for the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), joined with six or eight [verses];
or, having offered three, five, or eight [oblations], it should be given within the range of the fire.
Each [rite] should be performed individually when the possibility for the ritual procedure exists;
forty-eight such purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are declared for those of the Brahmin caste.
Having always united [the self] with Brahman through the heart,
everything thereafter becomes Brahman for one who is impelled by the injunctions of the Sūtras.
One should always perform oblations into the fire of Śiva by means of the yoga of the placement of the lotus (padmanyāsa) and so forth,
using the ghee of a tawny cow indeed for the purification of the bonds.
Alternatively, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the reality of the mantra as previously stated, using seventeen [oblations].
Thus has been described the work of the fire, which burns away the fetters. Immediately after that, one should then explain the sequence of the mandala.
O Guha, I shall now describe that which performs all rites, is pure, bestows all accomplishments, and is endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Thus ends the chapter on the eight-flower offering and the fire ritual within the *Kālajñāna* consisting of one thousand three hundred [verses].
Having thoroughly purified the ground and having dug it to the proper measure, one should remove ashes,
brick-dust, charcoal, bones, gravel, and potsherds.
Wood, hair, and other such things, as well as a mallet, must be thoroughly purified during the ritual acts;
however, one should not perform a sacrifice for a temple or a city gate on ground that contains hidden impurities.
It causes many defects; therefore, one should avoid the splinter. If a splinter from an elephant causes death, it may be so if it has been made by a dog.
In the *pauruṣa* [yantra], there is the destruction of the family; for a crow, there is expulsion.
For a cat, there is the ruin of the family and so forth; likewise for a vulture, a jackal, and a mouse.

If there should be a splinter among these, it will cause disease; if it falls on the ashes, it is said that the offspring will have short lives; and if it falls on the hair, the progeny will be short-lived.
In the Aṅgāraka [yoga], there is fire and water; in the Śarkarā [yoga], there is destruction by cattle.
In the Kāṣṭha [yoga], grain is obtained; in the Kapālika [yoga], there is miscarriage of the fetus.
But if there is a thorn, O child, it will come to pass; therefore, one should avoid a thorn.
The ground of a thornless [site] should be level and free from hollows.
That ground was very lush and well-nourished, granting all desires;
it was enriched with grass, water, fruits, and flowers, and was most sacred.
That earth should be known as beautiful when it is very cool and pleasant to walk upon;
it is also auspicious when there is a previous depression in the northeast.
One should not take any other types of plavas, for they are remembered as causing many defects;
likewise, those that are elevated like an elephant’s trunk or shaped like a tortoise are born from fire.
One should recognize her as auspicious and a promoter of nourishment;
however, if she has the form of a camel and is killed by her master, she causes the destruction of grain.
In the case of a *yavamadhyā* figure, there are losses and even childlessness;
because of the abundance of defects such as the triangular shape, it should be avoided by the wise.
White, red, yellow, and black— these four types of *dhātrī* should always be taken according to the sequence of their colors.
Sweet, salty,
and pungent, as well as bitter— these very tastes should be avoided with great effort.
Other tastes that produce defects should be avoided with effort;
one should recognize that [the taste] which is pure as being free from even a trace of defect.
Alternatively, O Six-faced One, when the time is short and the kingdom is threatened by an enemy,
no examination should be performed due to incapacity.
Initiation, which leads to the destruction of worldly existence, must indeed be performed at all times;
however, it is simply not possible to perform its purification instantaneously.
Therefore, O Guha, its purification must be performed according to reality;
one should first purify it with the Astra-mantra, and afterwards perform the purification with the Bhūtas.
It should likewise be purified by the Brahmans; in this way, purification will always be achieved.
Then, having made a fine plastering, [one should strike] with auspicious mallets made of Palāśa wood.
Then the wise one should perform a smearing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
upon that, a smearing with cow dung should be performed.
After the cow dung, the calf should be smeared with sandalwood;
furthermore, one should smear it with various other fragrances produced through yogic practice.
