One should perform the smearing according to the prescribed rite, accompanied by a scattering of flowers;
then one should worship with bilva leaves and perform purification with mantras.
The preceptor, whose defilements are purified, should have a pavilion constructed resembling crystal and should draw the sky in its center.
The knower of Tantra, always composed, upright, and silent,
should first prepare a thread made from the hair of a virgin, consisting of three strands.
Whether it be made of cotton, tree bark, linen, or some other auspicious material,
one should begin with darbha grass and so forth and take hold of it for the sake of prosperity.
O Guha, it should be known that thread made from cotton or tree bark grants all desires;
the thread should be one *ahama* in thickness and five *vyāmas* in length.
That which is proclaimed as the span for a two-cubit pavilion shall be seven spans for a four-cubit one; thus it is enjoined in the Tantra.
It should never be made three cubits long with nine sections of five finger-breadths each;
for such [measures] cause many defects and are intended for rites of killing and expulsion.
Therefore, one should cause the extent of the mandalas to be made as six,
eight, ten, twelve, sixteen, or eighteen cubits.
Beyond this, one should not perform [the rite]; it must be free from a small undertaking.
A ritual joined with excessive elaboration will result in many obstacles.
And for these very [deities], a thread should be prepared according to the characteristics of the proper rule;
it should be ten, twelve, twenty, or twenty-five units in height.
Therefore, that sūtra must not be made, for it would cause defects;
first, a triple-stranded cord should be made, circular and facing upwards, which is auspicious.
Having again tripled it by means of the upward sequence, the substance is called "ninefold"; one should then begin to triple it once more.
Thus it is said that there are twenty-seven [threads], as prescribed by the scriptures;
and that too must be wound upwards, produced from threads of the three qualities.
This threefold [system] has been declared; now I shall proclaim the deities:
Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Space as the fifth.
O sinless one, smell, taste, form, touch, and sound— these,
along with the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and the nose as the fifth, [are the objects and senses].

O Śāṅkarī, speech, the two hands, the two feet, the anus, and the generative organ—these indeed are to be known as the performers of action; they are the primary instruments of cognition and sensation.
The twenty are thus enumerated, as well as Manas, Ahaṃkṛti,
the Unmanifest (Avyakta), Puruṣa, Vatsa, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These deities are indeed proclaimed in the sūtra by those who construct the maṇḍala; he who understands them as they are enjoined in the sūtra of the thread [understands] those gods within the sūtra.
One should not perform the rite for severing all bonds with wood,
a clod of earth, charcoal, or even with the fingernail.
A wise person should not draw the Karaṇī with any inferior material;
it is proclaimed to be pure, arisen from the Bindu, and partless (niṣkalā).
With that, the wise one should draw the foundation and the vows of the mandala;
by means of that, O Lord of Gods, nothing remains deficient and everything proceeds.
Awakening, action, birth, and likewise the production from the *mātṛkā* arise from the chalk;
therefore, it is remembered as being born of Śiva.
But the teacher,
O auspicious one, being established in the ritual procedure, bestows grace upon the world through the sound.
Otherwise, that awakening does not lead to true enlightenment;
for without her, O Lord of Birth, there is no fire—therefore, she is remembered as the Supreme.
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣaparvata, Pāriyātra, Vindhya, and the great mountain Himavat;
At Śrīśaila and Arbuda, chalk is remembered as auspicious;
so too are other meritorious mountains and regions possessing auspicious characteristics.
Therefore, one should take chalk that grants all desires—
perfectly pure, proven, white, smooth, stainless, and free from defects.
It should be taken with effort on an auspicious lunar mansion and day,
or else by a wise person observing a fast during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism.
Having secured the body through offerings, incense,
worship, and so forth, one should perform the ritual worship according to the rules for the hosts of obstructing mothers and other such beings.
O Six-faced One, having first performed the great worship of Śiva,
the two best of the twice-born should sprinkle that place with purifying substances where they are to receive [the offerings].
One should perform the touching with the *sahya* mantra; O Guha, the sprinkling with the *guhya* mantra;
having lifted [the vessel] with the *aghora* mantra, one should consecrate it with the *puruṣa* mantra.
One should form the fist-mudrā in the northeast and protect it with the Śivāstra mantra;
one must first take great care not to dig into that [ground].
One should bind the directions for them; one should not conceptualize them as tenfold.
One should veil [the deity] with the armor-mantra and establish [him] with the heart-mantra.
Then, O one of great wisdom, one should remember the weapon-mantra at the crest of the ocean;
one should place Śiva there, together with the Lord Bindu.
In this manner, it should be established and grasped in due order;
then, having opened [the door] with the Astra-mantra, one should meditate upon Bindudeva.
One should perform this rite joined with the heart-mantra;
thus grasped, O Guha, that Goddess becomes the bestower of success.
For one desiring liberation, there shall be liberation; for one desiring prosperity, there shall always be prosperity.
The knower of mantras should cause [the hand] to revolve to the left in a circular motion.
Thus, the pericarp known as eight finger-breadths wide is said to be the bearer of Śiva;
likewise are the filaments, the petals, and the subsidiary petals.
O son of Pārvatī, those three wise ones should rotate it in due order by means of the eight,
twelve, and sixteen-fold yogas.
O Guha, one should rotate that [mandala] made of threads in its own form as circular,
square, and likewise twice-four (eight-sided) again.
Indeed, this single measure is prescribed for the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions,
as well as for the pericarp, the filaments, the petals, and the secondary petals.
The lotus is said to be thirty-two finger-breadths in measurement;
one should make the pericarp yellow, while the filaments are white and red.
Offered to the Viśvedevas with the leaves of the *taru* tree, it increases wealth, grain, and enjoyments;
or rather, when procured according to the prescribed rite, it grants all desires.
With that [line], one should cause the entire mandala, which grants all desires, to be made;
it should have beautiful lines with a gnomon situated in the center, or else a point for the Lord.
If a fault occurs when the peg is pierced, one should not strike the peg again; rather,
one should know that the work performed at the point where the mark was made bestows all desires.
The wise should draw the lines for each individual spoke so that they are auspicious.
This is declared to be the *garbha* (inner sanctum) measured at two cubits;
one should arrange the doors and other features according to a measurement of four parts.

East, south, west, north, and northeast, as well as southeast, southwest, and northwest— from the southeast onwards— these eight directions beginning with the Hotṛ are traditionally known as the Kṣura directions.
O Six-faced One, where neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate directions waver;
That sūtra is described in the tantra as bestowing the fruits of all desires;
the pathway (vīthī) should be equal to the womb (garbha), and the enclosures (āvaraṇas) should be half [that size].
One should place the weapons outside the pavilion itself;
these lines are declared to be of four kinds, based upon the Śaiva [tradition].
Among those,
O Guheśvara, the width of the door should be prepared as one part, while the ornaments should be of equal parts.
The *tatra* (central part) there should consist of half a *śobhā*; the two cheeks (*kapola*) are the *krauñcamardana*.
The *upaśobhā* is equal to that, along with the cheek; of this there is no doubt.
Having fixed it with the entire [line], one should grasp it at the front and rear on both the north and south sides, marked by lines at the doors.
The remaining two [deities] are likewise situated in the directions of Varuṇa and Indra; thereafter,
the remaining [deities] should be placed according to the sequence starting from the eastern door.
From the east toward the west, and from the south,
one should open the door situated in the western direction.
All this has been explained to you in brief as its defining characteristic;
and the various types of weapons of the world-protectors have already been described by me previously.
O child, those protectors against obstacles should be given accompanied by mantras;
having thus laid out the lines, one should always cast the colored powders.
The wise should cast down the fourfold, most subtle dust,
having the deities Vāyu, Agni, Mahendra, Varuṇa, and others as its presiding divinities.
One should know that white belongs to Varuṇa, while the color said to belong to Agni is red;
Vāyu is black in color, and the King of the Gods (Indra) is yellow.
One should know that Śveta is Brahmā, the red-colored one is Janārdana,
the black-colored one is Rudra, and the yellow-colored one is Sahasradṛk (the Thousand-eyed).
The Rajas are proclaimed as the presiding deities for Mahāsena;
for the purpose of subjugation, the Guru should cause them to fall by means of the fist-yoga using colored powders.
It should be drunk from the tips of the fingers for the increase of nourishment and peace;
by employing the *apasavya* method, it accomplishes all desired aims.
One should draw [the lines] with well-stabilized fingers so that no defect arises;
O Guha, one should always draw the lines in a perfectly pure manner.

The men were neither too stout nor too thin, nor were they sunken or deformed, nor did they press against one another; they were not disjointed, nor were they marked with drops of sweat, nor were they stretched out, nor were they hunched, nor did they have upturned faces.
O wielder of the Pināka bow, the auspicious [line] measuring a thumb's breadth should be drawn with white powders prescribed for the rite by the Guru,
who is ever composed, within the maṇḍala.

The *vicchinnā* causes fear of weapons and a weak husband; the *nimnonnata* brings disease; the *saṃśliṣṭā* leads to quarrels; the *śubhā* brings auspiciousness; and the *puruṣā* destroys the mouth, life, and friends.
In this mandala of the Enemy of Kāma, a line that is uneven, adorned with dots, and causes great calamity and incomparable loss of wealth, produces what is disagreeable.
I shall now fully explain the arrangement situated within the walls and enclosures,
according to the true characteristics and the specific distinctions of the syllables of the mantra.
One should first place the earth element (dharitrī), then water (āpaḥ), fire (jyotiḥ), and likewise wind (marut);
and space (ākāśa) should be placed with effort in this very sequence.
O Lord, my son, [I shall describe] the arrangement of those elements above,
together with the grace associated with the Brahmās, including all the limbs and sub-limbs.
Vāma, Aghora, Puruṣa, Īśāna,
and Aghora— these are declared to be the forms (mūrtis) of Śiva that one should install within his body.
O son of Pārvatī, the wise should briefly perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five Brahmans upon Śānta, so that he may accept the worship.
Otherwise, the partless Supreme Lord does not grasp at all;
the one of firm vows should place Sadyojāta upon the feet in all the Mothers.
One should place Bahurūpa in the secret region, indeed in the secret part;
one should place Vaktra in the region of the face, and Īśāna on the head of Śiva.
One should constantly worship the god Śiva, who possesses a manifested form and is endowed with the twenty-eight [attendants], the bestower of the fruits of liberation and desired objects.
The heart [mantra] is joined with eight lotuses, while the secret [mantra] consists of ten syllables;
the face is situated with eight [syllables].
Five seed-syllables of Īśāna have been declared;
one should assign them to the limbs and sub-limbs as the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon.

Having placed the heart-mantra upon the heart, one should join the head-mantra to the head; likewise, the crest-mantra is to be established in the location of the crest, situated in the south-western direction.
One should thus assign Dharma to all the limbs and the weapon to the direction of the hand;
having thus assigned everything, one offers the complete favor accompanied by flowers.
One should place the auspicious Sadāśiva upon that [lotus], in the pericarp;
his body is the color of a swan, and his feet are the letter Ū.
Through the union of the bindu, nāda, head, and neck, he is known as Puruṣa;
having thus established the deity, both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), according to the prescribed rite.
Then, one who desires accomplishment should perform the ritual of worship:
Sadyojāta is in the western part, while Vāmadeva is situated in the north.
One should place Bahurūpa to the south and Puruṣa to the east;
one should then conceive of Īśāna as being in the portion of the head, thus [the deity] is arranged fivefold.
I shall now fully describe the limbs, beginning with the heart, in their proper order:
having placed the heart on the southeast petal, one should place the head on the northeast petal.
One should visualize the goddess Vikṣyā in the southwest and Puruṣṭuta in the northwest;
one should place the Eye-mantra in the position of the eyes, and the Weapon-mantra starting from the eastern petal and so forth.
One should station them in the south, the west, and the north;
one should also install the protectors of the second enclosure and of the worlds.

O Lord of Yoga, one should place [the syllables] starting from the east: Śakra (Indra), Agni, Padma (Yama), Nairṛtya, Vāri (Varuṇa), Vāyu, Indu (Soma), and Śaṅkara (Īśāna), continuing until the [syllable] born of Rudra (Hūṃ).
The third enclosure consists of three [rings] which are to be joined in the ten directions:
the vajra, the śakti, the daṇḍa, the khaḍga, the pāśa, the aṅkuśa, and the gadā.
The trident is declared as the eighth, and the lotus and the discus make ten;
these too one should employ with the previously mentioned yoga.
O child, one should place the discus and the lotus in the lower and upper directions; the discus should be placed in the lower part, while the lotus should be assigned to the south-west.
And Padma is indeed in the portion of Īśa; this rule was seen in ancient times.
Furthermore, in all cases where [deities] have not been mentioned, one should employ the Heart-mantra.
Everything previously performed shall become accomplished; there is no doubt regarding this.
It should be performed according to the application of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and mudrā as taught in the Tantra.
"The instructor goes to hell if he does not know this procedure.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of the mandala in the *Kālajñāna*, consisting of one thousand three hundred [verses].
Now I shall explain the initiation (*dīkṣā*) which was previously mentioned by me—
that through the mere knowledge of which the accomplishment of liberation (*mokṣasiddhi*) arises.
O Skanda, the body of all living beings is composed of the five principles;
it must be purified with effort when the time for initiation has arrived.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these are the five elements by which the entire world is pervaded.
In brief, all principles (tattvas) are to be seen therein;
pervading the earth and the intermediate space, they are established as such.
Withdrawal (nivṛtti) is to be known as Varuṇa, while Pratiṣṭhā is said to be Water;
Vidyā becomes Fire, and Śānti is established in Wind.
Having known that supreme space beyond peace, which is all-pervading and the liberator from bonds, one should initiate even those of one's own school, O Mahāsena.
I shall explain their classification; listen attentively, O Guha, so that you may understand the initiation that liberates one from the great cycle of transmigration.
It has been said that one part of him is the Lord of the Lord of the Senses (Gandharveśvara).
That would be the foundation there; it is said to have become a mere fraction (kalā).
Within that, another reality (tattva) remains, situated as its nourisher.
It is declared to possess four qualities; when pure, it becomes a single quality.
It arises in the form of rasa; know this to be the state of cessation (nivṛtti).
O Skanda, to whom does this [power] belong—whether it is called "the elemental" (bhūtākhyā) or "the originating" (sambhavā)?
For fire is indeed composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), yet even that is pure in its essential form.
If it is abandoned, it becomes pure; a fraction of it arises as the remaining progeny.
Even though impermanent, there is complete purification; through the excellence of sound, it is purified.
One should know the form of touch (to be) Hari, the Lord of the Three Worlds;
he exists in five states, consisting of the threads and endowed with the constituent parts (kalās). (p. 23a)
Its purification must be performed as long as it remains within a single sheath;
indeed, its very quality is characterized by peace.
Beyond tranquility is the supreme ether, soundless and pure, O Guha;
one should know that as the end of *nāda*, bowed down before the abode of Śiva.
Sound is declared to be *nāda*, characterized as the quality of space;
it is purified by initiation, and indeed, in reality, by means of higher knowledge.
O Guha, this is the complete and partless purity of the principles;
it is the complete state for those established in the manifest world, while the partless is known as the subtle powers.

"O child, this thorough knowledge has been taught for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). O sinless one, I shall now proclaim it to you at the conclusion of the ritual application of initiation."
Withdrawal is not established in the heart; its station is in the head.
Then, one should place the Vidyā in the crest-lock and Śānti with the armor-mantra.
One should perform the fire-oblation with grace to the supreme deity who transcends peace;
this has already been fully explained specifically in the section on the extraction of mantras.
The purification for them has been described by me exactly as it is;
for each one, a hundred oblations are to be offered, and indeed five hundred are proclaimed.

O six-faced one of excellent countenance, one should offer the oblations with clarified butter alone, not with the milk of a tawny cow; and at the end, O Ṣaṇmukha, one should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra of grace.
O best of Brahmins, for the sake of purification through expiation, one should offer oblations of individual sticks in sequence,
beginning with the *śikhā* and *astra* mantras, in their proper order.
These initiations are fully described as being devoid of [the ritual of] birth and so forth;
yet, even when the oblation has been performed, practitioners are not liberated from the bondage of birth.
This, however, is proclaimed as the first initiation, called "the elemental" (bhūtadīkṣā);
by means of this, those who assume the form of the kalās become purified by me.
Now I shall describe the second [purification] for the sake of purifying the limbs:
one should perform the purification of the elements by means of the *bhūtaśuddhi*, conjoined with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
A wise person should offer one hundred oblations for each of them in successive order; thus, six hundred oblations are prescribed.
Before that, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with that very same clarified butter;
one should offer a hundred oblations for each of them in their proper sequence.
The third, which is conjoined with Śiva, has been declared by the Brahmins;
O child, the fire-oblation (homa) prescribed therein removes all sins.
At its conclusion, however, that oblation which has been described should be offered;
indeed, O son, five hundred oblations must be performed for it.
Alternatively, one should offer their hearts into the fire in successive order;
one should declare that their purification consists of exactly sixteen voids.
Alternatively, the knower of the seed-mantras should truly offer each one individually into the fire, having encased it with the Śakti-mantra born of Śiva.
The sequence of oblations previously described as ordained by the scriptures—
thus has initiation been fully explained, which is auspicious and the destroyer of all fetters.
Having performed the placement [of mantras] beginning with the womb (yoninyāsa) and having also extracted the western [mantra],
the wise should always carry out the sequence of purification.
The placement of the womb (yoni-nyāsa) has already been fully explained by me to you previously;
that womb is the supreme, partless reality for all embodied beings.
This body was previously described as consisting of seven times ten;
likewise, O sinless one, the five elements are designated as the five Brahmās.
And likewise, O Six-faced One, there is another six-limbed [mantra] preceded by the *yoni*;
for without the *yoni*, the limbs of Brahmā are not born.
Therefore, with every effort, you should understand the deposition in the womb (yoninyāsa);
for that which is the measure (mātrā) and the digit (kalā), my child, is established at the very end.
She is declared to be the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), spreading forth like the growth of a seed and sprout;
she is the womb of all beings, the Mother who brings about procreation.
O child, those seventeen [sages] are proclaimed as being endowed with that [power];
otherwise, their birth would not have occurred, for they were devoid of a womb.
She should be appointed with a devoted heart;
by that means, one should perform the entire ritual procedure as proclaimed by Śiva.
Worship, sprinkling, withdrawal, as well as striking,
conjunction, scattering, and again worship in that same manner.
The rite of conception (garbhādhāna) must be performed in due order,
as well as birth, empowerment, enjoyment, and likewise dissolution.
Once it has been heard, one should cause a hundred oblations to be offered with the Heart mantra;
likewise, one should perform the severing of the bonds with the Astra mantra and offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order.
One should perform the extraction in successive order, joined with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
according to the sequence of the vowels, and in due order within the limbs of the Brahma-mantra and so forth.
One must perform the withdrawal as well as the progressive expansion of the principles (tattvas);
one should practice yoga in the sequence of the mantra-principles in due order.
Seventeen mantras have been proclaimed; these seventeen imperishable principles (tattvas), joined with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, are indeed to be employed in the sacrifice to Śiva.
This ritual action has been fully explained by me to you for each respective reality (tattva).
O child, when purified in this manner, they do not assume a body again.
Otherwise, practitioners who are devoid of the prescribed rules will never be liberated;
therefore, one should proceed from the beginning with Īśāna up to the end with Śivāstra.
In each caste, however, one should perform the rites beginning with the *āmvara* and ending with the *yāntika*.
At the conclusion, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* and likewise the fourth oblation.
At the end of the vowels, one [letter] is indicated; at the end of the letters beginning with *ka*, the second;
at the end of the letters beginning with *ya*, the third; and at the end of *kṣa*, the fourth.
Thus have the initiations been fully described, established upon the path of reality;
and the application of mantras has already been told by me previously, O sinless one.
Initiation, which liberates one from bonds, has been declared to you as fivefold:
the first initiation is by means of the elements (bhūtas), and the second is by means of the Brahmans (brahmans).

The third, O Aṅga, is the initiation of the limbs (aṅgadīkṣā), while the fourth is the ontological (tātvikī). That which is taught at the end of the fifty [phonemes] should be known as the ontological, O Guha.
The fifth [tithi] is said to be joined with grace by the Kalas;
that fifth is designated as bestowing the fruit of nirvana.
O auspicious one, without the *kalās*, the Lord of Grace does not proceed;
Kubjikā is to be known as the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), while that ritual action is indeed *Dvikubjikā*.
Having placed that [power] in the middle, the descent of water is known to be below it;
this is called Nivṛtti, while Śikhā is proclaimed as being above it.
O child, the Vidyā of Agni is situated above the two Kubjas;
it is declared to be Śānti-bindu, the carrier of the principle of Anila.
Beyond that is the supreme void, which is indeed declared to be Nāda;
this, O Skanda, has been described as the grace (prasāda) conjoined with its digit (kalā).
That fifth initiation, which leads to nirvāṇa, has been fully described;
at the conclusion of the final oblation, one should then contemplate the nectar of immortality.
One should place [the drop] flowing onto the crown of the head and nourish the *bindu* in the heart;
for in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*), this supreme procedure has been observed in such a manner.
The nectar was previously described by me to you at the conclusion of the ritual procedure;
the line of the womb (yonirekhā) has been fully explained, as well as the Śakti endowed with its defining characteristics.
The detailed account has been told, O dear one, as previously declared by me;
I shall now speak in brief so that you will certainly understand it.
By means of the yoga of the equinox, one attains the supreme state;
having attained the yoga of the equinox, who indeed would not be liberated from bondage?

And what of earth and the others? Indeed, they are not the first; rather, they are known as the presiding deities of the mantras, consisting of qualities such as sound and so forth, along with the winds, which were previously mentioned as belonging to the *kalā*.
These aforementioned beings, beginning with the earthly element, possess great austerity; they are all-pervasive and supreme seeds—now hear from me their pervasion.
They are taught at the end of the *hṛdaya* and proclaimed at the end of the *tattva*;
they are established according to the divisions of Brahmā and the other deities.
Their true nature has been explained to you in brief, O Six-faced One; previously, my child, I told you merely their designations.
I shall explain in detail that by which they may understand in truth the equinox (viṣuva) which is proclaimed as bestowing liberation and granting the supreme state.
The supreme, partless, and pure reality is declared to be that of Īśvara;
through the yoga of the Viṣuva, it ascends as far as the crown of the head within the Deity.
From space arises the drop (bindu), and that is proclaimed to be wind;
at the end of the Tantra, that is designated as the eternal state of Sadāśiva.
From the drop (bindu), the Vidyā is produced; the principle of fire (agnitattva) is manifested. From fire, water is produced; from water, the earth arises.
O high-minded one, the heart of the universe has been declared by these;
now hear from me how it is dissolved at the end of the Mātṛkā.
The digits previously described by me to you, beginning with Nivṛtti, are situated below;
above them are established Pratiṣṭhā, Tejas, and Bindu.
I shall now describe the division of those digits (kalās) together with the deities,
beginning from Sadyojāta up to the position of the head.
For these vowels have arisen in their peaceful state in succession from of old:
Sadyojāta, Hṛdaya, Vāmadeva, and Śiras as the fourth.
The four Bindu-devas have arisen as the supreme seed-syllables:
Aghora, the Goddess Śikhā, Puruṣa, and Varma.
One should indeed know these four vidyās as originating from his splendor:
the god Īśāna, Pluta, Netra, and the Astra of the wise one.
Indeed, these four supreme principles remain established through cessation;
however, the four neuter ones are those which consist of anger, death, and old age.
One should recognize disease at the end for one who understands it at the foundation;
furthermore, O fair-faced one, others [recognize it] by means of the path as a maiden at birth.
O fair-faced one, Nivṛtti is to be known as Vāruṇī, designated by the syllable *u*;
one should understand that she is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of twenty-four leaders (*nāyikā*).
That is designated as Vāruṇī; they know Śakrajā to be [the other].
O child, that which arises from the syllable *ha* becomes Dvikubjā.
One should know that the Vidyā is fiery (āgneyī), characterized by the syllable *u*;
it should be known as residing in the letter *e*, and likewise as abiding in existence (*bhāva*).
One should recognize the syllable *bhā* as the form of the Lord who pervades fifty [letters];
it is the child (*śiśuka*) of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Peace arises from the Maruts; the principle of the Bindu consists of the Kalās.
O Skanda, these indeed are said to be the Kalās established within the Tattva.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these are declared to be the five elements, conjoined with their respective vowels.
Furthermore, I shall explain the classification accepted in all tantras,
which bestows every accomplishment upon both the vowels and the *kalās*.
The vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga* are indeed remembered as sixteen;
starting from *śānti*, they are traditionally taught in groups of four.
From the letter *a* up to the head [of the alphabet], these arise from the body through tranquility;
the fifth is the long *ū*, and likewise the two phonemes *ṛ* and *ṝ*.
These, which arise from knowledge, should indeed be known by those intent on accomplishment;
they are situated beginning with the letter *ḷ* and ending with the letter *ai*.
These foundations and origins should be known as arising from cessation;
cessation has been described by others, while that called the letter *rū* belongs to Varuṇa.
Nivṛtti is to be known as belonging to the earth, and Pratiṣṭhā is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa; this second division is said to be endowed with the essence of the Kalās.
I shall now fully explain the third division, which is extremely difficult to obtain,
established within the vowels, the musical notes (kalās), and the elements.
O child, the first and last vowels are said to be the source of the Vidyā;
you should know those four to be A, Ā, Bindu, and that which is born from Visarga.
O sinless one, when the two *ī* sounds are uttered, they are *e* and *ai*;
these four are also declared to be *Pratiṣṭhā*, arising from the body.
Two faces with double lips and four colors are proclaimed;
those born from Nivṛtti should be known by those intent on attaining perfection.
I shall now describe the four neuter vowels of the *kala*:
the vowel *ṛ* is born from the letter *sa*, and the vowel *ṝ* arises from the letter *śa*.
The letter *ḷ* is the ground of stability (*pratiṣṭhā*), while the letter *ḹ* arises from cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Thus the vowels are produced, arising both collectively and individually.
Therefore, one should know that from those [elements] they arise; hence they are known as the "givers of desire.
Now I shall describe the conjunction of the objects of touch, which is joined with the elements.
O Lord of Guha, the Ka-varga is born from Śānti, and that which arises from the Vidyā-mantra is born from the [Sa-]varga;
however, the Ṭa-varga has emerged from Pratiṣṭhā.
The labial class (tavarga) is to be known as Vārija; O sinless one, Nivṛtti is Prabhava.
Some desire Pṛthivī to be Nivṛtti, while others [desire] Pārvatī’s son [to be it].

O Śakra and Guha, know that in this tantra, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is indeed water; there is no doubt about this. In other tantras, however, the consecration is declared to be born of lightning (śakrajā).
Nivṛtti is to be known as Vāruṇī; these two are remembered as a pair.
Pratiṣṭhā is the consort of Śiva, while Śānti is remembered as Māheśvarī.
The Vidyā is said to belong to Viṣṇu, while Nivṛtti is the speaker of Brahman. Brahmā is the seed of the universe, and Viṣṇu is the womb; of this there is no doubt.
The seed-syllable, Māheśvara, Śiva, and the Neuter—
this quartet is one's entire essence, which is very difficult to obtain even for the gods.
The supreme true nature of Śiva must be guarded with great effort;
the principle of Śiva’s installation is proclaimed in all the Tantras.
That deity who is "twice-curved" (dvikubja) is that very reality, the Supreme Lord;
she is designated as Earth, this womb which is both supreme and non-supreme.
The principle of Vidyā is declared to be at the summit of the Śiva-principle;
O you who are equal and fearless of worldly existence, the principle of Ātman is said to be Nivṛtti.
The fifth class, the crest-jewel of the classes, has arisen from the body of Nāda;
this is what is called "this class," at the end of which is the Lord (Īśvara), the ultimate reality (tattva).
The letter Ma is said to be bent; it is the essence of the Bindu.
The Supreme Lord bestows liberation and brings about the destruction of suffering.
Thus have the contacts been fully described; these are the digits (kalās) arising from the body. O child, they are called the "intermediate" ones, residing within the bodies.
The Vidyā of Śānti is said to be in the northwest; the Vidyā of Āgneyī is proclaimed [to be in the southeast];
the one named Pratiṣṭhā is in the northeast, and Nivṛtti is remembered as being in the west.
Through the practice of inhalation (pūraka) and the others, the triad of principles is established:
the letter *sa* is declared to be inhalation, and the letter *pra* is remembered as retention (kumbhaka).
The *recaka* indeed has the form of the syllable *sa*; these are remembered as the three types of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
The entire realm of speech, including all that is moving and unmoving, is said to consist of the syllable *ṛ*.

O observer of excellent vows, how is the pervasion of the elements maintained? I have explained it to you in its entirety; yet, without knowing these principles that reside in the letter *ha*, [the truth remains hidden].
He does not release one from the bonds, nor is he a teacher upon the surface of the earth;
this is declared to be the Viṣuva, endowed with the dhāraṇās.
O Guha, through the three-fold regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma) alone, the state of the equinox (viṣuva) occurs;
O Maheśāna, he who is joined with these is always possessed of the sleeping elements (dhātus).
O child, why do you wander with the notion of body and the embodied? The Supreme Lord is all-pervasive.
With reference to the seven constituent elements (dhātus), the pacification of the vital winds (marut) and so forth have been proclaimed.
Is this body Śiva? It wanders among all living beings;
by means of the yoga of gradual progression, it is situated on the left and the right.
Joined with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), Śiva, who is partless (*niṣkala*) in the sequence,
should fill [the body] while stationed within the center of the body, and then remain motionless once again.
For a single moment, Śiva delights in the body within the range of the *vaṃśa*;
this is proclaimed as the *recaka* [exhalation] on both the right and the left.
One should know that the northern [course] occurs when the sun is in the south, and it enters the south when it is in the north;
these two solstices are declared to be mutually transitive at the junctions.
O child, at the equinox, the transition [of the breath] is proclaimed to be equal;
by means of that yoga, one should perform that which liberates the bound soul (paśu).
The connection between the openings of the channels consists of upward-stalked [tubes] that are indeed downward-facing;
all of them are provided with two knots and are recited [as mantras] ending with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
The Pārthiva and the others were previously described by me in connection with the *granthi* yoga;
one should know them to be two-faced, flowing always both downwards and upwards.
The Sadyojāta deity is situated in the feet; the Vāmadeva is established in the private parts;
the Aghora resides in the heart; and the Vaktṛ (Vaktra) is established in the mouth.
Īśāna is situated in the region of the head; these five locations have been proclaimed.
Indeed, these five knots are to be untied, as they flow along the downward path.
O Mahāsena, for the ignorant [the path is downward], while for the wise it is upward-bound. I shall declare their knowledge by which they flow upward.
Those who are Brahman become the elements, and those who are the elements know [Brahman] again;
there is indeed no doubt that they are Brahman—I shall describe their distinction to you.
The Earth is to be known as Sadyojāta, while Water is proclaimed as Vāmadeva; Fire is said to be Aghora, and Wind is remembered as Tatpuruṣa.

Īśāna is indeed the ether; thus are the elements established. It should be known that when situated in Brahman they grant liberation, but when situated in the elements, the wise know them to be bondages.

Those beings who have arisen from the constituent parts (kalā) are proclaimed as "bhūtas. They are called "bhava" because they come into being; thus, the bhūtas are established within the state of becoming (bhūta).

Because they exist within the fourteen-fold cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), they are known as "beings" (bhūta). The divine realm is said to be eightfold, while among the animal species it is fivefold.
A single human birth proceeds within the sphere of beings;
that is declared to be the Earth (pṛthivī), and the letter va is remembered as Varuṇa.
The letter *ra* is fire and also wind;
O Skanda, the supreme lord, it is space and the soundless resonance (*vināda*).
Listen now to the truth regarding these elements, the principles, and the seed-syllables residing within Brahman:
the principle that culminates in the *bindu* and *nāda* is proclaimed as Sadyojāta.
Its third [face] is the left one, while the fifth is Bahurūpaka;
the third [face] beginning with Aghora is the deity whose nature is Tatpuruṣa.
Īśāna is to be known as "Om"; thus Brahmā is established. O wise ones, through yoga, I shall now declare the distinction between their constituent parts (kalās).
The letter *śa* is proclaimed to be in the middle of the letters beginning with *a*;
its presiding deity is Śakra, and it is declared to be the earth (*pṛthivī*).
The vowel *i* is the left [hand] of the first [deity], while the two *ku*s are the humpbacked one (*kubja*).
That which follows is the beloved of Vāmadeva; it is proclaimed as belonging to Varuṇa.
He then becomes the supreme deity; now I shall proclaim the third:
it is called the "Aghora Splendor," situated above the two hunchbacks.
Fire is its deity, and Puruṣa is situated in the head;
one should know the all-pervading Lord Anila (Wind) as its presiding deity.
Īśāna is said to be the sky, the presiding deity of the *viṣanta*;
he is the form of the *bindu*, and that *bindu* is remembered as the *praṇava*.
These arts have been fully described as being endowed with the practice of Brahman;
now, O son, I shall explain that which is joined with the five principles.
The *brahmāṇi* is said to have twenty-four *vṛtti*s;
the *pañcaka* has twenty-four *nāyaka*s, and the *ṣaṭka* is likewise described.
This yoga has been fully described; it is difficult to be attained even by those who know themselves.
Viṣṇu is the foundation where that reality is established.
In the inexpressible, my color is devoid of the sphere of form;
it is tranquil, free from all color, and therein alone is it established.
"O dear son, it was previously stated by me that Śakti resides at the end as Śiva.
That which is called Vaiṣṇavī Śakti is indeed declared to be Pratiṣṭhā."
O observer of excellent vows, I shall explain this division that exists above him, by knowing which one situated there in the Supreme Lordship becomes immortal.
O Skanda, I shall describe the partless Śivatattva, which exists in eight divisions; one should know that it constitutes the head which has been proclaimed.
This thread pervading all castes must be known by those desiring liberation;
otherwise, O Skanda, the progression of saṃsāra would not exist.
There are no castes, nor mantras, nor sounds, nor deities;
there are no elements, nor assemblies of beings, nor existents, nor likewise sense-objects.
Neither does the mind nor the intellect proceed from egoism;
neither the unmanifest nor the Puruṣa exists, nor indeed is there any necessity.
O Lord of Vows, neither Time, nor Māyā,
nor Vidyā can act in manifold ways upon the Śiva-tattva.
May the Supreme Lord, the liberator, who dwells above Śānta, grant peace;
by him, may the ears indeed attain manifestation according to his will.
Above that is the Lord Sadāśiva in the form of sound (nāda);
he is liberation, he is emancipation, and he is the absolute cessation of that [sound].
That supreme cause is peaceful, undecaying, eternal, and immutable;
it is called Sadāśiva—ever-abiding, immovable, and constant.
That, however, is declared to be the Supreme, beyond which nothing higher exists;
it is the state that reaches the end of the eighteen [places], where the lotus of the end of sound (nādānta) is found.
This consciousness, O Skanda, which severs the knots, has been explained to you. I shall further declare another [consciousness] established in the yoga of initiation.
The earth [element] should be joined with the mind and conjoined with the mantra,
by which one pierces the lower knot and goes to supreme Śiva.
O one of great asceticism, having placed the seed-syllable of Śakra below that of Śānta,
one should make it conjoined with the long vowel and endowed with the bindu.
Having first placed the *sapluta* [vowel] and at the end the *astra* [mantra] accompanied by the *śikhā*,
one performs the mantra with very long [breaths] until it is completely filled on all sides.
O best of Brahmins, by means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*) in a long form,
the breath (*prāṇa*), which bestows liberation, remains steady during the retention (*kumbhaka*).
As long as the body is not completely filled, the wise one should indeed fill it;
then, by means of the supreme deity at its end, with the crest-weapon (śikhāstra).
The wise one should perform its severance at the end, conjoined with exhalation (recaka),
by means of five upward thrusts (udghāta) of the earthly element (pārthiva-tattva).
O auspicious Guha, purification has been described as being both external and internal;
however, in each and every reality (tattva), they should be seen as dissociated and free from all marks.
In this way, the earth should be understood as all-pervading by those seeking liberation.
Concentration is known as the mind, and the knower is proclaimed as awareness.
By means of that, one should perform the stretching [of the body] so that it becomes upward-facing.
In this manner, one should undertake this application of the water-element;
it should be joined with the limb of Śiva, while the remaining four are subordinate.
Just as through prior application, one purifies the earth element and the others in sequence; likewise, by means of four upward thrusts, one should purify the state of being obstructed by water.
One should recognize fire by three [elements], while wind is traditionally said to consist of two;
one should purify space with one, and there is no conflict with grace.
However, with a purified [mantra], the purification of the *bhūtārgala* should be performed;
by that, O best of Brahmins, the auspicious striking of the *śikhā* and the *astra* [is accomplished] in the five [limbs].
By means of this, the unborn one (Aja) indeed destroys the spirits that have been summoned;
this secret mantra is considered the destroyer of the bolt of the spirits.
By which the arising of beings occurs no more and no longer;
having broken through the bolt, one should place [the mind] in the *yoni* and unite it with each principle (*tattva*).
Having performed the nourishment with the Śakti-mantra, one should deposit [the offering] ending with *vauṣaṭ*.
For the Śakti becomes the reality (*tattva*); there is no reality devoid of the Śakti.
The reality situated at the end is the Śakti, which is difficult to discern even for the gods;
having encased [the mantra] with that on both sides, one should perform the four [steps] in sequence as before.
For them, a single method has been proclaimed, established through reintegration (sandhāna).
I shall fully explain that reintegration, by which one shall go to that supreme state.
The letter *u* dissolves into *Kuṭilā*, O Six-faced One;
the letter *ū* and *Kuṭilā* themselves are established within *Tāmasī*.
I am the arm of Tamas, residing within the body of knowledge;
that which is called the body of knowledge goes to dissolution through peace.
Even the Śāntā dissolves after having consumed all that is moving and unmoving;
one should know the principle of Bindu, and the principle of Nāda is very difficult to attain.
O Mahāsena, having gone there through the practice of concentration, yogins [attain] Śiva, the supreme cause, the God who is beyond sound.
When a living being does not grasp that which is proclaimed as the "elemental" (bhūtākhya),
this is called "union" (saṃdhāna), which severs all fetters.

This yoga is not to be told to a person of wicked character, nor to one who is impure, nor to one who is undisciplined; it is for the benefit of one who is pure, self-controlled, and of restrained mind.
This yoga should be told to him, but never to anyone else;
this second supreme junction has been declared—now listen.
One should grasp the first [finger] with the second; O Śivā, one should cause the body and the embodied soul to be drawn together by means of a fist in brief.
That which is the supreme seed-syllable, the ultimate reality, abides within the heart;
for the Vīra, O Six-faced One, the supreme station is at the end of the heart.
By means of that fist-technique, one should quickly draw [the essence] from all sources;
one should not release the fist until the city is completely filled.

But when [the breath] is purified, O highly fortunate one, that fist which was previously enveloped should be projected forward by means of the Weapon-mantra (astra) stationed at the limit of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
In the great yoga of equal day and night, which is partless and free from worldly existence,
the embodied soul should finally apply himself there, by means of which he is not born again.
Thus, those who are devoid of the observances (samaya) go to a state of union with the [lower] powers. The observances are said to be ten, proclaimed as beginning with Yama and the others.
Furthermore, there are other observances (niyamas) for the sake of understanding their designations:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in diet,
and vigilance— these five are proclaimed as the observances (niyamas).
The Yamas should be known as the first-born; these indeed are proclaimed as the ten. These are known as the Samayas, the lineages born of such Dharma.
Fortitude, forbearance, and so forth; non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, modesty, knowledge, lack of envy, and freedom from anger—this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma.
But those men who are devoid of these [virtues] and are possessed by a flood of sins,
they too, O Mahāsena, go to the auspicious state through the practice of *sandhāna*.
As it was stated in the previous sūtra: "The liberation of the practitioner occurs;
those who are free from the [ordinary] observances go to the supreme abode."
Whatever is performed that is indescribable and unknown becomes fruitless;
O Guha, the action performed with him as the objective bestows liberation.
One should contemplate the entire world, including all that is moving and stationary, as having become Śiva;
one should reflect again and again on how it proceeds through all its activities.
Whatever inauspicious action a person of deluded mind performs,
by that very nature of his action, he is seized hundreds of times.
Therefore, in all ritual actions, one should always contemplate Sadāśiva,
by which the attainment of the fruits of action occurs for the practitioner.
Thus ends the chapter on initiation in the thirteen-chapter *Kālottara*.
I shall now describe the process of departure, by which one certainly ascends;
having performed the eclipse of the sun, the wise practitioner should perform the āyāma.
O child, at the end of the length [of the cord], one should always perform the cutting with a very sharp,
flowing weapon (*kṣarāstra*); then it will certainly ascend.
And the Sun, together with the entire reality conjoined with the equinox,
should be united with the Supreme Lord through a very long lineage.
Having closed the mouth, one should utter the syllable Śiva;
having filled both cavities with the emission (visarga), one shall be liberated.
And thus, for one who knows the true meaning of reality, that power departs quickly;
I shall now explain the second type of departure, which bestows bondage.
And by this method, even a practitioner who is not yet fully disciplined can quickly ascend;
I shall now explain with certainty this very process of immediate ascension.
The snares knotted by the mind are like clusters of gems on a thread; from the heart-lotus up to that [supreme] lotus, they are strung together by the threads of the mind.
The jewels have already been mentioned, as well as those elements that were proclaimed; these are called knots, and the jewels have been described in detail.
Those nooses are to be understood with effort as the binders;
however, for this great-souled one, their piercing must be performed within those very [nooses].
He is declared to be the weaver, the supreme lord who pierces;
impelled by the lineage, he proceeds from the heart-lotus to that [supreme] lotus.
The earth dissolves into water, and water dissolves into the three qualities;
the three qualities dissolve into wind, and wind enters into space.
And it goes beyond the ether into the eternal abode of Śiva;
this indeed is known as the "thread" (tantuka), the supreme piercer of jewels.

From the heart-lotus up to that [supreme] lotus which has been described by you as being of the nature of Śiva—having seen that, one should perform its severance through the activity of the mind; thus one should cut away the mind.
Having severed the mind with the mind alone, one never again has power over anything else—
not by speech, nor by beings, nor indeed by the objects of the senses at that time.
All these have ceased when the wind has arisen among the elements;
and this [aroma] is produced from scent, not from another taste, nor from fire.
That which is devoid of consciousness, devoid of stability, devoid of contact,
and devoid of sound and the rest— that is proclaimed as the supreme state.
Some declare that in this case, the mental [obstacle] is the one that causes the interruption;
having once severed that [interruption] by means of the mind of the thread-bearer.
O Supreme Lord, how can that [desire] be turned back from the mind? O dear one, when the mind has desisted, the liberated one becomes solely the Knower.
This secret which brings about liberation has been told to you;
it is that supreme state which was spoken by Svahe, Hema, Kuṣṭena, and Teka.
This application of the *saṃdhāna* has been proclaimed to be of various kinds; the first yoga is born of the elements (*bhūtaja*), which destroys the obstacles to the attainment of liberation.
One should commence the third yoga of the mind by means of the mind alone;
for this initiation has been described as that which burns away the fetters.
Whoever should undertake initiation and ritual action without understanding this yoga will indeed be cooked for a long time in the Avīci hells, where there is no end.
This knowledge is not to be told to a person of wicked character.
"The most excellent of all secret knowledge should be given to one of virtuous conduct.
Thus ends the chapter on initiation in the *Kālottara*, consisting of thirteen hundred verses.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord of Gods, for the practitioner who has been initiated and is utterly pure,
and who is appointed to Śiva— how should his consecration take place?
"O Mahādeva, Lord of Pārvatī, let there be no planets for me; let Viṣṇu, Yama, and Vināyaka be [favorable] toward me, since I have been initiated by you."
O Lord, what kind of consecration is prescribed for Śiva,
who is liberated from all bonds, yet whose body remains?
When his body has been exhausted through the application of the remaining mode of life, he shall go to Śiva;
how, then, should the consecration of that initiated one be performed?
Īśvara said:
Listen, O son of great wisdom, to the words you have uttered;
I shall explain to you the means for resolving that inquiry.
Initiation is prescribed for the purpose of attaining the reality of knowledge;
this threefold initiation must be performed for him by the Lord of Sādhakas.
When the consecration has been performed first, initiation is prescribed as liberation;
the second, however, is the initiation of knowledge (*vidyādīkṣā*), wherein knowledge is bestowed.
O best of the twice-born, for the practitioner during an affliction, there is the third type;
thus indeed has the threefold consecration been described by me to you.
I shall explain the ends of the divisions so that no delusion may arise;
first, the empowerment of knowledge (vidyābhiṣeka) must be performed by the practitioners and others.
Having first performed the initiation into the Vidyā, one then performs the consecration of the Vidyā;
therein the severing of the bonds of the practitioner is carried out.
O Skanda, that initiation which bestows liberation is the giver of nirvāṇa;
by means of knowledge they are not burned, but by initiation they [are freed] from the domain of the bonds.
Furthermore, because it is at the end of knowledge (*vidyā*), it is called "knowledge" (*vidyā*) here;
by means of which [knowledge] the wise are united with the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).
Indeed, those bonds are not severed by arrows or missiles;
rather, it is the initiation into the Vidyā that subsequently brings about the burning away of the bonds.
Burnt by her, O son of the River, the nooses do not take root;
yet, through the state of residual existence, she moves toward the fruit of the three worlds.
In that case, there shall be initiation through knowledge (vidyā-dīkṣā); hear now its definitive explanation, O Guha: whatever fruit is enjoyed by means of this very body.
Let the reality of knowledge arise; there is no need for deliberation here.
The characteristic sign of the perfection of the pill is the upward movement through the underworld (pātāla).
By means of collyrium, yellow orpiment, sandals, and likewise gorocanā,
one attains the station of a Vidyādhara and achieves oneness with the Yoginīs.
O twice-born one, he shall gradually attain sovereignty over the world of mortals as he desires;
the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā* are his portion— this is remembered as his remaining mode of life.
There are various kinds of food and drink, consisting of the four types and the six tastes;
having thus eaten properly, the practitioner will then undoubtedly [attain success].
He goes to the supreme abode and never again enters the realm of the womb;
when the body is destroyed, he enjoys the fruit for the sake of liberation from the bonds.
O Guha, by means of this very body, the fruit of knowledge is enjoyed;
I shall now describe its sacrifice upon a perfectly purified surface of the earth.
The wise one should construct the mandala with pure and auspicious powders;
it should be made four-cornered and adorned with four gates.
In its center, one should draw a white lotus endowed with eight petals,
possessed of a pericarp and filaments, radiant and intense with splendor.
One should scatter the colored powders in sequence according to the previously stated procedure.
Having scattered the powders, O child, perform the preliminary placement and worship.

Invocation, the offering of water for the feet and the guest-water, worship, as well as bathing, incense, fragrance, the purifying thread, the food offering, and the traditional oblation of rice grains.
In this manner, every rite whatsoever must be performed according to the prescribed rule;
as for the fire-ritual (agnikārya), it has already been explained by me to you previously.
The knower of reality should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) according to that very same procedure;
this is declared to be the initiation of knowledge (vidyādīkṣā), which bestows all enjoyments.
For one who has been purified by the initiation of knowledge (vidyā-dīkṣā), the initiation of liberation (mukti-dīkṣā) is prescribed.
I shall now explain, according to reality, this distinction between the mandalas.
The preceptor should perform the sacrifice for the sake of enjoyment and liberation to the god who grants all desires, the supreme Maheśvara-maṇḍala, and the Vāruṇa-maṇḍala.
A nine-naveled [mandala] should be made for the sacrifice and for the consecration with weapons;
for killing, it should be triangular, and for paralyzing, it should have the shape of a bow.
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), it should be known as circular; for inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), it is five-cornered. O Guha, these are indeed the mandalas prescribed in the *Svatantra*.
And in the previously mentioned square mandala, which fulfills all desires and bestows divine accomplishments, there is the consecration of knowledge (vidyābhiṣecana).
The lords of teachers, for the sake of the welfare of their disciples,
should perform everything endowed with the proper characteristics while stationed in the northeastern direction.
One should fashion a lotus with fifty petals and a pericarp;
one should then place the seed-syllables of the Mātṛkā letters therein in the sequence as before.
That which is at the end, the principal seed-syllable, emerged from the group of eight;
it is purchased as residing in the jar, joined with the bindu, and arising from me.
At the edge of the pericarp, one should place a water-pot with the seed-syllable mudrā;
it should be endowed with all auspicious characteristics, free from blemishes, straight, and beautiful.
It was stainless, free from dust, variegated, and either white or red;
it had a broad neck and ears, and a large belly with a great abdomen.
One should have it cooked well, neither overburnt nor undercooked;
it should be free of swirls, not black, and highly auspicious.
It was filled with heaps of gold and jewels, as well as beautiful medicinal herbs;
and the river Savaṇī was filled with water rising from its own source, emitting fragrant vapors from its mouth.
Having filtered it with fragrant substances and mixed it with sandalwood and camphor,
one should smear its exterior with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
One should wrap his neck with a new, variegated, ten-fold *dukūla* cloth,
or, if that is unavailable, with one made of *kṣauma*.
O auspicious one, having first prepared it thus with that divine, fresh cotton of Śukra, the ritual placement (nyāsa) is subsequently performed.
O best of Brahmins, one should consecrate [the rosary] with the Aṅga-mantras, the Brahma-mantras, and the Bhūta-mantras,
using a rosary that has been obtained according to the prescribed rule.
One should especially prepare eight hundred of those gems;
there, O Skanda, the practitioner should install the Vidyā and pray to her.
The knowledge of Brahmā is [attained] through lotus seeds; the Vaiṣṇavī knowledge through conch-born [seeds]; the knowledge of Rudra through rudrākṣas; and the Mahendrī knowledge through indrākṣas.
The Vidyā that belongs to Bhāskara should always be deposited with crystals;
but the Vidyā that belongs to the Vidyādharas, one should fashion with pearls.
O Mahāsena, one should always recite the Yakṣa-vidyā with gold, silver, and the like; the Gāndharva-vidyā with *vakula* and *kadamba* flowers.
The Rākṣasīs should always have an ālikā made with nimbā and riṣṭa;
the Mothers, with candrakānti, desire the increase of nourishment.
The Gaṇas and the Nāgas likewise...
[with] crystal for the purpose of nourishment, and with pearls for the sake of increasing one's lineage;
however, for the purpose of exterminating a family, one should perform it with Nimba and Ariṣṭa.
One should always have a golden garland made for the purpose of subjugation;
for the purpose of causing enmity, a garland of bitter and pungent fruits is prescribed.
The Brahma-vidyā is indeed swiftly perfected by means of lotus seeds;
that Vaiṣṇava Vidyā which belongs to the Vedas is certainly accomplished through the [Vedic] branches.
They desire liberation through the recitation and the wearing of rudrākṣas;
O child, the wearing of rudrākṣas has been praised by me at various places.
Indeed, even mothers do not harm one who wears a rudrākṣa.
O Guha, what more need be said? One who recites a mantra with rudrākṣa beads, which are born of Rudra, shall obtain merit a hundred million times greater than that gained from reciting it even once.
O child, those who hold the water of the Nyāya [stream] contained within the hollow of a rudrākṣa fruit,
joined with mantras, indeed roam about as Rudras.
O Skanda, one who is not Rudra never wears the rudrākṣa like Rudra;
they always place it within thousands of Rudra-liṅgas.
O child, even those who are in a state of sin, if they always wear the rudrākṣa,
they too become liberated without a body and go to Śiva at the dissolution of their physical frame.
The lord of yogis should always wear that which is well-spined, very broad, free from blemishes,
heavy, stainless, and bestowed by his guru.
How may one obtain purity through the purification of the fast-day (upavāsa) in accordance with the Dharma?
The mouth should be joined with the mouth, and the anus with the path of the snake.
It is taught that one should tie a triple knot upon the *gaṇa* using either a cotton thread, an auspicious thread made of *darbha* grass, or a pure bark-fiber thread.
Then, one should have a rosary made according to the procedure prescribed in the *mantra-kalpa*,
by which the practitioner attains all fruits.
O best of the twice-born, one should place it upon a large Audumbara pedestal that is free from blemishes and made of ivory, facing either eastward or northward.
Then the wise one, having consecrated the disciple with pure water over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times in succession, [should proceed].
They should perform the consecration while wearing fragrant and pure garments,
using *śrīphala* fruits, *jātī* flowers, and auspicious, fragrant green leaves.
It was filled with medicinal herbs as well as gold and silver,
with various fine garments, and with white creatures born from eggs and born from wombs.
One should wrap the neck of the jar with well-perfumed *vikaṅkata* twigs;
meanwhile, the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*) should be performed, accompanied by the resounding noise of musical instruments.
With the sounds of stringed instruments and songs, with the shouts of "Victory!
from bards reciting aloud, and with various kinds of narratives derived from the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
With the sounding of conchs, cymbals, drums, and sweet-toned instruments,
one should thus offer the vidyā together with the rosary.
Having bowed to it, the wise man, being pure, joyful, and satisfied, with his body covered in horripilation, should receive it with devotion upon his head.
One should prostrate like a staff before the Guru,
saying: "O Great-Souled One, by your grace, may I always attain perfection."
Having said, "So be it," the Guru should then cause [the disciple] to rise;
immediately thereafter, the worship of the Guru must be performed.
Indeed, one's own wealth, life, servants, sons, and even grandsons—
all these belong to others as long as they remain within the domain of the lord of the twice-born, until their very lives depart.
Having thus introduced himself to the instructor, O Guha,
that great being will then surely attain the supreme accomplishment.
In this manner,
O best of Brahmins, the preceptor should bestow the initiation of knowledge (vidyābhiṣeka) according to this rite, and thereafter the initiation of the principles (tattvābhiṣecana).
The initiation of knowledge (vidyābhiṣeka) should be performed by the preceptor with the Brahmans;
however, the initiation of reality (tattvābhiṣeka) must be bestowed with the reality itself for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and supernatural powers.
The knower of mantras should bestow the Śiva-natured consecration with all the mantras for the office of Ācārya, together with the parasol and the throne.
The crown is joined with a pair of scissors, and a bracelet is prescribed for the hand;
one should wear these made of gold or silver, or else of rudrākṣa.

The knowledge-consecration (vidyābhiṣeka) should be performed; the parasol is used, but it is devoid of a pedestal. An uṣṇīṣa is not to be worn by him, nor is there the taking up of a pair of scissors.
If one is assailed by obstacles during the weapon-consecration (astrābhiṣeka) performed with the Astra-mantra,
one should perform the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) for the purpose of dispelling them.
O auspicious one, when the Astra-yāga has been performed, the consecration with the Astra-mantra follows;
thus have these various consecrations been described individually.
The first is the initiation of knowledge (vidyābhiṣeka); the second is known as the ontological (tāttvika);
the third is the reality of the preceptor (deśika-tattva); and the fourth, O Guha, is that which arises from the weapon (astraja).
O child, the ritual procedure for practitioners and others has been explained regarding the two-syllable mantra.
Thus ends the chapter on consecration in the Kālajñāna consisting of one thousand three hundred [verses].
Kārttikeya said:

O Lord of the Gods, the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) and likewise the transition of the individual soul (*jīvasaṃkramaṇa*) have been explained by me through the method of rapid practice; it is not for you to know them.
O Lord of Gods, how many channels (nāḍīs) are there, and how many winds (vāyus) are traditionally taught?
And in which junction do they flow day and night for Śambhu?
What is this transmigration of the soul, or what indeed is the soul conceived to be?
Where does it move, and how is the all-pervading Supreme Lord situated?
And since it is omnipresent, how does it move among the elements and the vital breaths?
How is it that, though divided within the body, it remains undivided by those [elements]?
O Śaṅkara, tell me this: how does that Lord take upon Himself the sin committed over seven lifetimes? This has been declared regarding eight births; explain it to me.
The Lord said:
I shall now describe the wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra), which is established in ten ways and is always pervaded by those numerous channels.
In the center of the body is the navel, and there the *kanda* is situated;
the supreme deity, abiding in the letter A, is all-pervasive and resides in the head.
From his body emerged the seeds which indeed lead to the sprout;
you should know them to be sixteen, and likewise another thirty-two.
The six syllables are proclaimed according to the division of the eight vowels:
*ṛ*, *ṝ* (with visarga), *ja*, *ka*, *ra*, and *sa*; these indeed are the syllables.
The enumeration of qualities is performed; the remainder, both higher and lower, is otherwise.
That is the life-force (jīva) of all beings, while the castes (varṇa) possess a body of three syllables.
O Six-faced One, all things arising from the syllable *A*— both external and internal— are to be known as the channels and the vital winds.
I shall describe their division according to how that which is designated as the eight-spoked wheel, situated within the heart, revolves.
It is completely surrounded on all sides by ten subtle channels:
the iḍā, the piṅgalā, and the suṣumṇā as the third.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, as well as Masā;
Alaṃbuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
These ten vital-breath channels are indeed established in the form of a wheel;
the *iḍā* is said to be on the left, while the *piṅgalā* is remembered to be on the right.
Between those two, however, is the Suṣumṇā, which is the source that brings about creation;
O Mahāsena, I shall now describe the remaining channels.
And for those abiding in Kālacakra, I shall explain in due order, according to the sequence of the eight constituents, through the application of other designations.
And for those situated in the ten directions, [the goddesses] are, in order:
Jvālinī, Tapanī, Dhūmrā, Kāmadā, and likewise Vijayā.
Amūlā, Bahumūlā, Pakṣiṇī, Uddhagāminī,
Alambu, Mātā, and Jihvā— these ten are the vital channels (prāṇanāḍīs).
Listen with focused attention, my child, to their detailed classification:
Jvālinī is the element of air (vāyu-tattva), while Tapanā is said to be fire (vahni).
One should know Dhūmrā to be Kāla; Kāmadā is remembered as Aruṇī.
In Vijayā, however, the syllable *ī* is said to be Amūlānāpa.
O Rudra, the heart should be Bahumūlā; that is the reality, there is no doubt.
Know that Pakṣiṇī is the Praṇava, while Alaṃbuṣā is the Mātṛtattva.
The palate and the tongue are declared [as the locations for the remaining letters], and the tenth is the crest of the group.
These have indeed been described in brief; now hear their detailed classification.
Jayā, Vijayā, Gāndhārī, Talavāhinī,
and the one known as Haritajihvā— these carry [the breaths] within the fivefold vital energies (prāṇapañcaka).

Intellect, mind, the origin of the elements (ahaṃkāra), the ego (asmitā), and the individual soul as the fifth—this is the pentad of intellect; he who restrains the vital breaths and so forth is the subduer.
When Vāyu recognized the syllable *ya* as his own name, Vijayā was designated as his consort;
they know Gāndhārī to be the wife of Śakra.
Talavāhī is to be known as Kuhū; she is named after the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa).
Hastijihvā is Raudrī; she resides in the vital breath within the pentad of breaths.
First, the pentad of intellects is declared to be the seed-syllable Sadyaḥ;
the principle of the letter *ma* is known as the mind (*manas*), which pervades the primordial elements.
The mind is declared to be the fire, and the individual soul (jīva) is called the dissolution;
this pentad of intellects is described as being within the range of the channels (nāḍī).

One should know these very things; however, O highly fortunate one, I shall describe them individually. Their foundation is established within the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) and resides in the channels.
Piṅgalā and Iḍā are situated on the right and left [respectively];
the movement of the transits, equinoxes, and so forth occurs within the range of the cakras.
By means of the union of the left and right [channels], according to the sequence of half-yāmas,
the rudra-tattva is proclaimed to precede that of Piṅgalā.
O observer of noble vows, the Iḍā flows having taken its station on the right side;
the Kuhū, however, is known as Vāruṇī and is situated on the left.
By these channels within the scope of the cakras, all this is pervaded through the union of the left and right, according to the sequence of half-yāmas.
Through the application of the division of parts (kalā) in the sequence of the eight elements,
the vowels from 'a' to 'sa' are known as short and long syllables.
Residing in the heart within the range of the wheel, they flow constantly at all times;
the movement of the entire [system] occurs at dusk and at sunrise.
The month of Māgha is declared to increase the strength of yogis;
there, everything flows together as one with the Sun.
And the King of Nagas, who is the limit of tranquility, carries the long-shaped form in color;
he carries the wind residing in the vital breath (prāṇa), and he always carries that which resides in the sun.
When there is no doubt that [the breath] remains undivided for half a watch (yāma),
then the threefold division— consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm— is declared.
O son of Pārvatī, let there be this separation of them for but a single moment;
however, that conjunction which proceeds from the moon and the sun shall continue.
They should recognize the [proper] time and not cause the destruction by means of the winds and so forth;
the soundless movement of the partless one is to be known as being on the left.
Vāsuki and Soma always carry it alone;
it is likewise designated as Apāna and Niśā, belonging to Śaṅkara.
And in the first half,
O Lord of the Gods, it is said that [the breath] moves together with the intellect during its external course for the duration of one *prahara*.
It is undoubtedly the half-duration of the second watch.
Is that wheel of yours also like this? It has been declared by the son of the Moon and Sun to be the movement in emptiness; and the planet is remembered as Aṅgāraka.
Takṣaka, however, is declared to be joined with Samāna;
he is non-different from the Lord, and the letter *I* is indeed on the right.
O Mahāsena, for half a watch (ardhayāma), one should carry [the breath] steadily through Piṅgalā;
the letter *ī* is to be known as the youth, and Sadāśiva resides within the first digit (kalā).
Joined with Udāna and the wise Karkoṭa, the second watch is declared to be for external movement; of this there is no doubt.
The path born of the Moon has been described to you as the left;
on the new moon day, the pervasive life-force is situated in the southern direction.
The planet Bṛhaspati was there, as was Padma, the king of the Nāgas;
he made the sky clear for the Lord, remaining absorbed in meditation throughout the day.
Through the conjunction with the vowel *u*, the channels are known to be all-pervasive;
one should understand that Piṅgalā remains for the fifth half-watch.
The syllable *u* is declared to be semen (*śukra*), and the serpent (*nāga*) is proclaimed to be the wind (*vāyu*).
Within that very [place] is the great lotus (*mahāpadma*), and there is also the movement of the one who has destroyed [the afflictions] (*kṣapaṇa*).
The southern course has been described, as well as the night belonging to Śaṅkara;
O child, the third watch has been explained by me from the external perspective.
In this wheel of the circle of vowels, the state of *iḍā* is fully described;
the goddess Gāndhārī, born of Śakra, is situated in the southwestern direction.
Kūrmāra is fully described as flowing together with Kṣayānta;
Saturn is to be known as the planet there, and Śaṅkhapāla is the king of the nāgas.
The letter *ṛ* carries the breath there, while in the right nostril it carries a long vowel;
O fortunate one, it always flows undivided through that channel.
The seventh is declared to be the half-watch (ardhayāma) as it arises in sequence;
it is declared to reside in Piṅgala, and this yoga is conjoined with the long [vowel].
Iḍā is said to be the syllable Ṛ, joined with the syllable Ṝ;
it is declared by the wise to be Kulika, formed with the throat and the lips.
Rāhu is known as the planet; the eighth half-watch is said to be the auspicious day, O observer of good vows, while the exterior [time] belongs to you.
O Mahāsena, if the channels are obstructed, four days and nights pass within [the body]; of this there is no doubt.
These four pure channels, situated within the cakras, flow in a sequence of half-yāmas during the state of the south.
Piṅgalā, Dhruvā, Amā, Gandhārī, and Svarā— these eight,
as well as others, are situated within the individual channels (nāḍīs).
One should indicate the letters from *a* to *kṣu* in their daily course;
those which are short are here considered in the left [channel] as the digits of the moon (*candrakalā*).
O highly fortunate one, those [veins] situated to the long right of the sun—
listen to me regarding their designations within that arrangement of channels.
Pūṣā, Āyuṣmatī, Manasā, Prīti, Tuṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti,
and Dhṛtikarī— these eight digits (kalās) are thus established.
O highly fortunate one, one should sequentially place Piṅgalā and the others, ending with Gāndhārī;
two by two, according to the yoga of short and long [vowels] and so forth.
O one of great austerity, one should place the eight Nāgas in the [eight] directions in reverse order:
Ananta is said to be long, while Vāsuki is called short.
Takṣaka, however, is long, while Karkoṭa is situated in the short [category].
O child, Padma is long, and Mahāpadma is in the short [category].
Furthermore, one should designate Śaṅkhapāla as long and Kulika as short;
thus do these planets come to be, in the sequence beginning with Āditya.
One should know that Bhāskara, Aṅgāraka, Guru, and likewise Śani— these are long, flowing within the solar orb.
Abiding in the center of the lunar mandala, they flow unimpeded:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The Nāga, Kūrma, and Kṛkara always carry [the breath] in succession;
Āditya is said to be Prāṇa, and Soma is called Apāna.
Samāna is to be known as Aṅgāraka (Mars), while Udāna is remembered as Budha (Mercury). Vyāna is to be known as Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), and Nāga is said here to be Śukra (Venus).
One should know that Kūrmāra is Śani and Niśa is indeed Graheśvara;
Kṛkara is declared to be Rāhu in this wheel within the domain of Māḍi.
O illustrious one, Devadatta is Anila established in Time;
Dhananjaya, however, is the Lord of the Group, as was previously told by me.
And during the great conjunction of the equinox, it flows into the *suṣumnā*;
this is declared by the wise to be the primary flow of that deity.
Śinīvālī and Kuhu are to be known according to their diminished conjunction;
they are proclaimed as Amāvāsya on the right and on the left respectively.
Both these, the moon and the sun, have gone to dissolution within Śeṣinī.
That which is called the sixteenth is the partless (*niṣkalā*) digit residing in the moon.
One should know that Śinī is indeed Bālī within the solar orb;
she is to be known at the "end of the twelve," for they become one.

But when the flow has ceased, O child, whether it be on the right or within the domain of the left, and when the nostril-passage is well-cleansed, O Skanda, whatever remains there— whatever little is left— [that is the essence].
She who is Śinīvālī should be known as that which is celebrated as Amāvāsyā;
even by knowing her, those who are disciplined are liberated through the power of Śaṅkarī.
O Dhanañjaya, this is declared to be the state of equal flavor (samarasa) belonging to Śiva;
for within these [energies], the power known as Nīlā proceeds as one alone.
The entire *pravaha* is said to be that in which [the breath] proceeds;
elsewhere, O Lord of the Gods, it should be known as *niṣkala*, wherein yoga has perished.
The immutable Lord Anāma does not flow at all when in a state of equilibrium;
just as ghee existing within milk is not seen without the application of a process.
