Likewise, Śiva would not always be perceived as being in the state of Dhanañjaya;
for he, the all-pervading Jīva, causes everything to flow forth.
O auspicious one, accompanied by the vital breath (prāṇa), it is situated at the mouth of the channel;
it migrates at all times as long as it does not abandon [the body].
The remaining [vitality] flows through the middle of the left channel in its own essential form;
when one abandons it at the proper time, the cage that produces many defects is cast off.
Then, by means of the upward flow, it moves within the cave;
thus is the night described, arising from the seizing of the wind and the serpent.
By means of that yoga which has been described through the various divisions of the eight Śivas,
the further differentiation of the channels (nāḍīs) and the vowels (svaras) is now prescribed.
Gāndharvā, Jayā, and Vijayā as the third;
Kuhū is likewise proclaimed, and Śinīvālī is the middle one.
The Gāndharvā is said to be in the west; the syllable *a* is the supreme seed-syllable. Jayā is situated in the northwest, residing in the position of the syllable *ya*.
Vijayā has Soma as her deity and is supported by the letter *i* in the north;
Kuhū is situated in the portion of Īśāna and is established in the syllable of Varuṇa.
Śinīvālī resides in Kāla, and Dhanañjaya resides in Suṣumṇā;
the two vowels ḷ and ḹ belong to the Gandharvas, while e and ai are in the sphere of Vāyu.
The two vowels *o* and *au* are the states of victory; *ku* arises from the bindu and the visarga.
The long vowels are to be known as being on the right, while the short vowels are situated on the left.
The vowels are indeed said to be in the center of the Vāma [nāḍī], increasing the heat;
the Gāndhārī flows during the first watch by means of the flow through both ears.
In the night, the one who contemplates the night is designated by the *svaraja* [mantra];
in the second watch (*yāma*), however, it is *jayā*, according to the yoga previously described.
Vijayā also always flows during the third watch,
beginning from the first watch by means of the flow through both ears.
Kuhū is to be known as the portion of Iḍā; it constitutes the fourth watch.
Described according to the previously mentioned sequence, this is for the benefit of yogins.
Beginning from *sakala* and continuing as far as the final [vowel] ending in the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*),
the *nāgas*, *agrahas*, and *prāṇas* always circulate in succession.
Beginning from the first watch of the night, they are declared to be struck by two notes in succession;
listen now to their names.
Pūṣā, Amasā, and likewise Saumyā; Marīci, Suvāmā, and likewise Śaṅkhinī, as well as Aṅgirā, are indeed present in the full orb of the moon.
The sixteenth [digit] is to be known as Amṛtā, which is situated at the end of the night;
it is the state of Gāndhārī-Piṅgalā, attained without being joined with force.
She flows with a long-colored [wind] in a reverse order;
she flows with a short [wind] when situated on the left, and is said to flow when situated in the *iḍā*.
That which is designated as a collection of entities is called a "cultivated dream";
furthermore, whatever action is performed during the day, whether consecrated by mantras or otherwise, [is likewise so described].
One situated in the *bhāva* sees a thread during the first quarter of the night;
O son of Kṛttikā, one should know that such a dream occurring on a Monday (*jayā*) is of the nature of wind (*vātika*).
In the third watch, the wind-based (vāttika) dream occurs; during Vijayā, however, one remains awake. In the latter half of the night, the phlegm-based (śleṣmika) dream is said to occur.
This [state], consisting of a combination [of the humors], proceeds uninterruptedly;
when one *prahara* remains of the night, it is called *uṣā*.
One should know that what is seen by one afflicted by wind and other humors is mixed and false;
however, that which is yet to be experienced is to be understood as being of two kinds, established as either auspicious or inauspicious.
One should know that prosperity is found in the *iḍā*; otherwise, there is the opposite.
Among all the channels (*nāḍī*), the channel called *iḍā* is the one that flows [toward] the channels.
Piṅgalā is declared to be the Kālanāḍī on the right side;
when the vital breath moves within her, one should examine the time.

Then, O Skanda, one should move the vital breath (prāṇa) within the heart through the combined application of both the collective and individual methods; listen to how this is accomplished in conjunction with the channels (nāḍīs).
Whatever color one relies upon while moving along with the channels,
that very form shall belong to that Lord of immeasurable power.
The vital breath (prāṇa) indeed wanders through the Āmā, which is like the space within a seed;
the mind is composed of the imperishable and other elements, O Brahmins who have reached the further shore of the Vedas.
O Lord of Guha, he beholds all those [visions] in the Gāndharva state:
in the Mānasī state, there is the enjoyment of food, combat, and various excellent women.
In Vijayā, one perceives celestial garlands, excellent ornaments, and the like;
as well as naked women, those belonging to the Pāśupata sect, shaven-headed women, those with matted hair, and those bearing the Śiva-linga.
In this Piṅgalā, within the range of the sequence of Rudra,
one perceives meditation like that of a bird, as well as chatter and the act of speaking.
O Guha, one who sees mounting or entering during the Jayā yoga will suffer from fire and heat; however, during the Brava yoga, one will become afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Seeing this, there is no doubt that Śiva is established in fire;
he is fully satisfied with the body and, together with the Ṛṣis, emits semen.
Gāndhārī, joined together with him, beholds all those horses, chariots, vehicles, and lion-thrones.
When situated in Kuhū, [the Moon] brings rain from the ocean and its watery reservoirs,
cold weather and the like, thunderbolts, and a host of agitated hooded serpents.
The individual soul, however, always perceives while resting upon the water-channel;
it perceives the abode of Yama while resting upon the *śinī* and *vālī* channels.
And he, abiding in time, beholds many terrible hells situated for both restraint and favor within the range of his own movement and perception.
With the vital breath (prāṇa) resting in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), the individual soul (jīva) beholds the supreme Śiva;
it beholds him as non-different [from itself] through the channel (*nāḍī*).
O child, one should move by means of the right [channel], relying upon the wheel of channels;
those of evil nature, devoid of the true meaning of reality, do not perceive that reality.
Since the channels (nāḍīs) are proclaimed to be dissolved in one place alone,
the individual soul (jīva) resides within the Suṣumnā, supported by the filament of the lotus.
That deity moves among the openings of the channels.
By that [means], consciousness proceeds;
when the mind situated in the waking state pervades the cage of effects.
Śiva moves day and night through the channels of the hair-pores;
[He resides] in the sixth station above the nose.
When the Lord Sadāśiva has reached the state of the Fourth (turya), he awakens;
he is declared to be undivided among those who are undivided, [but] for one who is divided...?
Guha, it is accepted; indeed, there is no fault in those [cases]. "One should give," so said the Supreme Lord.
O Guheśvara, when the division of the measures (*mātrā*) occurs for one who carries [the breath] for one watch (*prahara*) in the Piṅgalā,
then one should know it to be broken.
But by whichever month it may be excessive, one should offer it as a gift.
In brief, there is agitation...
O son of Kṛttikā, in the fourth watch there is loss of wealth;
however, in the fifth watch of the night, when it flows in a divided state...
Then, there is no doubt that for objects, [the connection] becomes severed;
in the sixth [month], one should know the destruction of the lineage (gotra), and in the seventh, it becomes immovable.
Death should be known to occur within three years by means of the flow [of breath] itself during the day and night.
O Skanda, when the breath flows through both nostrils simultaneously for a full day and night,
his death should be known to occur within two years.
If Sadāśiva always flows for three nights toward the right of a person, that embodied being shall live for one year; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of the Gods, for one who carries [the burden] for even one night or a single day, death shall occur within six months; such is the certainty of the scripture.
He who practices for two watches lives through the night;
O fair-faced one, Piṅgalā is thus designated as the channel of time.
One should recognize Kāla as the Sun; when he flows to the south, he declares life to be certain, provided that one does not choose otherwise.
The gentle channel is called Iḍā; it is of the nature of Varuṇa and is situated on the left.
O observer of noble vows, because it flows separately for the duration of a *mātrā* of the sun, it is so designated.
Then, by that very same sequence, one should indicate it according to prior knowledge;
she, namely the Iḍā pierced by the Sun (Bhāskara), carries [the breath] for one watch (prahara).
Whatever defects arise therein are always pacified by the application of mantras and burnt offerings, or by well-conceived acts of giving.
Or whoever, through the variation of time, becomes happy, he shall become a Śivida;
those who are born under Soma, O Lord of Sādhakas, indeed possess distinction.
Those defects which have been proclaimed as arising from the passage of time come to rest for him; thus Rudra is glorified.
They constantly announce their own death step by step, until the end of their lifespan is reached; however, for a single day, it belongs to Śaṅkara.
In the western quarter (vāruṇa), the afflictions are pacified through rituals performed according to the rules;
they should be known as yielding only slight suffering at every watch of the day.
Know that the second [day] is excessive; in the third, there is disease;
and in the fourth, O Guha, the destruction of one's sons and wife occurs.
In the fifth [watch], however, there will be great affliction that brings an end to life;
in the sixth and likewise the eighth watch, there is the crushing of Śakra.
One's own life remains intact while others meet with the opposite;
thereafter, situated in the western direction, she causes [the enemy] to be eradicated.
There will be various kinds of bondage, as well as the cutting off of ears and nose;
within ten days, one shall fall under the power of enemies due to the flow [of the breath].
By these means, death shall not occur, nor the extremely difficult-to-cross states of existence;
furthermore, one should give gifts according to one's ability, in consideration of the recipient and the time.
By performing a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and recitations (japa), one who possesses the *sivindu* shall become happy.
Thus, O auspicious one, have I explained to you the mutual relationship of the channels (*nāḍīs*).
The method for the channels and wheels has been taught by me in the Kālacakra.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, consisting of one hundred and thirty verses, on the Knowledge of Time, the eighth [chapter] concerning the Wheel of Time.
I shall explain the Kālacakra as it is established in its major and minor limbs;
where the wrist occurs, that is the location of the forearm.
When the deity does not move, one should predict death within eleven months; there is no doubt that it occurs within five months from the middle of the arm.
O Lord of the Best, it is taught that [the path] passes through the middle of the armpits in three months;
at the region of the ankles in eight [months], and in seven [months] through the middle of the thighs.
And the knees, O Mahāsena, are produced in six months;
the anus, O Ānanda, in five months, when it moves through the middle.
Then death indeed occurs; this has been clearly told to you.
But if it does not throb in the fourth region, the temple of Śaṅkha, O Lord of Guha.
One should indeed report the measurement at the base of the ear after three months;
at the neck after two months; and in that region [of the heart] after one month.

If [the breath] does not move at the throat, death shall occur within half a month when it is located in the region of the heart, or after five days when it is below the heart; however, if it remains at the throat, death shall occur in a single day and night.
The child lives for one watch (three hours), O dear one, indeed due to the lack of movement in the womb;
that channel which has reached the eyes is the fortunate portion of the bindu.
That Lord, having abandoned his station, is declared to be the all-pervading life-force (jīva);
indeed, for half of a half-watch (one hour), the life-force becomes omnipresent.
Having pierced through the aggregate of reality and the domain of the collection of senses,
and having abandoned that which is bound to the channels of the vital breath, he goes to the supreme Śiva.
By means of the path of the head, however, the Supreme Lord within proceeds to His own abode, from which there is no return.
O Lord of the Best, for those who are ignorant and are declared to be the most sinful, endowed with the defects of their actions, [the soul] goes downward into the interior of the belly.

This destination has been declared for those who have performed great sacrifices according to the sequence prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, through the downward breath (apāna); of this there is no doubt.
Their movement is said to be circular, while the knowledge of Brahman is on the left;
O highly fortunate one, the knowledge of Sāṃkhya is on the right.
The northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is said to be the path that leads to return;
however, those who know Śiva travel by way of the equinox (viṣuva).
By which there is no further birth and no further acquisition [of rebirth]—
this entire procedure of Kālacakra has been explained to you.
O illustrious one, out of affection for your son you have related this movement of the soul;
you too must never hastily disclose this to anyone.
Likewise, the wealth of the wicked must be guarded with great effort.
Thus ends the chapter on the vital points (*marmādhyāya*) in the *Kālajñāna* consisting of one thousand three hundred [verses].
O Lord born of fire, the sphere of the movement of the vital breath has been explained through the application of the Kālacakra for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
Kārttikeya said:
O Supreme Lord, this movement of the individual soul (jīva) which has been described consists of ten subtle channels and is joined with the vital airs (vāyus).
O Mahādeva, I did not know this eternal reality of the living soul (jīvatattva),
which is this that vibrates within your body on every side.
That wind is said to circulate through the channels at the vital points (marmans);
O Lord of Gods, where does the living soul reside? Tell me this according to the truth.
Devoid of tone and color, and free from the domain of form;
when the sense-faculties have passed away, it is devoid of intellect and ego.
How can that *jīva* be known as being entirely free from other principles—neither by means of sound, nor by form, nor by wind? (Narasena)
That Lord of the gods, the imperishable Master, cannot be grasped by means of fragrance;
thus has the true nature of the individual soul been previously explained to you, O Lord of Umā.
Tell me, O Great Lord, so that they may know with certainty [the sequence] through the yoga of the ten movements, starting from Ūnarā and so forth in due order.
O Lord, how does the embodied soul move within the wheel of channels situated in the heart?
Though I am ignorant, O Master, may you explain this even without being asked by me, who am devoid of wisdom.
O Lord, please recount them as well for the sake of showing compassion.
The Lord said:
Excellent, excellent, Mahāsena! You have asked a most wonderful question.
It is marvelous that, having heard and experienced this great [teaching], another person asks about it.
That which was previously described as the one called the *jīva* within the sphere of the channels (*nāḍī*),
and which was specified in the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*), is indeed the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
I shall declare to you the definitive conclusion of those who know reality regarding that which is proclaimed as the fourfold, all-pervading, and supreme reality.
In its center abides that Jīva, the supreme cause,
which is indefinable and nameless, moving like the wind situated within the breath.
The eleventh is said to be the successor of the ten;
in whatever place they reside, they always remain there by virtue of their rising.
Situated on the path of the vehicle of the wind, utterly purified, and supremely auspicious—
that *jalya* which is always within the body— I shall now describe that reality (*tattva*) to you.
O you who observe the vow of the digits (kalāvrata), through its application, it wanders in the midst of the lotus;
like one struck by the play of a ball, it constantly performs rising and falling.
O sinless one, I shall tell you of the deity who resides in the midst of that which is proclaimed as the fourfold body of reality.
Through clear, diverse, and auspicious practice,
I shall explain the reality to you so that you may understand it according to its true nature.
Having cleared away all those great beings who were present there,
he related the entire account of his life.

That which is the inhalation is known as the *putrakalā* (the digit of the son), and it is remembered as the *vāyavyā* (pertaining to wind); that which was previously described as being situated there, he flows forth from.
But when it is joined with Śakti and likewise with Vahni,
it is designated as the Māhendrī Śakti, as was previously declared.
By her, moreover, that all-pervading Lord, the individual soul (jīva), is supported;
and that goddess is likewise surrounded on all sides, enveloped by fire.
The fire-maṇḍala is said to be Śakti herself, abiding in her own place;
within that maṇḍala, O Mahāsena, Soma is carried by them.
O King, Lord of the Gods, one should know that cessation arises from the Imperishable (akṣara) within the heart;
thus, O King, does it abide in the state of four parts.
They say that the city is the body, which is proclaimed to be fourfold;
the Lord, the Master of all, is the deity residing in its center.
But when a deity moves there with a face turned away, one should know that she is Śāntā; the wise know this through the Āgneya-dhāraṇā.
The third breath control is declared to be *recaka*;
it is that which issues forth from within and touches the Imperishable.
Then that [breath] should be known as Vāruṇī when accompanied by inhalation (pūraka);
indeed, there is no doubt regarding Vāruṇī—this has been told to you who have asked.
The Goddess remains in the center of the body, restrained by the *kumbhaka* [breath-retention];
she flows through the right channel (*sāṅga*), endowed with the letter *ṇa* and the *tattva*.

From the head to the end, one should practice the Lord; O child, that other [practice] which was previously described is devoid of the natural flow (pravaha), whereas that reality (tattva) flows with the natural flow.
That sound which is heard abiding within the heart is declared to be the *ghoṣa*; it is that Goddess who expresses the reality (*tattva*) within the heart for one who possesses true knowledge.
This sevenfold constituent has been described as the embodiment of reality;
furthermore, the four types of *dhāraṇā* have been declared as belonging to the *kalā*.
Another threefold breath control, beginning with inhalation (pūraka) and so forth, has been proclaimed;
yet this [system] consisting of the seven constituents is not understood by those of unrefined self.
Covering that face with his own, he [remained] there for a full day and night, right up to the nostril apertures at a distance of twelve finger-breadths.
That very sound, which is indeed the supreme power of the Lord, touches the ears;
the Goddess, resembling the lowing of a cow, is heard when enveloped by Śakti.
O illustrious Guha, she carries that reality through the mouth;
indeed, by means of ten applications, she moves through the deficient nights and so forth.
The emission of phlegm is the omitted night (ūnarātra), and yawning is the intercalary month (adhimāsa).
Coughing becomes the lunar mansion (ṛkṣa), and exhalation is said to be wealth (dhana).
The northern [channel] is to be known as the southern, and the left is designated as the right;
in the middle is declared the equinox (viṣuva), which issues forth from both nostrils.
The transition (saṃkrānti) should likewise be understood as occurring from one's own place to that very place;
for the upward vital breath (prāṇa) and the downward vital breath (apāna) are indeed night.
This movement of power (śakti-sañcāra), established in ten ways,
has already been explained previously by means of the group of seven, and not by means of yoga.
Out of affection for my son and as a favor, that which was not to be spoken has been told;
this tradition has been declared, having come down through the lineage of gurus.
O child, the Supreme Lord is indeed devoid of names, forms, and the means of valid cognition; He is beyond perception and inference, and inaccessible to logical reasons.
It has already been fully explained that it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru;
the oral tradition has been fully described as being established within the mouth of the Guru.
O son of Pārvatī, the "mouth of the Guru" has been fully explained;
indeed, the first mouth is said to be white and joined with two bonds.
At the end of the head (mūrdhan), however, there is the fourth; these are the faces of the Unborn (aja).
That Guru is said to be the Unborn, and he moves within the midst of the faces.
The oral instruction of the Guru is declared to be distinguished by the tradition;
the Lord should always move about with a measurement of half of half a tala.
O Mahāsena of noble vows, established as the support for the Śakti through these faces, it is impossible for anyone to seize her.
Through instruction and by virtue of his own gentle nature, the wise one perceives Sadāśiva as the subtle body; otherwise, he would not be grasped.
I shall fully explain an illustration that serves as the cause for grasping reality,
by which a concentration (*samādhi*) arises that is free from all activity, O Guha.
O son, just as those two previously mentioned, the great maidens who are now young,
have not yet experienced human enjoyment that produces pleasure or pain.
When those who serve one another are joined together with ease by a single [woman],
then that second girl shall be the fashioner of their destiny.
"O fortunate one, what kind of pleasure do you experience arising from the bodiless god?
O auspicious lady, speak to me in such a way that I may understand it."
Thus questioned, that maiden spoke of that supreme happiness:
"O friend, such and such is the happiness you shall have with the most excellent ones."
When this was said, the maiden, seeking happiness, became enraged;
for he had either told her out of meanness or concealed it out of wickedness.
"O Six-faced One, because of her backbiting, her wickedness, and her lack of propriety toward what was auspicious,
that second maiden was thus beaten."
Do not be angry; for this has been said as an illusion and cannot be realized.
Truly, truly, again truly: such is not that supreme happiness.
The second, however, is the state of becoming (*ṛbhāvasthā*); yet it does not experience that bliss.
Nevertheless, due to its unmanifest nature, that constituent (*kalā*) does not perceive it.
In no long time at all, that happiness was attained by her.
That which is known through self-realization cannot be taught;
that maiden was pleased with him, yet I became angry in vain.
O friend, this bliss is to be known by oneself; how can it be described?
Thus, the investigation into the nature of the living being remains hidden within one's own secret cave.
That deity cannot indeed be described through the means of direct perception;
he is to be known through the oral tradition by those adorned by their masters.
O Maheśvara, O Nātha, you who abide in the half-palm, in the sky, and in the power of the void,
are grasped as residing in the heart within the three traditions.
O Supreme Lord, endowed with the eight groups of eight, it flows through the eight constituent elements in due order, beginning with *saka* and so forth.
These sixty-four states have been declared to be of the nature of Śiva;
they are not understood by those who rely on fallacious reasoning arising from webs of sophistry.
A blink (nimeṣa) joined with an opening (unmeṣa) is called a tālikā;
the fourth part of that is said to be a tuṭi.
O Śiva, the measure of that movement has been declared by him;
O Guha, that which was previously described as being situated in the void is indeed blissful.
At its end flows the Śakti, endowed with the seven constituents;
within that [Śakti] also resides the Jīva, which is perceived only through subtle observation.
That Self has but one characteristic: it is the power whose face is the drumstick.
This is declared to be the measure [of the Self], and the principle of the individual soul (jīvatattva) has been described.
O son, this has been clearly explained to you;
for these words, which bring about the perfection of one's commands, indeed bring an end to the asuras.
And it cannot be turned back by any other web of arguments—
that which is devoid of means of valid cognition and free from the two types of statements.
The speech of the *paśu* is established as twofold, bringing about both success and failure;
however, the speech of Śiva is declared to be tenfold, along with its defining characteristics.
O observer of excellent vows, it is like a perfected state— profoundly deep, very firm, well-established,
auspicious, stainless, pure, and peaceful— and it is the attainment of mastery through command.
That which is proclaimed as *vidhivāda* (injunction) is not *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), for it has Śiva as its essence;
whereas that which is seized by defects such as passion and ignorance would speak untruth.
If those [scriptures] were composed by Īśvara, how could he have spoken otherwise? For they were taught by Śiva, who is omniscient and free from all defects.
The most excellent and stainless word is authoritative; of this there is no doubt.
The words of worldly beings are afflicted, unstable, and trivial.
These are mixed, impure, and based on false reasoning;
they consist of networks of causes and are primarily characterized by the members of inference.
O son of Kṛttikā, not even a trace of truth exists in them;
they are supreme liars, deceivers, and creators of strife.
For the sake of protecting the reality (tattva), great obstacles have been fashioned;
that which proceeds as direct perception is here called scripture (āgama).
O gentle one, without direct perception, false cognitions indeed arise;
the origins of mantras are manifold, and their seeds are likewise remembered as many.
Regarding these, O Six-faced One, consciousness is direct and not indirect;
for that state which is indirect, O Guha, is established by means of the direct.
For that state is indeed free from conceptual construction for the practitioner;
just as it is difficult for one blind from birth to perceive white or red.
Just as it is impossible to establish that qualities such as white or red are [inherently] red by means of individual instances,
so too is the realm of heaven beyond the scope of animals who lack direct perception.
The purification of a scale, as well as the blazing of fire without fuel; the rendering of seeds seedless, and the sprouting of what has been burnt.
It effects the possession of healthy persons, as well as the immobilization of those to be subdued;
it brings about enmity and eradication, and the destruction of malevolent planets and rākṣasas.
The dispersal and withdrawal of poison, the summoning of serpents,
the uprooting of mountains, and the winning of divine maidens.
The arrival in the form of a pill, the bursting forth of the earth,
the invisibility of the body, and the utterance of divine speech;
Knowledge of future objects, the manifestation of powers such as *aṇimā*,
and many other various [powers] of this kind.
The thousands of means of valid cognition established in the Śiva-scriptures are directly perceived; there is no doubt regarding this, for it is the very nature of Śiva.
O Guha, all those things spoken by the animals— whether true or false—
are surpassed by the direct knowledge of the supreme scripture, which is endowed with reason.
O lords of men, perfection is attained by this very body;
however, O lowest of men, it is not achieved through other systems of the bound (paśutantra).
Therefore, the great purification must be performed according to the teaching of Śiva,
so that those who know the scripture and the meaning of the scripture may go to that state.
But how can there be liberation for the bound souls (paśus), whose minds are afflicted by māyā? O Mahāguha, they have merely performed protection through the recitation of the Śiva-scriptures.
It is difficult to traverse, difficult to cross, hard to pierce, and hard to surmount;
it is defiled by those who grasp at injustice, and crowded with nothing but truth.
The intellect, spreading like water, has plunged into the fathomless ocean of egoism, which is overwhelmed by the waves of sense-objects and shrouded in darkness.
The bud of the three qualities (guṇas) is well-adorned with the elements and the senses,
and the Unmanifest (avyakta) has been made its girdle by means of vast flashes of lightning.
Thus indeed, O child, the trench (parikhā) of the Śiva-tattva is established,
by which [people] do not know that reality which bestows all accomplishments.
Those men devoted to dharma have certainly been seized by her;
therefore, this truth which grants grace and delivers one from rebirth is difficult to penetrate.
The Supreme Lord, established in the state of the partless (niṣkala), residing in the Haṃsa,
is described as being free from action and its causes, and devoid of both the seen and the unseen.
It is unapproachable and inconceivable, residing within the body yet devoid of a body;
it is like the heat residing in a gem, or like fire residing in wood that is not visible.
Just as butter resides within milk, so does the Lord reside within power;
just as fragrance resides in the earth, so does taste reside in water.
O Skanda, the wind has touch as its domain, and Śiva has entered the sphere of power;
just as the path of birds flying in the sky cannot be perceived.
Likewise, O Lord of the Gods, the deity abiding in the body is not known;
however, by means of subtle practice, he is known by the masters among practitioners.
I shall fully explain the practice by which you may recognize Śiva—
[the practice] endowed with thirty-eight kalās, possessing four divisions, and born from the five elements.
Having realized the Supreme Lord as united with the five Brahmans,
one should know that Nivṛtti is the earth and Pratiṣṭhā is said to be the waters.
The Vidyā is declared to be fiery (āgneyī), while Vāyu and Śānti are proclaimed [as the next two];
the supreme Vyomana is beyond Śānti, which is indeed what is designated as Nāda.
The five elements have been fully described; O Brahmā, hear what follows.
Nivṛtti is said to be Sadyojāta, and Pratiṣṭhā is called Vāmadeva.
Vidyā is to be known as arising from Aghora, while Śānti is to be known as Pauruṣī;
Nāda is said to be in Ākāśa—thus the five Brahmans are proclaimed.
Sadyojāta is to be known as having eight kalās; the wise know Tridaśa as Guhyaka. Aghora, moreover, has eight [kalās], and Puruṣa has four kalās.
Īśāna is indeed with five; thus thirty-eight kalās are traditionally taught.
They say that the Ṛgveda is Nivṛtti, while Pratiṣṭhā is traditionally associated with the Yajurveda.
The Sāmaveda is known as the Vidyā, and the Atharvaveda is called the Bindu;
that which is the peaceful, supreme Divinity is recited as the fifth.
They call the pervasive womb "space" (ākāśa);
one should know that subtle sound (nāda) from which everything has issued forth.
The five divisions have been fully described; now hear concerning the Yugas.
Kali is to be known as the first, and Dvāpara is remembered as the second.
The third is designated as Tretā, and the fourth is called Kṛta;
this is declared to be the Great Yuga (Mahāyuga), while the fifth is established in Nāda.
That age established in time is declared to be inaccessible—
immovable, eternal, divine, and devoid of valid means of knowledge or traditional authority.
O Six-faced One, beginning with Nivṛtti and so forth, one should arrange them in successive order: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and ending with Kailāsa.
Know that *nāda* is indeed the fifth; these are proclaimed as the presiding deities (*adhideva*).
Brahmā is designated as *anivṛtti*, and Viṣṇu is to be known as *dvikubjaka*.
Mounted upon the letter 'ma' of Rudra, it is known as the Tāmasī Vidyā.
Rajas is said to be restless and crooked, while sattva is called tranquil;
that which is proclaimed as the Puruṣa is declared to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
That which is beyond Sadāśiva is proclaimed as the fifth;
O highly fortunate one, it has a body of sound (nāda), and it is peaceful, eternal, and constant.
The hells, including Kālāgni, as well as the seven netherworlds (pātālas), are recorded;
likewise Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and Maharloka.
Janas, Tapas, and Satya are proclaimed as the seven worlds;
above them, however, the Rudras are established in a hundredfold manner.
In ten ways and again in ten ways, in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, above, and below,
the hundred Rudras of the wise one are thus described.
This is called the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), situated within the earthly enclosure;
originating from Nivṛtti, it is all declared to be the impure path (aśuddhādhvan).
Likewise, another group of five octads is situated above them;
beginning from the downward direction, one should then establish the veil of ego (ahaṅkārāvaraṇa).
Above that is the eightfold divine womb, situated within the veil of the intellect;
it is the supreme eightfold yoga, adorned by the veil of the qualities.
Likewise, the lords of wrath (Krodheśas) and the gods are also remembered as being eightfold;
they are unmanifest and enveloping, and they abide indeed as bestowers of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
The lineage of gurus is itself the grain; the creators are Manu and the others.
Likewise, they are established as the obstructions of day and night for one who has become ashes.

O Guha, that which consists of the eight means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is endowed with the eight sciences (vidyā); it is said to reside within the covering of the sciences and is born from the mouth [of the Lord].
The form consists of eight parts, as do the two Vidyās and the seat;
established within the enclosure of the Kalās, the Vidyā arises from the body.
O child, that which is proclaimed as the totality of all manifestations and the three principles (tritatva),
whatever it may be, is established beyond [the manifest world].
That state is declared to be inexpressible, peaceful, and eternal;
yet through tranquility, one attains the supreme thread, the sound that is most difficult to obtain.
That is declared to be Nirvāṇa, that is the auspicious, supreme state;
yet even beyond that is what has been placed within the mouth of the Guru.
Otherwise, those deprived of the teacher’s mouth do not know it at all;
this is called the grace, O Guha, which is both with parts and without parts.
This has been told; there is no doubt here—do not entertain a conceptualizing mind.
By this, O Guha, you will undoubtedly attain liberation.
O Lord of Guha, the Śiva-tattva has been fully explained in the Śiva-śāstra;
it is not known in other tantras, for those with the faces of bound souls (paśus) are always [obstructed].
O Guha, when a dwelling is made for birds in the sky,
then that reality consisting of Śiva is perceived by those with the knowledge of the bound souls (paśu).
O noble one, when rain falls even without clouds, then,
my child, through the knowledge of the animal, the reality of Śiva is attained.
O son of Pārvatī, when one obtains oil from the husk,
O child, Śiva is known as "the giver of a hundred" among the sciences of cattle.
When a woman gives birth to a son without a man,
then that son of Kṛttikā attains auspiciousness through the knowledge of the sacrificial animals.
But when milk is mixed with clarified butter, O Guha, it then becomes fit for animals as taught in the Tantras; [likewise] knowledge becomes fit for embodied beings.
When people fashion a cloth from a lump of clay,
or a jar from threads, then for those who know the cause, Śiva is the source.
He who is devoid of knowledge regarding Śiva yet desires to know Śiva strikes at the sky with his fist and drinks a mirage.
There is no liberation without Śiva; there is no goal without Śiva;
there is no happiness without Śiva—and yet, Śiva is difficult to know.
In this world, all these things that humans obtain here come from Śiva;
therefore, Śiva indeed should be known, for through him there will be an end to suffering.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Kālottara, consisting of one thousand three hundred verses.
